questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A female patient collapses soon after delivery. There is profuse bleeding and features of disseminated intravascular coagulation. Which of the following is the most likely etiology?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Amniotic fluid embolism

The given clinical scenario with a diagnosis of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) points to amniotic fluid embolism as the most likely etiology.

Amniotic fluid embolism presents with a classic triad of hemodynamic and respiratory compromise, along with DIC. Usually, it presents during the late stages of labor or immediate postpartum. Gasping for air, seizures, and cardiorespiratory arrest are other features. Clinical features are variable.

Diagnostic criteria for amniotic fluid embolism include:

• Sudden onset cardiorespiratory arrest, or both hypotension and respiratory compromise
• Overt DIC
• Onset during labor or within 30 minutes of delivery of the placenta
• No fever ≥38°C

Since there are no specific diagnostic tests, a clinical diagnosis has to be made. Other causes for a similar presentation such as myocardial infarction, pulmonary embolism, and anaphylactic shock needs to be ruled out.

Risk factors include rapid labor, meconium-stained liquor, and uterine tears. Post-term pregnancy, maternal age, and eclampsia are other predisposing conditions. The currently accepted mechanism is the entry of fetal material into the maternal circulation which leads to the activation of proinflammatory mediator systems. This results in pulmonary vasoconstriction and hypertension. The tissue factor present in fetal material also activates factor VII resulting in DIC.

The condition can be fatal and management includes cardiopulmonary resuscitation and advanced cardiac life support.

Other options:

Option B: Post-partum hemorrhage is the loss of ≥500mL of blood after the third stage of labor. Symptoms and signs of hypovolemia are commonly seen.

Option C: Peripartum cardiomyopathy presents with features of heart failure in the last month of pregnancy or within 5 months of delivery. Probable causes include viral myocarditis, malnutrition, and hormonal interactions.

Option D: Rupture of the uterus is a disruption in the continuity of all the uterine layers anytime after 28 weeks of pregnancy. Clinical features depend on the specific cause and include abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, fainting attacks, and rapid pulse rate.
questions.learning: Amniotic fluid embolism — The given clinical scenario with a diagnosis of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) points to amniotic fluid embolism as the most likely etiology.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: You see a child with delayed speech development as part of a health visit at a local school. The otoscopic appearance of the ear is shown below. Hearing loss of 20 dB is detected in audiometric tests. What is your diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Serous otitis media

The given clinical scenario and image suggest a diagnosis of serous otitis media.

The golden yellow discoloration of the tympanic membrane is caused by the clear watery straw-colored effusion filling the middle ear. Since the fluid is clear, one can see the structures of the middle ear quite clearly on otoscopy.

Patients having serous otitis media will have hearing loss that rarely exceeds 40 dB. This deafness can pass unnoticed, and maybe accidentally discovered during audiometric screening tests. Because of hearing loss, the development of speech is delayed or defective.

Otoscopic findings in serous otitis media:

* Fluid level and air bubbles are seen when fluid is thin and the tympanic membrane transparent.

* In chronic cases, the fluid becomes very sticky. Hence, the name glue ear.

* The tympanic membrane is often dull and opaque with a loss of light reflex.

* The mobility of the tympanic membrane is restricted.
questions.learning: Serous otitis media — The given clinical scenario and image suggest a diagnosis of serous otitis media. The golden yellow discoloration of the tympanic membrane is caused by the clear watery straw-colored effusion filling the middle ear.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 26-year-old male presents with chronic abdominal pain, recurrent episodes of non-bloody diarrhea, significant weight loss, low-grade fever for 8 months, occasional perianal discomfort. On examination, mild pallor and tenderness in the right lower quadrant are noted. Laboratory investigations reveal anemia, raised ESR, and hypoalbuminemia. CECT abdomen shows segmental bowel wall thickening of the terminal ileum with engorged mesenteric vessels. Biopsy reveals non-caseating granulomas. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Crohn's disease

Crohn’s disease is a chronic, relapsing inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) characterized by transmural granulomatous inflammation that can affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract, with a predilection for the terminal ileum.

The diagnosis is suggested by:

• Chronic abdominal pain
• Chronic non-bloody diarrhea
• Weight loss
• Low-grade fever
• Perianal disease
• Terminal ileal involvement
• Non-caseating granulomas on biopsy

Key differentiating features:

• Intestinal tuberculosis:

• Usually ileocecal region
• Caseating granulomas
• Confluent granulomas with acid-fast bacilli may be seen
• Necrotic lymph nodes and ascites are common

• Ulcerative colitis:

• Begins in the rectum with continuous proximal spread
• Inflammation limited to mucosa and submucosa
• No skip lesions or transmural involvement
questions.learning: Crohn's disease Crohn’s disease is a chronic, relapsing inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) characterized by transmural granulomatous inflammation that can affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract, with a predilection for the terminal ileum.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: HPV infection is most commonly associated with which type of cancer?
questions.explanation: High-risk Human Papillomavirus (HPV) infection, particularly with HPV-16, is strongly linked to a rising subset of oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinomas, including those of the tonsils and base of the tongue. HPV is also classically associated with cervical and other anogenital malignancies. Lung cancer (Option A) is primarily associated with environmental factors like smoking and radon rather than viral infection. Stomach cancer (Option C) is most commonly linked to Helicobacter pylori infection. Esophageal cancer (Option D) risk factors typically include alcohol, smoking, and Barrett’s esophagus. Because HPV selectively targets the mucosal surfaces of the oropharynx, it has become a major causative factor for these specific head and neck cancers
questions.learning: High-risk Human Papillomavirus (HPV) infection, particularly with HPV-16, is strongly linked to a rising subset of oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinomas, including those of the tonsils and base of the tongue.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which chemotherapeutic drug is most likely to cause extrapyramidal symptoms such as acute dystonia, bradykinesia, and tremors in a patient receiving chemotherapy?
questions.explanation: Metoclopramide is a commonly used anti-emetic, particularly in patients undergoing chemotherapy. It acts primarily as a dopamine D₂-receptor antagonist. Because it readily crosses the blood–brain barrier, metoclopramide blocks dopamine receptors in the basal ganglia, which can lead to extrapyramidal side effects (EPS). These include acute dystonia, parkinsonism (bradykinesia, rigidity, tremors), and akathisia, and they occur more frequently in children and young adults. Ondansetron (Option A) is a 5-HT₃ (serotonin) receptor antagonist and does not interfere with dopaminergic pathways; therefore, it does not cause EPS. Meclizine (Option C) and scopolamine (Option D) are antihistaminic and anticholinergic agents, respectively, used mainly for motion sickness and vestibular disorders, and they are not associated with dystonic reactions. Acute dystonic reactions due to metoclopramide can be rapidly reversed with anticholinergic agents such as diphenhydramine or benztropine. With prolonged or high-dose use, metoclopramide carries a risk of tardive dyskinesia, which may be irreversible, hence the drug carries a black-box warning
questions.learning: Metoclopramide is a commonly used anti-emetic, particularly in patients undergoing chemotherapy. It acts primarily as a dopamine D₂-receptor antagonist.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient involved in a road traffic accident was admitted to the emergency department. During the first 2–4 hours, he received 4 units of packed red blood cells. Which of the following complications is most likely to occur in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hypocalcemia

Stored blood contains citrate

↓

Citrate binds calcium

↓

↓ Ionized calcium

↓

Hypocalcemia

Answer is B because stored blood contains citrate as an anticoagulant, which binds ionized calcium during rapid or massive transfusion, leading to hypocalcemia.

Mechanism:

This can cause tetany, hypotension, and arrhythmias during transfusion.

Sodium abnormalities and hypocitratemia are not typical complications of blood transfusion.

Massive Transfusion Complications-

| Complication | Mechanism

| ------------ | ---------

| Hypocalcemia | Citrate binding

| Hyperkalemia | RBC lysis

| Hypothermia | Cold blood

| Acidosis | Poor perfusion

Prevention:

• Monitor calcium
• Give IV calcium gluconate if needed

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 2-year-old child presents to the emergency department with a barking cough and noisy breathing. Anteroposterior neck X-ray reveals a steeple sign. What type of stridor is most commonly seen in this condition?
questions.explanation: In a child with croup (acute laryngotracheobronchitis), the presence of a steeple sign on AP neck X-ray indicates subglottic narrowing. This region lies between the vocal cords and upper trachea, so obstruction here affects airflow during both inspiration and expiration, producing biphasic stridor. Although croup is commonly associated with inspiratory stridor in mild cases, classically and in exam context, subglottic involvement leads to biphasic stridor, especially when narrowing is significant. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Inspiratory: Seen in obstruction above the vocal cords (e.g., supraglottic), not typical for subglottic lesions. (B) Expiratory: Seen in lower airway obstruction (bronchi, bronchioles), such as asthma or bronchiolitis. (D) Uniphasic: Not a standard clinical classification of stridor and is not used diagnostically

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A patient undergoing surgery receives succinylcholine for muscle relaxation and later develops hyperthermia, rigidity, tremors, and tachycardia. What is the most appropriate treatment for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Dantrolene

The above clinical scenario is suggestive of malignant hyperthermia. The drug of choice for the condition is dantrolene.

Dantrolene is a direct-acting skeletal muscle relaxant that acts on the RyR1 (ryanodine receptor) calcium channels in the sarcoplasmic reticulum of skeletal muscles and inhibits calcium-induced calcium release. This results in the uncoupling of membrane depolarisation and muscle contraction, thus inhibiting muscle contraction.

Malignant hyperthermia is a genetic condition in which mutated RyR1 receptors are present in the skeletal muscles. In the presence of certain triggers, this mutated RyR1 causes severe dysfunction in the RyR1 channels. This leads to the accumulation of calcium ions in the skeletal muscle, resulting in sustained muscle contraction, rigidity, increased heat production, acidosis, hyperkalaemia, and increased end-tidal CO₂.

Drugs triggering malignant hyperthermia:

* Succinylcholine

* Halothane

* Isoflurane

* Sevoflurane

Susceptible patients:

* Patients with a positive family history. It can be inherited as an autosomal dominant trait.

* Patients with congenital myopathies.

Treatment:

Dantrolene sodium is the drug of choice for malignant hyperthermia. Once the diagnosis is made, the causative inhalational agent should be stopped immediately. Supportive treatment with rapid cooling, inhalation of 100% oxygen, control of acidosis, and treatment of hyperkalaemia should be given.
questions.learning: Dantrolene — The above clinical scenario is suggestive of malignant hyperthermia. The drug of choice for the condition is dantrolene.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is a heat-sensitive indicator of vaccine viability?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Vaccine vial monitor

Vaccine vial monitors (VVM) are the only heat-sensitive indicator of vaccine viability that are routinely used in vaccines throughout the supply chain.

VVM records cumulative heat exposure through a gradual change in color. If the color of the inner square is the same or is darker than the outer circle, the vaccine has been exposed to too much temperature and should be discarded.
questions.learning: Vaccine vial monitor Vaccine vial monitors (VVM) are the only heat-sensitive indicator of vaccine viability that are routinely used in vaccines throughout the supply chain.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient presents with pain abdomen, diarrhea, and a stepladder pattern of fever for the past five days. He also complains of a headache and malaise. Which of the following is the best screening test to perform now if typhoid is suspected in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Blood culture

The best test to screen a symptomatic patient for typhoid in the first week is blood culture.

Enteric fever (typhoid fever) is caused by Salmonella species. The patient presents with stepladder pyrexia (fever), abdominal pain, diarrhoea, headache, and malaise.

Diagnosis of enteric fever:

*

Blood culture: It is more sensitive during 1st week than in the subsequent weeks. It rapidly becomes negative on treatment with antibiotics.

* Antibody testing: WIDAL test to detect rising titers of H and O agglutinins against salmonella typhi and paratyphi. Agglutinins appear by the end of the first week and rise steadily up to the 3rd or 4th week, after which they disappear.

*

Stool culture: It yields positive results from the 3rd week onwards.

*

Urine culture: Results may be positive after the 2nd week.

*

Bone marrow culture remains positive for 5 days even after the start of antibiotics and is the most sensitive test in the first week. The culture of duodenal aspirate may yield positive results when bone marrow culture is inconclusive.

Empirical treatment of typhoid fever includes management with ceftriaxone 2g/day intravenously for 10-14 days along with azithromycin  1g/day for 5 days. Other antibiotics such as ciprofloxacin, chloramphenicol, and amoxicillin should be considered in resistant cases.
questions.learning: Blood culture — The best test to screen a symptomatic patient for typhoid in the first week is blood culture. Enteric fever (typhoid fever) is caused by Salmonella species.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child transfers an object from one hand to another. What does it signify?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ability to compare objects

The milestone of transfer of objects from one hand to another in a child signifies the ability of the child to compare objects. The transfer of objects is a motor milestone occurring at 6 months of age.

Other options:

Option A: When the child reaches for objects it implies the onset of visuomotor coordination. It is attained at 4 months

Option C: Thumb finger grasp implies the ability to handle small objects. It is attained at 8 months.

Option D: The voluntary release/ Release phenomenon is used to denote the disappearance of the palmar grasp, which is seen at 4 months.
questions.learning: Ability to compare objects — The milestone of transfer of objects from one hand to another in a child signifies the ability of the child to compare objects.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 40-year-old male presents with diffuse abdominal pain. He has a known history of Crohn's disease . Physical examination reveals rigidity and guarding. On imaging Ileal Perforation is diagnosed. What is the next best step in the management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Urgent surgical exploration with ileostomy

The clinical vignette with Ileal perforation and physical examination findings of rigidity and guarding suggests peritonitis due to perforation. The next best step in the management of this patient is urgent surgical exploration with an ileostomy.

Perforation of a viscus is a life-threatening condition that occurs following the rupture of the alimentary tract. Common causes include iatrogenic (surgery, scopes) blunt or penetrating injury, bowel obstruction, peptic ulcer disease, corrosive agents, or particular medications.

This leads to the leakage of the enteric contents, thereby leading to acute bacterial peritonitis. Peritonitis is the generalized or localized inflammation of the peritoneum either due to the free spillage of fluids into the peritoneal cavity or secondary bacterial infection.

Clinical features of hollow viscous perforation occur due to the developed peritonitis and the features include abdominal pain and distension, nausea, vomiting, tachycardia, tenderness, rebound tenderness, decreased or absent bowel sounds, and guarding on palpation. Fever may be present. Sometimes, features of septic shock can be seen at later stages.

Investigations include estimating the white blood cell count, urea, serum electrolytes, and an erect abdominal radiograph showing free gas under the diaphragm. A supine radiograph may show dilated gas-filled loops of the bowel, suggestive of paralytic ileus. The below image shows a hollow viscus perforation.

Management - Initial management includes intravenous (IV) fluid therapy, cessation of oral intake, and broad-spectrum antibiotics. Indications for immediate bowel exploration are

* Sepsis/diffuse peritonitis(as in this patient)

* Bowel ischemia

* Complete or closed-loop bowel obstruction

Resection or repair of the perforated site with or without drainage and diversion is usually undertaken. Duodenal perforations, on the other hand, are generally treated with omental patch repair without resection.
questions.learning: Urgent surgical exploration with ileostomy — The clinical vignette with Ileal perforation and physical examination findings of rigidity and guarding suggests peritonitis due to perforation.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A total of 2000 individuals were screened for HIV, of whom 200 were confirmed to be HIV- positive. A new ELISA screening test was then applied to the same population and identified 260 individuals as positive, but only 130 of these actually had the disease. What is the specificity of this test?
questions.explanation: Specificity is defined as the ability of a test to correctly identify those without the disease (True Negatives / Total Actual Negatives). From the data: Total patients = 2,000; Actual positive = 200; Actual negative = 1,800. The ELISA test gave 260 positives, of which 130 were true positives (TP), meaning 130 were false positives (FP). To find true negatives (TN), we subtract false positives from total actual negatives: . The formula is . When rounding to the provided choices, 96% (Option A) is the closest standard value, although the exact calculation is ~93%. Option B (80%), C (72%), and D (68%) are significantly lower and would imply a high rate of false positives. A high specificity is essential for screening tests to minimize unnecessary psychological stress and follow-up costs for healthy individuals
questions.learning: Specificity is defined as the ability of a test to correctly identify those without the disease (True Negatives / Total Actual Negatives). From the data: Total patients = 2,000; Actual positive = 200; Actual negative = 1,800.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The protein in the glomerular basement membrane responsible for charge-dependent filtration is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Heparan sulfate

The protein in the glomerular basement membrane responsible for charge-dependent filtration is heparan sulfate. It prevents filtration by repelling negatively charged proteins.

Collagen type IV, fibronectin, entactin are structural components of basement membrane.
questions.learning: Heparan sulfate — The protein in the glomerular basement membrane responsible for charge-dependent filtration is heparan sulfate. It prevents filtration by repelling negatively charged proteins.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following statements is FALSE regarding deep second-degree burns?
questions.explanation: The false statement regarding deep second-degree (partial thickness) burns is that they are "painless." In reality, deep second-degree burns remain painful to pressure because the pressure-sensitive nerve endings in the deeper dermis are still functional, even if superficial pain receptors are destroyed. True "painless" burns are Third-degree (full thickness) burns, where all dermal sensory structures are completely destroyed. Other statements are correct: deep second-degree burns do result in damage to the deeper dermis (Option C); they show "less blanching" or delayed capillary refill because the superficial dermal vessels are damaged (Option B); and they frequently heal by scar deposition and may take 3 to 6 weeks to close (Option A) . Identifying the depth of a burn is essential for determining if a patient requires skin grafting or conservative dressing management. Because deep second-degree burns retain pressure sensation, labeling them as painless is medically inaccurate

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following are clinical features of Parkinson’s disease? I. Reduced eye blinking II. Drooling of saliva III. Soft voice IV. Macrographia
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. I, II and III

Parkinson’s disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder caused by degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta, leading to dopamine deficiency in the nigrostriatal pathway. It is characterized by both motor and non-motor symptoms.

The classic motor features are:

• Bradykinesia (essential feature) ⭐
• Resting tremor
• Rigidity
• Postural instability

The following are characteristic clinical features of Parkinson’s disease:

• I. Reduced eye blinking: Due to facial bradykinesia, producing a masked facies (hypomimia).
• II. Drooling of saliva: Caused by reduced spontaneous swallowing, not excessive saliva production.
• III. Soft voice (Hypophonia): Speech becomes soft, monotonous, and low in volume.

Why is IV incorrect?

• IV. Macrographia: Parkinson’s disease causes micrographia (progressively smaller handwriting), which is a classic feature due to bradykinesia.
questions.learning: I, II and III Parkinson’s disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder caused by degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta, leading to dopamine deficiency in the nigrostriatal pathway.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: The radiograph shown below is done for better assessment of the sinuses. What is the common name of this view?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Towne's view

The radiograph shown above shows Towne's view.

Towne's view is taken with the patient in the supine position and lying on his back with the chin often depressed into the neck. The X-ray camera is angled at 30 degrees towards the feet so that the rays enter the head at the level of the hairline.

* This is usually taken for acoustic neuroma and apical petrositis.

* Bilateral petrous pyramids are visible in this view and hence can be compared.

Structures seen are:

* Arcuate eminence and superior semicircular canal.

* Mastoid antrum.

* Internal auditory canal.

* Tympanic cavity.

* Cochlea.

* External auditory canal.

The image below shows Towne's view

Other options:

Option A: Waters' view (also known as the Occipitomental view or nose-chin position) is a radiographic view, where an X-ray beam is angled at 37° to the orbitomeatal line. The rays are passed from behind the head and are perpendicular to the radiographic plate. It is commonly used to get a better view of the maxillary sinuses.

Option C: Caldwell's view (also known as the occipitofrontal view or nose-forehead position) is a radiographic view of the skull, where the X-ray plate is angled at 15° to the orbito-meatal line. The rays pass from behind the head and are perpendicular to the radiographic plate. It is commonly used to get a better view of frontal sinuses.

Option D: Submentovertical view/ Hirtz view/ basal view is taken with vertex near the film and X-ray beam projected at right angles to the film from the submental area. It is commonly used to get a better view of the sphenoid sinuses.

Pearl PF1596: Radiographic views of paranasal sinuses and mastoid

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which fetal vessel is assessed by doppler to indicate fetal anemia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Middle cerebral artery

Fetal anemia is assessed using the peak systolic velocity (PSV) of the middle cerebral artery (MCA) on Doppler.

Fetal middle cerebral artery doppler measurements of peak systolic velocity(PSV) are the recommended test for the detection of fetal anemia. In the anemic fetus, blood is shunted preferentially to the brain to maintain adequate oxygenation. As a result, the velocity rises because of increased cardiac output and decreased blood viscosity.  MCA PSV is used for the monitoring of fetuses of Rh-negative sensitized mothers, and if it exceeds 1.5 MoM and the gestational age less than 34 or 35 weeks, fetal blood sampling followed by transfusion is considered.

Serial measurements of the peak systolic velocity of the fetal MCA are reliable and noninvasive. The threshold value to identify fetuses with anemia is 1.5 MoM (multiples of the median) for gestational age and is 100% sensitive. If the PSV is between 1.0 and 1.5 MoM and the slope is rising and approaching 1.5 MoM, fetal surveillance is increased to weekly doppler examination. If the MCA peak systolic velocity > 1.5 MoM and the gestational age is <34 or 35 weeks, fetal blood sampling should be considered and followed by fetal transfusion if needed. If the gestation age is >/=34 weeks, delivery is considered.

Other options:

Option A: Umbilical artery- S/D ratio:  Abnormal flow patterns on the umbilical artery doppler:

* Reduced end-diastolic flow: Uteroplacental insufficiency.

* Absent end-diastolic flow: Fetal compromise.

* Reverse end-diastolic flow: Impending doom of death.

Option C: Uterine artery: The presence of a diastolic notch indicates incomplete trophoblastic invasion of the uterine spiral arteries and is associated with an increased risk of developing pre-eclampsia, intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR), and even fetal demise.

Option D: Umbilical vein: Doppler assessment of the venous system (ductus venosus and umbilical vein) gives insight into cardiac forward function by evaluating cardiac compliance, contractility, and afterload.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Renal compensation in metabolic acidosis takes time because:
options: Initially the pH of tubular fluid increases
Low pH normally decreases bicarbonate excretion
It takes hours to days for kidney to synthesize enzymes that produce NH4+
Other ions in the tubule interfere with buffer action
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. It takes hours to days for kidney to synthesize enzymes that produce NH4+

Compensation in metabolic acidosis happens late in the kidney because it takes hours to days for it to synthesize enzymes that produce NH4+(ammonium ions).

Acid-base balance equation: CO2 + H2O -----> H2CO3 -----> H+(acid) and HCO3-(base)

• First line of defence (in seconds): Buffers ( phosphate and ammonium )
• Second line of defence (in Minutes): Lungs
• Third line of defence (in hours - days): Kidney

The kidneys regulate the acid-base balance by two major mechanisms: the reabsorption of bicarbonate and the generation of new bicarbonate via ammonia production and distal nephron acid secretion. Urinary NH4+ is produced primarily in the proximal tubule cells by converting glutamine to glutamate.

Renal failure leads to a buildup of acids due to loss of excretory function of the kidney. The decreased glomerular filtration rate also leads to diminished excretion of the renal buffers phosphate and ammonium. Thus, bicarbonate reabsorption decreases, resulting in metabolic acidosis.
questions.learning: It takes hours to days for kidney to synthesize enzymes that produce NH4+ Compensation in metabolic acidosis happens late in the kidney because it takes hours to days for it to synthesize enzymes that produce NH4+(ammonium ions).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 55-year-old man sustains a head injury involving the left temporal region following a road traffic accident. After regaining consciousness, he speaks fluently, but his speech is irrelevant and meaningless, and he is unable to comprehend spoken language. Which cortical area is most likely affected?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Wernicke's area

Wernicke’s area, located in the posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus of the dominant (usually left) hemisphere (Brodmann area 22), is responsible for language comprehension. Lesions produce Wernicke (receptive/fluent) aphasia, characterized by fluent but meaningless speech, impaired comprehension, impaired repetition, and poor awareness of the language deficit.

FMGE/NEET PG Pearl

• Broca’s area (BA 44, 45) → Non-fluent, effortful speech with intact comprehension.
• Wernicke’s area (BA 22) → Fluent but nonsensical speech with impaired comprehension.
• Arcuate fasciculus → Conduction aphasia with impaired repetition but relatively preserved fluency and comprehension.
• Primary auditory cortex (BA 41, 42) → Receives auditory input; lesions cause cortical hearing deficits rather than aphasia.
questions.learning: Wernicke's area Wernicke’s area, located in the posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus of the dominant (usually left) hemisphere (Brodmann area 22), is responsible for language comprehension.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following finding is shown in the given image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Linea nigra

The given image shows Linea nigra.

Linea nigra is a brownish-black pigmented area that stretches from the xiphisternum to the symphysis pubis in the midline. The pigmentary changes may be due to melanocyte-stimulating hormone from the anterior pituitary. The pigmentation disappears after delivery. Similar changes are observed in women taking oral contraceptives may be due to estrogen and progesterone may be related to it as.

Other options:

Option A: Striae gravidarum is slightly depressed linear marks with varying length and breadth found in pregnancy. They are predominantly found in the abdominal wall below the umbilicus. They appear pinkish in color. They can sometimes be found over the thighs and breasts. These stretch marks represent the scar tissues in the deeper layer of the cutis.

Option B: Chloasma gravidarum also called pregnancy mask is an extreme form of pigmentation around the cheek, forehead, and around eyes. It may be patchy or diffuse. It disappears spontaneously after delivery.

Option C: Initially, striae gravidarum are pinkish but after the delivery, the scar tissues contract and obliterate the capillaries and appear glistening white. They are called the linea alba.
questions.learning: Linea nigra — The given image shows Linea nigra. Linea nigra is a brownish-black pigmented area that stretches from the xiphisternum to the symphysis pubis in the midline.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following is transmitted by all the components of blood?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Malaria

Among the options provided, Malaria is the only disease transmitted by all components of blood.

Malaria is primarily spread through the bite of infected Anopheles mosquitoes, which inject sporozoites into the bloodstream but can also be transmitted by transfusion of blood and blood products.

other options:

Option A : Syphilis is primarily transmitted through direct contact with syphilitic sores (chancres), which can occur on the genitals, lips, mouth, or anus during sexual activity.In most cases, transmission via blood transfusion is rare.

Option C:  Filarial parasites are primarily transmitted through the bite of infected mosquitoes. However, they can also be found in the blood of infected individuals, which can potentially transmit the infection through blood transfusion. However, plasma and platelets may not typically harbor filarial parasites unless there's concurrent infection or contamination.

Option D: Toxoplasma is transmitted through various routes, including ingestion of contaminated food or water, contact with infected cat feces, and transplacental transmission from mother to fetus. However, it is not primarily transmitted through blood

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the term used for a communication format in which 4–8 participants discuss a given topic informally in front of a large audience, without a fixed agenda, prepared speeches, or a predetermined speaking order, and later engage with the audience?
questions.explanation: The description provided matches the specific format of a Panel Discussion. In this mode, a small group of experts (4 to 8) sit in front of an audience and discuss a topic conversationally. Unlike other formats, there are no formal speeches or fixed order; the moderator guides a spontaneous exchange of ideas, and the session concludes with audience questions. A Symposium (Option B) involves formal, pre-prepared speeches by each expert on different aspects of a topic. A Workshop (Option C) is focused on practical learning and skill acquisition through active participation. A Seminar (Option D) is a more academic setting where a lead speaker presents a paper followed by group discussion. Therefore, the informal, conversational, and audience-interactive nature of the experts defines the Panel Discussion format
questions.learning: The description provided matches the specific format of a Panel Discussion. In this mode, a small group of experts (4 to 8) sit in front of an audience and discuss a topic conversationally.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which artery is being assessed by palpation in the image shown below?
questions.explanation: The image shows palpation being performed posterior to the medial malleolus — the anatomical landmark for the posterior tibial artery, which runs in the groove between the medial malleolus and the calcaneus. Key Anatomical Features: 1. 1. Fingers placed behind medial malleolus 2. 2. Classic position for posterior tibial pulse assessment 3. 3. Important pulse for assessing peripheral vascular disease 4. 4. Absent in peripheral arterial occlusive disease Why other options are wrong: (A) Anterior tibial artery is incorrect because anterior tibial artery is palpated on the dorsum of the foot between first and second metatarsals : not behind the medial malleolus. (C) Dorsalis pedis artery is incorrect because dorsalis pedis is palpated on the dorsum of foot lateral to extensor hallucis longus tendon : not at the medial malleolar groove as shown. (D) Popliteal artery is incorrect because popliteal artery is palpated in the popliteal fossa behind the knee with knee slightly flexed : completely different anatomical location from what is shown here

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following statements are true about eutectic mixture of local anesthetic (EMLA)?
options: It is made of Lignocaine and ropivacaine
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Methohemoglobinemia is a side effect

Methemoglobinemia can develop when high doses of prilocaine are administered, typically over 600 mg.

EMLA (Eutectic Mixture of Local Anaesthetic) is a topical mixture containing prilocaine. The risk of methemoglobinemia is increased in neonates with metabolic disorders or in those receiving drugs that can impair the reduction of methemoglobin.

It is an eutectic(in fixed proportions) mixture, not necessarily equal (Option C). It consists of a 1:1 mixture of 2.5% lidocaine (Option A) and 2.5% prilocaine, not ropivacaine (Option D)

EMLA can provide adequate dermal analgesia for procedures like:

• Split skin-graft harvesting
• Venipuncture
• Intravenous cannulation in children
• Laser skin treatments
• Lithotripsy
• Circumcision

EMLA cream should not be used on mucous membranes, broken skin, infants younger than 1 month of age, or patients with a predisposition to methemoglobinemia. EMLA is applied 45-60 minutes before the procedure with an occlusive dressing. It provides analgesia up to a depth of 5 mm, which lasts for 1-2 hours.

Other side effects include- blanching of the skin, erythema, and oedema.
questions.learning: Methohemoglobinemia is a side effect Methemoglobinemia can develop when high doses of prilocaine are administered, typically over 600 mg. EMLA (Eutectic Mixture of Local Anaesthetic) is a topical mixture containing prilocaine.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: During a routine prenatal visit, a 25-year-old pregnant woman voices concern about traveling to a tropical area because of the risk of Zika virus infection. You counsel her on the importance of knowing the vectors involved in transmission. Which mosquito species is the primary vector responsible for spreading the Zika virus?
questions.explanation: Zika virus is primarily transmitted to humans through the bite of an infected mosquito from the Aedes genus. While Aedes aegypti is the world's most common primary vector, Aedes albopictus (the Asian tiger mosquito) is a significant and widespread secondary vector that is also capable of tr-ansmitting the virus (Option B). Aedes australis (Option A), Aedes mitchellae (Option C), and Aedes polynesiensis (Option D) are not the primary drivers of the global Zika epidemics. Zika infection during pregnancy is of major concern because it is neurotropic and can cause microcephaly and other severe fetal brain anomalies. Education for pregnant travelers focuses on using insect repellent, wearing long sleeves, and avoiding areas with known outbreaks. In many regions of the world where A. aegypti is absent, A. albopictus serves as the main threat. Therefore, among the choices provided, Aedes albopictus is the recognized vector for Zika virus transmission
questions.learning: Zika virus is primarily transmitted to humans through the bite of an infected mosquito from the Aedes genus. While Aedes aegypti is the world's most common primary vector, Aedes albopictus (the Asian tiger mosquito) is a significant and widespread…

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following post-translational modifications (PTM) is associated with the synthesis of haemoglobin, collagen and immunoglobulin?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Subunit aggregation

Haemoglobin, collagen, and immunoglobin are proteins that are synthesized as subunits and undergo subunit aggregation during post-translational modifications (PTM).

Adult haemoglobin is synthesized separately as 2 alpha chains and 2 beta chains and then aggregated together to form (α2β2) chains.

Collagen is synthesized as pre-procollagen inside cells and released as tropocollagen which aggregates into collagen fibrils through covalent bonds.

Immunoglobulins are components of the immune system and are divided into 5 classes. However, each immunoglobulin has two heavy chains and two light chains synthesized separately and then aggregated.

Post-translational modifications of the polypeptide chain include the removal of N- or C- polypeptides from zymogens to make mature proteins e.g. trypsinogen to trypsin. Also, covalent alterations of proteins in the form of phosphorylation, glycosylation, etc are considered post-translational modifications.

Subunit aggregation is an essential step that provides functional properties to the structural proteins. Error in aggregation can lead to disease pathologies like Amyloidosis-including ALS, Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and prion disease.

Other options:

Options A and C: Gene splicing and alternate splicing are post-transcriptional modifications occurring in mRNA.

Option D: DNA mismatch repair is a post-replication step.

Pearl PF2045: Structure of proteins
questions.learning: Subunit aggregation Haemoglobin, collagen, and immunoglobin are proteins that are synthesized as subunits and undergo subunit aggregation during post-translational modifications (PTM).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient sustains a road traffic accident and has a normal non-contrast CT scan of the head at admission. After several days in the ICU, the patient deteriorates into coma and subsequently dies. Brain biopsy reveals multiple punctate hemorrhages. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Diffuse axonal injury (DAI) is a severe primary brain injury caused by shearing forces during high-velocity trauma, such as a road traffic accident. These forces disrupt axons throughout the white matter, brainstem, and corpus callosum. A classic feature of DAI is that initial Non-Contrast CT (NCCT) scans are often normal or show only minute, subtle abnormalities. Diagnosis is frequently clinical, based on a prolonged coma without a lucid interval, or confirmed via MRI. Histopathology reveals multiple punctate, petechial hemorrhages within deep white matter tracts. Ischemic injury (Option A) typically presents with localized territorial infarcts. Intraventricular bleeding (Option C) and subdural hemorrhage (Option D) would be clearly visible on the initial CT as hyperdense blood collections within the ventricles or as a crescent-shaped mass, respectively. Thus, the normal CT followed by punctate hemorrhages on biopsy is pathognomonic for DAI
questions.learning: Diffuse axonal injury (DAI) is a severe primary brain injury caused by shearing forces during high-velocity trauma, such as a road traffic accident. These forces disrupt axons throughout the white matter, brainstem, and corpus callosum.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The function of the Golgi tendon organ is to _________
options: Sense changes in position of the muscle
Sense changes in length of the muscle
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sense changes in muscle tension

Golgi tendon organ sense changes in muscle tension.

Golgi tendon reflex (Inverse myotatic/ Inverse stretch reflex) is disynaptic, is the opposite of the stretch reflex.

When the tension in a contracted muscle is significantly elevated, the inhibitory effect from the Golgi tendon organ leads to instantaneous relaxation of the entire muscle. This effect is called the lengthening reaction.

It is a protective mechanism to prevent tearing of the muscle or avulsion of the tendon from its attachments to the bone.

Note: Muscle spindles senses changes in muscle length (stretch).
questions.learning: Sense changes in muscle tension Golgi tendon organ sense changes in muscle tension. Golgi tendon reflex (Inverse myotatic/ Inverse stretch reflex) is disynaptic, is the opposite of the stretch reflex.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 28-year-old man presents with a rash after a trip. You observe a vector on his skin. Considering common vector-borne diseases, what is the disease transmitted by the vector shown in the image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Scrub typhus

Scrub typhus is transmitted by chiggers (larval mites), not ticks, and should be suspected in patients with fever and rash after exposure in endemic areas.

• Causative organism: Orientia tsutsugamushi
• Vector: chigger (larval stage of mite)
• Classic feature: eschar at bite site
• Symptoms: fever, rash, lymphadenopathy
• Treated with doxycycline

Important distinction:

• Tick-borne diseases → Babesiosis, Anaplasmosis, Ehrlichiosis
• Mite-borne disease → Scrub typhus

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements does not apply during cross-examination in a court of law?
options: Witness is examined by the defense lawyer
Objective of cross-examination is to weaken case of opponent
There is no time limit to cross examination
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Leading questions are not allowed

Leading questions are allowed in a cross-examination according to Section 146 (4) of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA). However, they are not allowed during the direct examination conducted by the summoning counsel.

If the judge is satisfied that the witness is hostile, leading questions may be allowed during direct examination.

Leading questions (Section 146(1) of BSA) are defined as questions that suggest an answer that is favorable for the case of the summoning counsel or in alignment with their claim.

Other options:

Options 1, 3, 4 - In cross-examination, the witness is examined by the defense lawyer or adverse party with an objective to elicit favorable facts to their case, to test the accuracy of the witness statements, to unearth new or old facts, and also to discredit the witness.

While leading questions are allowed in cross-examination, the Judge can disallow indecent questions (Section 154 of BSA) or questions asked with an intention to insult or offend the witness in any form (Section 155 of BSA).

There is no time limit to the duration of cross-examination.

The sequence of examination in the recording of evidence is as follows -

Sequence of examination
Objective

• Examination-in-Chief/Direct examination by the party that summoned the witness
To elicit the facts of the case from the witness. Leading questions are not allowed.

• Cross-examination by the defense lawyer
To elicit facts favorable to their case and test the reliability of the witness. Leading questions are allowed.

• Re-examination by the party that summoned the witness
To resolve doubts that formed during cross-examination and re-emphasize the party's perspective
questions.learning: Leading questions are not allowed Leading questions are allowed in a cross-examination according to Section 146 (4) of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: In ophthalmic procedures, a specific dye is used to enhance the visualization of structures within the anterior chamber of the eye. Which dye is employed for staining the anterior chamber?
questions.explanation: In modern ophthalmic microsurgery, Trypan blue is the standard dye used to stain the anterior capsule of the lens during cataract surgery (specifically for continuous curvilinear capsulorhexis). By providing a sharp contrast, it allows the surgeon to clearly see the edges of the capsule, which is especially vital in cases of dense ("white") cataracts where the red reflex is absent. It is also used to stain the donor corneal tissue in endothelial keratoplasty. Brilliant blue (Option B) is primarily used to stain the internal limiting membrane during vitreoretinal surgery. Fluorescein (Option C, often greenish when viewed with cobalt blue light) is used for assessing corneal ulcers and tear film. Lissamine green (Option D) is used to stain devitalized conjunctival cells in dry eye diagnostics. Trypan blue is non-toxic to the corneal endothelium when used appropriately. Its introduction has significantly improved the safety and predictability of complex cataract procedures by providing superior intraoperative visualization of clear ocular structures
questions.learning: In modern ophthalmic microsurgery, Trypan blue is the standard dye used to stain the anterior capsule of the lens during cataract surgery (specifically for continuous curvilinear capsulorhexis).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 10-year-old child was brought to the OPD following a sting on his toe. On examination, he had tachycardia, hypertension, tongue fasciculations, hypersalivation, and dilated pupils. Local examination of the wound showed mild erythema. He remembers the animal having a curved tail upwards. Which of the following has most likely bitten him?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Scorpion

The clinical stem with the description of the animal is suggestive of a scorpion bite.

Most scorpion stings cause pain at the site of the bite. Systemic toxicity occurs in <10% of stings but is more commonly seen in infants and children. The venom is a clear, colorless toxalbumen and is generally classified as either hemolytic or neurotoxic.

The venom is a potent autonomic stimulator resulting in the release of massive amounts of catecholamines from the adrenals. It also has a direct effect on the myocardium.

It can present as neurotoxicity with restlessness or seizure-like activity, abnormal oculomotor function, loss of pharyngeal muscle control leading to respiratory compromise. Tongue fasciculations and hypersalivation are also common. Cardiovascular toxicity from systemic envenomation includes tachycardia, hypertension, pulmonary edema, and cardiogenic shock.

If the scorpion has hemolytic venom, the reaction is mainly local, with edema, pain, and reddening. This usually lasts for one to two hours.

Treatment:

* Pain- Paracetamol, NSAIDs, or opioids

* Sedation for agitation, oculomotor abnormalities, uncoordinated neuromuscular activity, muscle spasms- Benzodiazepines

* Hypertension and pulmonary edema -Prazosin counteract the adrenergic surge that can lead to these effects

* Cardiogenic shock- Antivenom, prazosin, nitroglycerin, dobutamine

* Cholinergic effects- Atropine

* Supportive care wound care

Note: Massive amounts of catecholamines are also released by a species of spider called the Black Widow spider which is fatal if bitten.
questions.learning: Scorpion — The clinical stem with the description of the animal is suggestive of a scorpion bite. Most scorpion stings cause pain at the site of the bite.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Identify the condition shown in the image below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Herpes labialis

The above image shows multiple vesicles & crusts clustered on an inflamed base around the lips which is characteristic of herpes labialis or cold sore.

It is commonly caused by herpes simplex virus type 1(HSV-1) and rarely by herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2). It begins with a prodrome of pain, burning, and tingling followed by the appearance of erythematous papules. The papules then become vesicular and may ulcerate.

It is treated with oral acyclovir 200 mg and 5% topical acyclovir.

Option B: Herpangina or vesicular pharyngitis is characterized by the presence of ulcerating small vesicles on the oral fauces and the posterior pharyngeal wall. It is commonly caused by the coxsackie virus.

Option C: Molluscum contagiosum is characterized by pearly white, wart-like umbilicated papules. It is caused by the pox virus.

Option D: Impetigo is characterized by golden yellow or honey-coloured crusts that form after the rupture of pustulating vesicles. Non-bullous impetigo is caused by both S. aureus and streptococcus. Bullous impetigo is caused by S. aureus.
questions.learning: Herpes labialis — The above image shows multiple vesicles & crusts clustered on an inflamed base around the lips which is characteristic of herpes labialis or cold sore.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following is the best method to assess the degree of muscle relaxation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Train of four

Train of four protocol is the best method to clinically assess neuromuscular blockade.

Train of four protocol is one of the methods used in the clinical assessment of neuromuscular blockade. It is done by stimulating the ulnar nerve with a stimulus and watching the contractile responses in the adductor pollicis muscle. Four successive stimuli of 2Hz strength are given at fixed time intervals and the response achieved is plotted as a graph.

Tetanic stimulation (Option A): It consists of a series of extremely rapid electrical stimuli typically applied over 5 seconds. This method has only 70% sensitivity to detect residual paralysis and its specificity is only about 50%, and is painful. Hence, this test is of limited value for assessing residual neuromuscular blockade.

Double-burst stimulation (Option B): Here two short bursts of 50 Hz tetanic stimuli is delivered, which are separated by 750 ms.

Electromyography (Option D) has been used to measure abdominal and thoracic motor function but is neither practical nor specific.
questions.learning: Train of four Train of four protocol is the best method to clinically assess neuromuscular blockade. Train of four protocol is one of the methods used in the clinical assessment of neuromuscular blockade.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A person reported to OPD alongside his 32-year-old brother working in a factory. The brother was recently subjected to a test – Coproporphyrin in urine. The physician should suspect:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Lead poisoning

Detection of coproporphyrin in urine is a characteristic finding in lead poisoning, due to inhibition of enzymes involved in heme synthesis.

Lead interferes with ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase, causing accumulation of porphyrin precursors that are excreted in urine.

In contrast, silicosis, byssinosis, and bagassosis are occupational lung diseases and are not associated with porphyrin metabolism abnormalities.
questions.learning: Lead poisoning Detection of coproporphyrin in urine is a characteristic finding in lead poisoning, due to inhibition of enzymes involved in heme synthesis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text:
Which of the following is not done during the primary survey in trauma management?

1. NCCT brain
2. Endotracheal intubation
3. Intercostal drainage
4. Chest X Ray
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1 only

NCCT brain is not done during the primary survey in trauma management. (Option C)

Endotracheal intubation is part of airway management in the primary survey. Intercostal drainage for hemothorax or pneumothorax and chest X-ray especially AP view is part of breathing component assessment of the primary survey in trauma management.

NCCT brain is a part of the secondary survey of trauma management and is performed after initial resuscitation and stabilisation. A CT scan of the head is performed within 1 hour if the GCS is <14 at the initial assessment. Other indications include a tense fontanelle, suspicion of an open/ depressed or base of skull fracture, abnormal pupillary response, abnormal posturing, and a focal neurological defect. A head CT scan should also be performed if there are three or more vomiting episodes, a witnessed loss of consciousness or amnesia for >5 minutes.
questions.learning: 1 only NCCT brain is not done during the primary survey in trauma management. (Option C) Endotracheal intubation is part of airway management in the primary survey.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Arrange the following steps of ventricular action potential in the correct order.

A. Opening of voltage-gated calcium channels
B. Repolarizing K+ currents
C. Opening of voltage-gated sodium channels
D. Transient outward flow of potassium
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. C, D, A, B

The correct sequence for ventricular action potential is as follows:

C. Opening of voltage-gated sodium channels
D. Transient outward flow of potassium
A. Opening of voltage-gated calcium channels
B. Repolarizing K+ currents

The events of action potential occur in the following sequence:

• Phase 0: Voltage-gated Na+ channels open in response to depolarizing stimulus (rapid depolarization phase)
• Phase 1: Inactivation of voltage-gated Na+ channels and transient outward flow of K+ causes rapid repolarization (rapid repolarization phase)
• Phase 2: Opening of slow voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels causes the influx of calcium into the cells and results in the plateau phase (plateau phase)
• Phase 3: Opening of various K+ channels results in the efflux of K+ from the cells and results in slow repolarization (slow repolarization phase).
• Phase 4: Return to resting membrane potential
questions.learning: C, D, A, B — The correct sequence for ventricular action potential is as follows: C. Opening of voltage-gated sodium channels D.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presented with anorexia, epigastric pain, jaundice, and pruritus for 2 months. The gallbladder is palpable but non-tender. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Carcinoma head of pancreas

Jaundice + pruritus → obstructive jaundice

• Palpable, non-tender gallbladder → distended GB
• Chronic symptoms (2 months)

👉 This points to malignant obstruction, most commonly →  Carcinoma head of pancreas

This case illustrates Courvoisier's Law: “In obstructive jaundice, a palpable non-tender gallbladder is unlikely due to gallstones.”

Why this happens

Tumor in pancreatic head compresses common bile duct (CBD) → Bile backs up → gallbladder gradually distends → No inflammation → non-tender

❌A. Gall bladder carcinoma → GB usually irregular, hard; not smoothly enlarged

❌B. HCC → liver pathology, not classic obstructive pattern.

❌C. Cholelithiasis → GB is painful & fibrotic (not palpable)

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: What is true about ovotesticular disorders of sex development?
options: Ovotestis is seen in the gonadal biopsy
The response of testosterone to hCG is increased.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ovotestis is seen in the gonadal biopsy

Ovotesticular disorder of sex development (DSD) is characterized by the presence of both ovarian and testicular tissue in the same individual. An ovotestis is present in approximately 2/3 of affected individuals.

Most affected individuals have a 46, XX chromosomal karyotype, which normally results in female sexual development. In about 10% of patients, testicular tissue in an individual with a 46, XX karyotype is present as a result of a translocation of the SRY gene on the Y chromosome to the X chromosome or another chromosome. There is a defect in R-spondin1 protein encoded by the RSPO1 gene, described in 46, XX ovotesticular DSD.

An abnormal vagina and an underdeveloped uterus are usually present. The testes are usually undescended, and the penis may present with hypospadias. Upon reaching puberty, breast development, feminization, and menstruation may occur. Most affected individuals are infertile, but ovulation or spermatogenesis is possible. The response of testosterone to hCG is normal or reduced.
questions.learning: Ovotestis is seen in the gonadal biopsy Ovotesticular disorder of sex development (DSD) is characterized by the presence of both ovarian and testicular tissue in the same individual.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 60-year-old patient with diabetes mellitus presents with severe ear pain and persistent otorrhea that has not responded to antibiotic therapy. On examination, granulation tissue is seen in the external auditory canal, along with facial nerve paralysis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Malignant otitis externa, also known as Necrotizing Otitis Externa, is a severe, life-threatening infection of the external ear canal and skull base. It occurs almost exclusively in elderly diabetic or immuno compromised patients. The hallmark clinical features include excruciating ear pain (disproportionate to findings), persistent otorrhea, and the presence of granulation tissue at the junction of the cartilaginous and bony canal. The involvement of cranial nerves, most commonly the facial nerve (CN VII) resulting in paralysis, indicates advanced disease and osteomyelitis of the temporal bone. Otomycosis (Option A) involves fungal growth but is not necrotic. Serous otitis media (Option B) involves painless fluid behind the drum. Eczematous otitis externa (Option D) is an itchy, skin-surface inflammation without deep invasion. Therefore, the combination of diabetes, granulation tissue, and nerve paralysis makes Malignant Otitis Externa the definitive diagnosis
questions.learning: Malignant otitis externa, also known as Necrotizing Otitis Externa, is a severe, life-threatening infection of the external ear canal and skull base. It occurs almost exclusively in elderly diabetic or immuno compromised patients.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A female patient presents with a swelling in the inguinal region that can be reduced through the deep inguinal ring, producing a gurgling sensation on reduction. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: An indirect inguinal hernia is the most common type of hernia in both males and females. The key diagnostic features in this case are its reduction through the deep inguinal ring and the presence of a "gurgling sound" upon reduction, which indicates that the hernia sac contains bowel loops (enterocele). Direct inguinal hernias (Option A) occur through Hesselbach's triangle medial to the inferior epigastric vessels and do not typically reduce through the deep ring. Femoral hernias (Option C) are more common in females but occur below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, through the femoral canal, not the inguinal rings. A pantaloon hernia (Option D) is a combination of both direct and indirect components on the same side. Because indirect hernias enter the inguinal canal via the internal ring, controlling the ring (the internal ring occlusion test) prevents the hernia from appearing, whereas direct hernias cannot be controlled this way. Surgical repair is indicated to prevent strangulation

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which artery provides the primary arterial supply to the palatine tonsils?
options: Tonsillar branch of the facial artery
Descending palatine branch of maxillary artery
Ascending palatine branch of facial artery
questions.explanation: The palatine tonsil receives a rich, multi-source arterial supply, but its primary and most significant source is the tonsillar branch of the facial artery. This artery reaches the tonsil by piercing the superior constrictor muscle. Other contributors include the ascending palatine branch of the facial artery (Option D), the descending palatine branch of the maxillary artery (Option B), the dorsal lingual branches of the lingual artery, and the ascending pharyngeal artery. The buccal branch of the maxillary artery (Option C) supplies the cheek and buccinator muscle rather than the tonsillar lymphoid tissue. Knowledge of this vascular anatomy is crucial during tonsillectomy, as the tonsillar branch of the facial artery is the most common source of significant intraoperative or postoperative primary hemorrhage. Identifying and ligating these vessels within the tonsillar bed is a standard surgical priority to ensure patient safety and prevent complications like airway obstruction or aspiration of blood
questions.learning: The palatine tonsil receives a rich, multi-source arterial supply, but its primary and most significant source is the tonsillar branch of the facial artery.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman has been diagnosed with cervical carcinoma and is planned for radiotherapy. What is the radiation dose delivered to point A in this treatment?
questions.explanation: In the radiotherapy planning for cervical carcinoma, Point A is a critical anatomical landmark located 2 cm superior to the lateral vaginal fornix and 2 cm lateral to the midline of the uterus. This point represents the area where the uterine artery crosses the ureter. The standard curative dose of radiation targeted at Point A, combining external beam radiation and brachytherapy, is typically 7000 to 8500 centigray (cGy). 5000 cGy (Option C) is closer to the dose often targeted at Point B, which is located 3 cm lateral to Point A and represents the pelvic wall lymph nodes. 2500 cGy (Option A) and 10,000 cGy (Option D) are outside the standard therapeutic range for definitive Point A dosing. Point A dosing is essential for achieving local tumor control while balancing the risk of radiation injury to the nearby bladder and rectum
questions.learning: In the radiotherapy planning for cervical carcinoma, Point A is a critical anatomical landmark located 2 cm superior to the lateral vaginal fornix and 2 cm lateral to the midline of the uterus.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Given a population of 10,000, what implication does a sex ratio greater than 1000 have?
questions.explanation: In demography, the sex ratio is typically defined as the number of females per 1000 males. Therefore, a sex ratio greater than 1000 (e.g., 1050) indicates that there are more females than males in that population. In a total population of 10,000, if the ratio is precisely 1000, there would be an equal split: 5000 males and 5000 females. If the ratio exceeds 1000, the female count must be higher than 5000, which logically necessitates that the male count must be less than 5000 (Option C). Option D is incorrect as it describes the opposite situation. Options A and B are numerically inaccurate as they suggest an impossible population distribution for a group of 10,000. A high sex ratio can be indicative of various social factors, including male migration, differences in life expectancy, or better health outcomes for women. Understanding these ratios is essential for community health planning and resource allocation. Thus, "males are less than 5000" is the definitive statistical implication of a ratio > 1000
questions.learning: In demography, the sex ratio is typically defined as the number of females per 1000 males. Therefore, a sex ratio greater than 1000 (e.g., 1050) indicates that there are more females than males in that population.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs used in the emergency management of asthma does not act by bronchodilation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hydrocortisone

Hydrocortisone does not act by bronchodilation while all other drugs mentioned act by bronchodilation.

Mechanism of action of Corticosteroids in an acute asthma attack:

* Increases responsiveness to Beta-2 agonists

* Decreases mucous secretion

* Decreases the inflammatory cell response.

Steroids increase the transcription of beta 2 receptor genes and hence increase responsiveness to beta-2 agonists. Beta-2 agonists, on the other hand, increase the effect of steroids by enhancing the action of glucocorticoid receptors.

Drugs used in the treatment of bronchial asthma

Bronchodilators

* Beta-2 sympathomimetics: Salmeterol, Formoterol

* Methylxanthines: Theophylline, Aminophylline

* Anticholinergics: Ipratropium bromide, Tiotropium bromide

Anti-inflammatory

* Corticosteroids (Inhalational): Beclomethasone, Budesonide, Fluticasone

* Corticosteroids (Systemic): Prednisolone, Hydrocortisone

* Mast cell stabilizers: Sodium cromoglycate, Ketotifen

* Leukotriene antagonists: Montelukast, Zafirlukast

* anti-IgE - Omalizumab

* anti-IL5 - Mepolizumab, Reslizumab(IL-5 antagonist), Benralizumab(IL-5 receptor antagonist)

* anti-IL4 receptor - Dupilumab

Treatment guidelines for different types of asthma are given below:

Step 1 (intermittent)
As needed low dose ICS + Formoterol

Step 2 (mild persistent)
Daily low-dose ICS

Step 3 (moderate persistent)
Daily low dose ICS + LABA

Step 4 (severe persistent)
Medium dose ICS + LABA +/- add-on therapy

Step 5
High dose ICS + LABA + oral steroids +/- add-on therapy

LABA - Long-acting Beta 2 Agonists, ICS - Inhaled corticosteroids
Add-on therapy includes long-acting anticholinergics, leukotriene antagonists, mast cell stabilizers, methylxanthines, and antibodies.

Other options:

Option A: β2 selective agonists like salbutamol, terbutaline, salmeterol, formoterol, etc, cause relaxation of the tracheal and bronchial smooth muscles by β2 receptor agonist action.

Option B: Ipratropium bromide acts by antagonizing muscarinic receptors in bronchial smooth muscle, thereby causing bronchodilation.

Option C: Theophyllines increase the effects of steroids by activating the enzyme histone deacetylase, which is the target for steroids as well.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 78 year old male presented with complaints of fatigue,breathlessness and palpitations.He has no co-morbidities and does not smoke or drink. On examination there was pedal edema and vitals were: PR-55, BP-100/70, Spo2-94%. An ECG was taken which showed no abnormalities after which he was given oxygen and an ECHO revealed restrictive cardiomyopathy. The physician in doubt of a disease did a cardiac biopsy which showed apple-green birefringence when viewed under polarized light after staining with Congo red stain. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cardiac Amyloidosis

The clinical scenario of breathlessness, pedal edema,ECHO finding of restrictive cardiomyopathy and the apple-green birefringence when stained with Congo red stain is suggestive of cardiac amyloidosis.

Cardiac amyloidosis:

* Amyloidosis of the heart can develop as a consequence of systemic amyloidosis or localized amyloidosis restricted to the heart, particularly in the aged (senile cardiac amyloidosis).

* It is seen in individuals 70 years and older, and it has a far better prognosis than systemic amyloidosis.

* Senile cardiac amyloid deposits are largely composed of transthyretin, a normal serum protein synthesized in the liver that transports thyroxine and retinol-binding protein.

* Cardiac amyloidosis most frequently produces restrictive cardiomyopathy. But, it can also be asymptomatic, manifest as dilation or arrhythmias, or mimic ischemic or valvular disease.

* Another presentation of cardiac amyloidosis is congestive heart failure due to systolic dysfunction, generally a later finding.

* In approximately 10% of patients with amyloidosis, orthostatic hypotension occurs and is presumed to be a result of amyloid infiltration of the autonomic nervous system.

* Morphology: The chambers are usually of normal size, but can be dilated and have thickened walls. Small, semitranslucent nodules resembling drips of wax may be seen on the atrial endocardial surface, particularly on the left.

* Histologically, hyaline eosinophilic deposits of amyloid may be found in the interstitium, conduction tissue, valves, endocardium, pericardium, and small intramural coronary arteries.

Image: Congo red stain viewed under polarized light, in which amyloid shows characteristic apple-green birefringence in the heart

Other options:

Option C- Hemosiderosis is characterized by deposition of hemosiderin, which is a hemoglobin-derived golden-yellow colored pigment. The deposition may occur in any organ or tissue. It is seen in conditions associated with iron overload.

Option D-Dystrophic calcification:When the deposition of calcium occurs in dead or dying tissues, it is called dystrophic calcification. This occurs in the absence of derangements in calcium metabolism, i.e the calcium levels are normal. Dystrophic calcification is seen in areas of necrosis of any type including coagulative, caseous, or liquefactive, and in foci of enzymatic necrosis of fat.
questions.learning: Cardiac Amyloidosis — The clinical scenario of breathlessness, pedal edema,ECHO finding of restrictive cardiomyopathy and the apple-green birefringence when stained with Congo red stain is suggestive of cardiac amyloidosis.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text:
An 18-year-old male presents to the emergency department with epistaxis and a nasal mass. What is the investigation of choice to evaluate his condition?

Contrast-Enhanced Computed Tomography - (CECT)

Paranasal Sinuses - (PNS)

Magnetic Resonance Imaging - (MRI)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. CECT PNS and nose

History of nasal mass and associated epistaxis in an 18-year-old raises the suspicion of nasopharyngeal angiofibroma. CECT of the PNS and nose can be done to evaluate the patient.

CECT of the PNS and nose is particularly useful for revealing characteristic findings such as the anterior bowing of the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus, known as the Antral sign or Holman-Miller sign (shown in the image below), which is indicative of nasopharyngeal angiofibroma.

Nasopharyngeal angiofibroma is a benign but locally invasive tumor that predominantly affects adolescent males aged 10-20 years. It typically originates from the posterior part of the nasal cavity near the superior margin of the sphenopalatine foramen and is thought to be testosterone-dependent. Clinically, this condition presents with profuse, recurrent spontaneous epistaxis, progressive nasal obstruction, conductive hearing loss, and otitis media with effusion. It may also cause additional features such as proptosis, cheek swelling, and broadening of the nasal bridge.

Diagnosis is primarily based on clinical presentation, with CECT serving as the preferred imaging technique to confirm the diagnosis and assess the extent of the tumor. Carotid angiography may be performed to evaluate the vascularity of the tumor and its feeding vessels, typically arising from the external carotid artery, and potentially from the internal carotid system in cases of larger tumors with intracranial extension. Biopsy of the mass is generally avoided due to the risk of severe bleeding.

Staging of juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma

Stage
Spread

IA
Limited to the nose and/or nasopharynx

IB
Extension into ≥ one paranasal sinus

IIA
Minimal extension into the sphenopalatine foramen with minimal part of pterygopalatine fossa

IIB
Full occupation of pterygopalatine fossa with Holman-Miller sign, may with erosion of orbital bones

IIC
Extension into the cheek, temporal fossa, or posterior to pterygoids through the pterygomaxillary fossa

IIIA
Erosion of skull base with minimal intracranial

IIIB
Erosion of skull base with extensive intracranial with or without cavernous sinus

Surgery is the treatment of choice. Embolization of the vessels can be done prior to surgery to reduce the risk of bleeding during the surgery. Radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and hormonal therapy can also be considered.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A truck driver came with complaints of a painless indurated genital ulcer after unsafe intercourse. Motility of the most likely causative organism can be detected by which of the following microscopes?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dark field microscope

The clinical vignette of a painless, indurated genital ulcer in a truck driver is most likely suggestive of syphilitic chancre / hard chancre caused by Treponema pallidum. The motility of the organism can be demonstrated by dark ground/ field microscopy.

Dark ground microscopy can be used to diagnose syphilis when an active chancre or condyloma lata is present to visualize Treponema pallidum. Dark-field microscopy images have a dark background with a refractile organism. The dark ground microscope has an optical system that enhances the contrast of unstained bodies. It is generally less sensitive.

Various types of Spirochetes and their appearances under a dark ground microscope:

• Treponemes generally are short, slender with regular and sharp spirals.
• Leptospira have a large number of closely wound spirals and characteristic hooked ends.
• Borrelia is large with irregular and wide open coils.

The image given below shows Treponema pallidum demonstrated by dark ground microscopy and the various appearances of other spirochetes respectively.

Other options:

Electron microscopy (Option-B) is not commonly used for diagnostics in laboratories. It generally helps in appreciating viral structures.

Light microscopes (Option-C) are commonly used in the labs to visualize the stained smears of various bacteria, fungi in 100x magnification. They are also used during the examination of stool specimens for identifying ova, eggs, or larvae.

Fluorescent microscope (Option-D) uses fluorescent dyes like auramine-rhodamine to appreciate Mycobacterial species and malarial parasites.

Syphilis:

Syphilis is caused by Treponema pallidum, a spirochete bacillus.

It shows corkscrew motility which can be demonstrated by darkfield microscopy. Smear specimens are stained using Fontana stain and pathological tissues are stained using Levaditi stain.

Serologic tests for syphilis recommended by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC):

1. Screening or diagnosis (RPR or VDRL),
2. Quantitative measurement of antibody to assess clinical syphilis activity or to monitor response to therapy (RPR or VDRL)
3. Confirmation of a syphilis diagnosis in a patient with a reactive RPR or VDRL test (FTA-ABS, TPHA, EIA/CIA)

Treatment of syphilis is with 2.4 million units of benzathine penicillin IM.

Note:

VDRL- Venereal disease Research Laboratory test

RPR- Rapid Plasma Reagin test

TA-ABS- Fluorescent Treponemal Antibody Absorption test

TPI-Treponema pallidum immobilization test

TPPA-Treponema pallidum particle agglutination assay

TPHA-Treponema pallidum haemagglutination test

EIA-Enzyme-linked ImmunoAssay
questions.learning: Dark field microscope — The clinical vignette of a painless, indurated genital ulcer in a truck driver is most likely suggestive of syphilitic chancre / hard chancre caused by Treponema pallidum.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 24-year-old female patient presents with a 3-day history of fever, headache, ataxia, nausea, and vomiting. On examination neck rigidity is present and there is hip and knee flexion on passive flexion of the neck. A lumbar puncture was done and CSF findings are as shown below. What is your diagnosis? Opening pressure - Increased Colour- Cloudy white WBCs - 7000/µl; neutrophil predominant Sugar- 15 mg/dl CSF/serum glucose ratio - 0.2 Protein - 70 mg/dl Latex agglutination - positive Limulus lysate test - negative
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Bacterial meningitis

The clinical picture and CSF examination findings are suggestive of bacterial meningitis.

The classic clinical triad of fever, headache, and neck rigidity is suggestive of meningitis. Other common complaints are nausea, vomiting, and photophobia. Nuchal rigidity (“stiff neck”) is the pathognomonic sign of meningitis. Hip and knee flexion on passive flexion of the neck is called Brudzinsky's sign.

<0.4

>0.45 g/L (>45 mg/dL)

Latex agglutination

May be positive in

Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, Haemophilus influenzae type b, Escherichia coli, group B streptococci

Limulus lysate
Positive in gram-negative meningitis

Positive in >80%

In partially treated bacterial meningitis, CSF can be clear, with normal glucose levels and lymphocyte predominance. Culture is usually sterile, and antigens can be detected by an agglutination test.
