questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Please identify the anatomical structure indicated in the provided image.
questions.explanation: The extensor pollicis longus (EPL) is a deep muscle of the posterior compartment of the forearm. It originates from the posterior surface of the ulna and interosseous membrane and its tendon passes around Lister’s tubercle of the radius. It then inserts into the base of the distal phalanx of the thumb. Its primary function is to extend the thumb at both the metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints, and it also assists in extension at the wrist. In anatomical diagrams, EPL is identified by its long tendon crossing obliquely toward the distal thumb, forming the medial boundary of the anatomical snuffbox. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Abductor pollicis brevis → Thenar muscle (palm), not forearm (B) Extensor pollicis brevis → Inserts into proximal phalanx (shorter tendon) (C) Abductor pollicis longus → Inserts into base of 1st metacarpal

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the procedure shown in the image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Whipple's procedure

The image shows the Whipple procedure which is a complex surgery done for carcinomas involving the head of the pancreas.

It is done only in cases when:

* The entire duodenum has to be removed e.g. in familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP)

* Tumor encroaches in the first part of the duodenum, or stomach

* A clear resection margin is not achieved by PPPD

The following structures are removed during Whipple’s procedure:

* Distal stomach

* Duodenum

* Proximal jejunum

* Head of the pancreas

* Gallbladder

* Common bile duct (CBD)

* Regional lymphatics

The reconstruction following Whipple’s procedure or pylorus-preserving pancreaticoduodenectomy involves anastomosis in the following order:

Pancreaticojejunostomy

↓

Choledochojejunostomy

↓

Gastrojejunostomy

This is controversial since there is a difference in the reconstruction procedures mentioned in standard textbooks:

Bailey and Love, 27th edition (Pg no: 1236) - Pancreaticojejunostomy + choledochojejunostomy + duodenojejunostomy

Schwatrz, 11th edition (Pg no: 1493) - Pancreaticojejunostomy + choledochojejunostomy + gastrojejunostomy/duodenojejunostomy

Sabiston, 20th edition (Pg no: 1546) - Pancreaticojejunostomy + hepaticojejunostomy + duodenojejunostomy

Pearl PF0333: Resection and Hybrid Surgical Procedures for Chronic Pancreatitis

Beger’s procedure: Duodenum-preserving pancreatic head resection (DPPHR)

* The completed resection after transection of the pancreatic neck and subtotal removal of the pancreatic head, with preservation of the distal common bile duct and duodenum (Marked A).

* Completion of the reconstruction of the anastomosis to the distal pancreas and to the proximal pancreatic rim by the same Roux limb of the jejunum.

Frey’s procedure:

* The local resection of the pancreatic head with longitudinal pancreaticojejunostomy (LR-LPJ) provides complete decompression of the entire pancreatic ductal system. Reconstruction is performed with a side-to-side Roux-en-Y pancreaticojejunostomy.

Warren’s modification of Beger’s procedure:

Berne modification (Beger + Frey) involves excavation of the central portion of the head without formal division of the neck.

(image below)

Hamburg modification of Frey’s procedure

Note:

Surgical treatments for chronic pancreatitis

Resection

* Pancreaticoduodenectomy (Kausch–Whipple procedure)

* Pylorus-preserving pancreaticoduodenectomy (Traverso–Longmire)

* Beger procedure

* Near-total or total pancreatectomy

Decompression/Drainage

* Duval procedure

* Puestow–Gillesby procedure

* Partington–Rochelle procedure (Puestow)

* Izbicki procedure

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: What is the function of tubuloglomerular feedback?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Regulate GFR

Tubuloglomerular feedback regulates glomerular filtration rate (GFR).

As the rate of ﬂow through the ascending limb of the loop of Henle and first part of the distal tubule increases, glomerular filtration in the same nephron decreases, and, conversely, a decrease in ﬂow increases the GFR.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following medications would be most helpful for a chronic smoker attempting to quit smoking?
questions.explanation: Pharmacotherapy for smoking cessation primarily includes nicotine replacement therapy (NRT) and two first-line non-nicotine medications: Bupropion and Varenicline. Bupropion is an atypical antidepressant that inhibits the reuptake of norepinephrine and dopamine, effectively reducing nicotine withdrawal symptoms and the urge to smoke. Varenicline acts as a selective partial agonist at the nicotinic acetylcholine receptors. It works by providing low-level stimulation to ease withdrawal while simultaneously blocking nicotine from binding, which prevents the rewarding effects of smoking. Mirtazapine (Option B) is an antidepressant with no established role in standard smoking cessation protocols. Clinical trials have demonstrated that both Bupropion and Varenicline significantly increase quit rates compared to placebo, with Varenicline often being the most effective single agent. Consequently, Option D is correct as it encompasses both validated pharmacotherapeutic options
questions.learning: Pharmacotherapy for smoking cessation primarily includes nicotine replacement therapy (NRT) and two first-line non-nicotine medications: Bupropion and Varenicline.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient's right hip drops when he takes the right foot off the ground. Which of the following would not be involved in the patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Sciatic nerve

A patient with dropping of the right hip on lifting the right foot off the ground, has a positive Trendelenburg’s sign. The sciatic nerve would not be involved.

A positive Trendelenburg's sign is seen in the paralysis of the gluteus medius and gluteus minimus muscles, both of which are supplied by the superior gluteal nerve. In the scenario mentioned, since the patient has dropping of the hip on the right side, the structures on the left side would be affected.

Mechanism of actions of gluteus medius and minimus:

• When the leg on one side is lifted off the ground,  making it the unsupported side,  gluteus medius and minimus muscles on the opposite side, which is the supported side, exert traction on the hip bone by acting from the femur. This action results in slight raising of the pelvis on the unsupported side, which helps maintain the trunk in the upright position.
• When the gluteus medius and minimus are paralyzed, the pelvis on the unsupported side sinks when the patient lifts the foot off the ground. This causes the patients to have a characteristic lurching gait.
questions.learning: Sciatic nerve — A patient with dropping of the right hip on lifting the right foot off the ground, has a positive Trendelenburg’s sign. The sciatic nerve would not be involved.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 60-year-old male with an acute ischemic stroke is undergoing thrombolysis with IV alteplase. He currently weighs 80 kg. What is the appropriate dose of alteplase to be given to this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 8 mg

The dose of alteplase for Intravenous thrombolysis is 0.9 mg/kg. This patient weighs 80 kg, therefore the required dose would be 0.9 x 80 = 72 mg. 10% of this is given as a bolus followed by the remainder of the total dose over 1 hour. So the required initial dose is 7.2mg ∼ 8mg

This should be immediately administered to patients with ischemic stroke who arrive in the window period within 4.5 hours of symptom onset.

Administration of rtPA:

* IV access with two peripheral IV lines (avoid arterial or central line placement)

* Review eligibility for rtPA

*

Give 0.9 mg/kg IV (maximum 90 mg), with 10% as an initial bolus. The rest of the is given as an infusion over 1 hour.

*

Frequent cuff blood pressure monitoring

*

No other antithrombotic treatment for 24 h

* If there is a decline in neurologic status or uncontrolled blood pressure, stop the infusion, give cryoprecipitate, and reimage brain emergently

* Avoid urethral catheterization for ≥2 h

Indications for thrombolysis in stroke

* Clinical diagnosis of stroke

* Onset of symptoms to time of drug administration <3 hours/4.5 hours

* Age ≥ 18 years

* CT scan showing no haemorrhage or edema of >1/3rd of the MCA territory

Contraindications of thrombolysis in stroke

* Sustained BP >185/110 mmHg despite treatment

* Bleeding diathesis

* Recent head injury or Intracerebral hemorrhage

* Major surgery in preceding 14 days

* Minor stroke symptoms

* Gastrointestinal bleeding in preceding 21 days

* Recent myocardial infarction

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child presents with abdominal distension and hepatomegaly, with the liver palpable 8 cm below the costal margin and smooth on examination. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Massive, smooth hepatomegaly in a child often points to metabolic disorders like Glycogen Storage Disease (GSD). In GSD subtypes such as Von Gierke disease, the liver becomes uniformly enlarged due to the excessive accumulation of glycogen within hepatocytes. The lack of nodularity or focal masses on palpation suggests a diffuse, infiltrative process rather than a tumor. Lysosomal Storage Diseases (LSD) like Gaucher or Niemann-Pick also cause hepatomegaly but are typically accompanied by massive splenomegaly and developmental regression, which are not described here. Hepatocellular Carcinoma (Option C) is rare in children and would present as a firm, irregular, nodular liver. Autoimmune hepatitis (Option D) usually causes milder enlargement associated with jaundice and fatigue. Thus, smooth, massive hepatic enlargement in early childhood is highly characteristic of a storage-related metabolic defect like GSD
questions.learning: Massive, smooth hepatomegaly in a child often points to metabolic disorders like Glycogen Storage Disease (GSD). In GSD subtypes such as Von Gierke disease, the liver becomes uniformly enlarged due to the excessive accumulation of glycogen within hepatocytes.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which neurotransmitter is secreted by the SA node in response to increased blood pressure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Acetylcholine

Acetylcholine is released in response to increased blood pressure.

In response to raised BP, there is inhibition of sympathetic system and activation of parasympathetic system. Acetylcholine is the universal neurotransmitter of PNS.

Baroreceptors are stretch receptors located in the heart and the adventitia of the blood vessels. They are stimulated by the stretching of the walls of the blood vessels when there is an increased volume or blood pressure in the vessel. They are important in the immediate management of blood pressure. They are of two types: carotid sinus and aortic arch receptors (high-pressure regions) and cardiopulmonary receptors (low-pressure regions).

An increase in blood pressure stimulates the baroreceptors. These signals are transmitted through small Hering’s nerves to the glossopharyngeal nerves and then to the nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS) in the medulla. These signals release glutamate and activate the caudal ventrolateral medulla (CVLM). This in turn inhibits the rostral ventrolateral medulla (RVLM) considered the vasoconstrictor center for the brain and the heart.

Simultaneously, this pathway also excites the vagal parasympathetic center. The stimulation of the vagus results in a slowing of impulse generation in the SA node and a slowing of conduction velocity in the AV node.

These neural changes produce vasodilation, venodilation, hypotension, bradycardia, and a decrease in cardiac output.

• NTS: Nucleus Tractus Solitarius
• CVLM: Caudal Ventrolateral Medulla
• RVLM : Rostral Ventrolateral Medulla (Vasomotor center)
• CVC : Cardiovagal center (Cardioinhibitory center)
• IML: intermediolateral nucleus
questions.learning: Acetylcholine Acetylcholine is released in response to increased blood pressure. In response to raised BP, there is inhibition of sympathetic system and activation of parasympathetic system.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Drug of choice for treatment of pregnant woman with bacterial vaginosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Metronidazole

The preferred treatment for bacterial vaginosis in pregnancy is either oral metronidazole 500 mg BD for 7 days (or intravaginal metronidazole for 5 days). Treatment is typically reserved for symptomatic women.

An alternative option is oral clindamycin, 300 mg BD for 7 days (or intravaginal clindamycin ovules for 3 days).

Bacterial vaginosis (BV) is characterized by a decrease in lactobacilli and an overgrowth of anaerobic bacterial species, including gardnerella, prevotella, mobiluncus, and bacteroides. Most women with BV are asymptomatic, but those with symptoms may experience a foul-smelling, thin vaginal discharge.

The clinical diagnosis of BV is based on the presence of three out of four Amsel criteria: elevated vaginal pH (>4.5), thin non inflammatory discharge, >20% clue cells, and a fishy odor (positive whiff test) after adding 10% KOH (potassium hydroxide) to a vaginal sample.

BV is associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes such as preterm birth, preterm premature rupture of membranes, and postpartum endometritis. It also increases susceptibility to sexually transmitted infections, including HIV.

The image below shows a vaginal epithelial cell, with adherent bacteria (clue cell) :
questions.learning: Metronidazole — The preferred treatment for bacterial vaginosis in pregnancy is either oral metronidazole 500 mg BD for 7 days (or intravaginal metronidazole for 5 days).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Classical galactosemia is caused by a deficiency of the enzyme:
questions.explanation: Classical galactosemia is an autosomal recessive metabolic disorder characterized by the inability to metabolize galactose, a sugar found in milk. The "classical" form of the disease is specifically caused by a deficiency of the enzyme galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase (GALT). This deficiency leads to the toxic accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate in various organs, including the liver and brain. Aldose reductase (Option A) converts excess galactose into galactitol, which contributes to cataract formation in untreated patients. Galactokinase deficiency (Option B) causes a milder form of the disease primarily characterized by early cataracts. UDP galactose-4-epimerase deficiency (Option D) is an extremely rare variant. Classical GALT deficiency presents in infancy with jaundice, hepatomegaly, failure to thrive, and sepsis if milk is not removed from the diet. Therefore, GALT is the definitive enzyme lacking in the classical presentation of this syndrome

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 23-year-old G3P1L1A1 at 37 weeks of gestation presents to the ER with labor pains. She has a previous history of emergency cesarean section and dilatation and curettage. During abdominal examination, fetal parts could be palpated easily. Per vaginal examination revealed a 5 cm dilated cervix and her vitals were: BP - 80/60 mm of Hg, RR - 20/ min, HR - 106/ min, SpO2 - 97% under room air. CTG showed a non-reassuring variable fetal heart rate pattern. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Uterine rupture

In the above clinical scenario of a G3P1L1A1 with previous history of emergency cesarean section and dilatation and curettage, presented with labor pain on abdominal examination, fetal parts could be palpated easily, with patient being hypotensive, tachycardic and CTG showed a non-reassuring variable fetal heart rate pattern points towards the diagnosis of the given clinical scenario is uterine rupture.

The risk factors of uterine rupture include:

* More the number (>2) of prior cesarean delivery

* lnterpregnancy interval <24 months

* Induced labor, especially with misoprostol

* Augmentation of labor with high dose oxytocin

* Women having single layer uterine closure in prior cesarean delivery compared to double layer closure

Hypotension, tachycardia, dizziness, confusion, abdominal pain, scar site tenderness are all the signs of uterine rupture. CTG in uterine rupture will show non-reassuring variable fetal heart rate which might progress to late decelerations and bradycardia.

Differential diagnoses for uterine rupture:

* Pre-eclampsia

* Eclampsia

* Pulmonary embolism - amniotic fluid embolism / venous embolism

* Abruptio placenta

* Anaphylaxis to anaesthesia

* Peripartum cardiomyopathy

Management of uterine rupture:

* Confirm the fetal station and arrest of labour

* Stabilize the patient's vitals

* Immediate laparotomy should be performed as early as possible to avoid neurological or hypoxic sequelae in newborns.

* Depending on the extent of rupture and vitals on the table decision of uterine suturing or hysterectomy or sub-total hysterectomy may be taken.

Other options:

Option A : Amniotic fluid embolism - can present with similar symptoms but oxygen saturation will be deteriorating to less than 95% and the respiratory rate will increase.

Option B: Placental abruption -The patient will present with painful vaginal bleeding. There is no history of hypertension and BP is not elevated

Oprion D: Placenta previa is characterized by abnormal implantation of the placenta over the lower uterine segment and presents with painless vaginal bleeding.

Pearl PF2186: Indications & contraindications for induction of labor

Indications:

* Uncontrolled maternal diabetes mellitus

* Gestational hypertension

* Pre-eclampsia

* Post-term pregnancy

* Abruption placentae

* Premature rupture of membranes

* Rh-isoimmunization

* Intra-uterine growth restriction (IUGR)

* Intra-uterine death (IUD)

* Oligohydramnios

Contraindications:

* Contracted/distorted pelvis and cephalopelvic disproportion

* Placenta previa or vasa previa

* Active genital herpes

* Pelvic tumor & carcinoma cervix

* Transverse lie or footling breech

* Appreciable macrosomia

* Severe hydrocephalus

* Umbilical cord prolapse

* High-risk pregnancy with fetal compromise

* Previous classical cesarean or hysterotomy

* Previous history of uterine rupture

* Pelvic surgeries like vesicovaginal fistula/rectovaginal fistula/pelvic floor repair (third or fourth-degree perineal tears repair)

* Previous 3 or more lower transverse cesarian sections.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Consider the following statements regarding the Central Drugs Standard Control Organization (CDSCO) in India: 1. The CDSCO is headed by the Drugs Controller General (India) at the Centre. 2. The CDSCO is a part of the Directorate General of Health Services. 3. The CDSCO is under the Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers, Government of India. 4. The CDSCO has a network of several port offices for monitoring the import and export of drugs. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2 and 4

The Central Drugs Standard Control Organization (CDSCO) is India’s national regulatory authority for drugs, medical devices, cosmetics, and clinical trials.

• 1. The CDSCO is headed by the Drugs Controller General (India) at the Centre. ✓

• The DCGI is the head of CDSCO and is responsible for the approval and regulation of drugs, vaccines, and medical devices.

• 2. The CDSCO is a part of the Directorate General of Health Services. ✓

• CDSCO functions under the DGHS, which is under the Ministry of Health & Family Welfare.

• 3. The CDSCO is under the Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers\, Government of India. ✗

• This is incorrect. CDSCO is under the Ministry of Health & Family Welfare, not the Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers.

• 4. The CDSCO has a network of several port offices for monitoring the import and export of drugs. ✓

• CDSCO operates port offices to regulate the import and export of drugs, cosmetics, and medical devices.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A neurologist notes the presence of a characteristic “wing-beating” tremor during examination of a patient. This clinical sign is most commonly associated with which underlying condition?
questions.explanation: The "wing-beating" tremor (also called a Rubral or Holmes tremor) is a coarse, proximal, high-amplitude tremor elicited when the arms are abducted and the elbows flexed. It is a classic neurological finding in Wilson's disease, which is a disorder of copper metabolism leading to copper deposition in the basal ganglia (especially the putamen) and liver. Huntington's chorea (Option B) presents with involuntary jerky movements (chorea) and cognitive decline, not this specific tremor. Parkinsonism (Option C) is characterized by a "pill-rolling" rest tremor, rigidity, and bradykinesia. Sydenham's chorea (Option D) is a manifestation of rheumatic fever involving purposeless movements. Patients with Wilson's disease also exhibit Kayser-Fleischer rings in the cornea and low serum ceruloplasmin levels. Treatment involves copper-chelating agents like D-penicillamine or zinc to prevent further neurological and hepatic deterioration
questions.learning: The "wing-beating" tremor (also called a Rubral or Holmes tremor) is a coarse, proximal, high-amplitude tremor elicited when the arms are abducted and the elbows flexed.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which structure does the anterior ethmoidal sinus drain into?
questions.explanation: The paranasal sinuses drain into the nasal cavity through specific meatuses located beneath the nasal turbinates. The anterior ethmoidal sinuses, along with the frontal and maxillary sinuses, drain into the middle meatus, primarily via the hiatus semilunaris or ethmoid infundibulum. The inferior meatus (Option B) is exclusively the drainage site for the nasolacrimal duct. The superior meatus (Option C) receives drainage from the posterior ethmoidal sinuses. The sphenoethmoidal recess (Option D), located posterior and superior to the superior turbinate, receives drainage from the sphenoid sinus. Understanding these anatomical drainage pathways is clinically essential for diagnosing sinusitis and for planning Functional Endoscopic Sinus Surgery (FESS). Obstruction of the "osteomeatal complex" in the middle meatus is the most frequent cause of chronic rhinosinusitis. Thus, the middle meatus serves as the primary drainage hub for the most commonly affected anterior sinuses

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following types of pain stimulus is associated with the Carrageenan-induced experimental pain model?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Inflammatory stimulus

The Carrageenan-induced pain model also called the Carrageenan-Induced Paw Edema model is a well-known model of acute inflammation.

It is employed to evaluate the anti-inflammatory properties of a variety of synthetic and natural substances. A non-antigenic phlogistic polysaccharide derived from red seaweed, carrageenan is frequently added to processed foods as a thickening, stabilising, gelling, and emulsifying agent. The activation of the complement system and inflammatory mediators is caused by the sulphated sugars found in carrageenan.

Carrageenan is injected subcutaneously into the plantar surface of the rat paw to cause inflammation. This process results in temporary inflammation and acute swelling, which peaks 3 to 5 hours after injection and subsides in 24 hours.

Postcapillary venules dilate due to the action of carrageenan, causing inflammatory cells and fluid to exude. During this process, a number of proinflammatory mediators are released. The cyclooxygenase pathway's activation is commonly associated with the carrageenan model. A biphasic curve represents the edema caused by carrageenan.

Part of the initial phase of inflammation caused by carrageenan is attributed to injection trauma and the release of acute phase mediators, particularly bradykinin, histamine, and serotonin. The second phase of carrageenan-induced inflammation, which happens about three hours after carrageenan is added, is mostly caused by prostaglandins.
questions.learning: Inflammatory stimulus — The Carrageenan-induced pain model also called the Carrageenan-Induced Paw Edema model is a well-known model of acute inflammation.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The artery that is palpated between the medial malleolus and the calcaneal tendon is?
questions.explanation: The posterior tibial artery passes behind the medial malleolus within the tarsal tunnel. It is standardly palpated at this location—midway between the medial malleolus and the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon—to assess the distal circulation of the lower limb. A useful mnemonic for the structures passing under the flexor retinaculum is "Tom Dick ANd Harry": Tibialis posterior, flexor Digitorum longus, posterior tibial Artery, tibial Nerve, and flexor Hallucis longus. The anterior tibial artery (Option A) runs in the anterior compartment and becomes the dorsalis pedis. The dorsalis pedis (Option C) is palpated on the top of the foot between the first and second metatarsals. The popliteal artery (Option D) is located behind the knee joint in the popliteal fossa. Thus, the posterior tibial is the only artery located in the medial ankle region specified
questions.learning: The posterior tibial artery passes behind the medial malleolus within the tarsal tunnel. It is standardly palpated at this location—midway between the medial malleolus and the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon—to assess the distal circulation of the lower limb.

questions.text: Common precursor amino acid for urea, creatine and nitric oxide is____.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Arginine

Arginine is the common precursor for urea, creatine and nitric oxide.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman with a known autoimmune rheumatological disorder presents with ocular symptoms. Different rheumatological diseases are associated with characteristic eye manifestations, which are often helpful in diagnosis and management. Which of the following disease–ocular manifestation pairs is not correctly matched, with respect to the most common ocular involvement?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Systemic lupus erythematosus — Cataract

Many rheumatologic diseases have characteristic ocular manifestations:

Correct associations:

• Ankylosing spondylitis → Acute anterior uveitis (most common extra-articular feature)
• Behçet’s disease → Panuveitis (can cause severe vision loss)
• Rheumatoid arthritis → Sicca syndrome (secondary Sjögren) and episcleritis/scleritis

Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) most commonly causes retinal vasculitis and keratoconjunctivitis sicca, not cataract. Cataracts in SLE patients are usually secondary to long-term corticosteroid therapy, not a primary ocular manifestation of the disease itself.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old HIV-positive male came with complaints of persistent cough and weight loss. He has skin lesions that appear as umbilicated papules and nodules predominantly on the face, trunk, and upper extremities. Chest x-ray showed multiple bilateral nodular infiltrates. His sputum CBNAAT for tuberculosis was negative and he has a low CD4 count. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. HIV with disseminated histoplasmosis

The diagnosis based on the given clinical scenario is HIV with disseminated histoplasmosis.

Progressive disseminated histoplasmosis (PDH) is seen in immunocompromised patients. Common risk factors are AIDS (CD4+ T-cell count, <200/μL), extremes of age, the administration of immunosuppressive drugs (e.g., prednisone, mycophenolate, calcineurin inhibitors), and use of drugs like methotrexate, anti-TNF-α agents, and other biologic response modifiers for autoimmune disorders. It most commonly involves the lungs and bone marrow.

Patients with PDH can present with diffuse interstitial or reticulonodular lung infiltrates that can cause respiratory failure, shock, coagulopathy, and multiorgan failure. Clinical features are fever, weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly, and thrombocytopenia. They may also present with meningitis or focal brain lesions, ulcerations of the oral mucosa, gastrointestinal ulcerations and bleeding, and adrenal insufficiency.

Cutaneous involvement is noted in about 10% of cases of PDH. Skin lesions can be caused by the fungus itself resulting in the formation of papules, plaques, nodules, or ulcers, or by an immune response to the infection causing erythema nodosum or erythema multiforme.

Laboratory investigations include looking for Histoplasma antigen in bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid, serum, and urine, IgG and IgM antibodies in serology, a fungal culture of blood or bone marrow aspirate, and cytopathology on biopsy of the affected organ.

Histoplasmosis caused by Histoplasma capsulatum is a thermally dimorphic fungus. The yeast form occurs mainly in tissues at a temperature of 37 °C and the mycelial form occurs in the soil at 25 °C. At room temperature, white, cottony, mycelial growth appears, with large (8-20 μ) thick-walled, spherical spores with tubercles (finger-like projections called tuberculate spores). Transmission is mainly via inhalation of microconidia.

Treatment involves liposomal amphotericin B,  followed by itraconazole for at least 12 months.

Other options:

Option B: If the disease involves skin with signs of meningitis, then HIV with disseminated cryptococcosis can be considered. Since the patient has no signs of meningitis, this option can be ruled out.

Option C: If the disease is restricted to the skin alone, it can be HIV with disseminated molluscum contagiosum. Since the question mentions lung involvement, the option is ruled out.

Option D: The question mentions that CBNAAT for tuberculosis was negative. Hence, this option is ruled out.
questions.learning: HIV with disseminated histoplasmosis — The diagnosis based on the given clinical scenario is HIV with disseminated histoplasmosis. Progressive disseminated histoplasmosis (PDH) is seen in immunocompromised patients.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: The following image shows which X-ray view?
questions.explanation: The image depicts the orientation of the skull for a Towne view (AP axial projection). In this view, the X-ray beam is angled caudally (downward), typically about 30° to the orbitomeatal line (OML), as shown by the green arrow passing from the frontal region toward the occipital bone. This projection is primarily used to visualize the occipital bone, foramen magnum, and posterior cranial fossa, and is especially helpful in assessing occipital fractures and posterior skull structures. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Waters view: Used for maxillary sinuses, with the head extended so the chin touches the cassette (occipitomental view). (B) Caldwell view: An AP projection with slight caudal angulation (15°), mainly for frontal sinuses and orbits. (D) Hirtz view (submentovertex): Beam passes from below the chin upward, used to visualize the base of the skull

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 40-year-old woman with a history of chronic sun exposure presents to the outpatient clinic with brownish pigmentation, as shown in the image. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The image illustrates Melasma, a common acquired hyperpigmentation disorder characterized by symmetrical, patchy, brownish macules on sun-exposed areas of the face, such as the cheeks, forehead, and upper lip. It is most prevalent in women and is strongly associated with chronic UV exposure, hormonal changes (e.g., pregnancy or oral contraceptives), and genetic predisposition. Freckles (Option B) are much smaller, discrete tan spots that darken with sun exposure. Melanoma (Option C) is a malignant pigment-cell tumor that typically presents as an asymmetric, irregular mole rather than a broad, symmetrical patch. Basal cell carcinoma (Option D) usually presents as a slow-growing, pearly nodule with telangiectasia. Management of melasma involves strict sun protection, the use of broad-spectrum sunscreens, and topical lightening agents like hydroquinone, tretinoin, and corticosteroids (Kligman's formula). It is often a chronic condition that requires long-term maintenance to prevent recurrence
questions.learning: The image illustrates Melasma, a common acquired hyperpigmentation disorder characterized by symmetrical, patchy, brownish macules on sun-exposed areas of the face, such as the cheeks, forehead, and upper lip.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A hypertensive patient is on metoprolol. If verapamil is added, there is a risk of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bradycardia with AV block

Metoprolol, when added with verapamil, leads to bradycardia with AV block.

Verapamil and β blockers have additive effect on inhibiting SA node and AV conduction, and the combination should be avoided to prevent severe bradycardia and conduction block.

These agents can also have additive effect on decreasing left ventricular function which could seriously impair cardiac output in a patient with heart failure.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Proper functioning of ICD tube is indicated by _____.
options: Continuous air bubbles coming out of the underwater drain
Oscillation of water column in the tube
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Oscillation of water column in the tube

Oscillation of the water column level (moving up and down during respiration) within the tube in the water seal chamber is indicative of a functioning (patent) ICD tube.

During spontaneous respiration, the water level rises with inspiration and falls with expiration. Whereas during positive pressure ventilation, the opposite occurs. This oscillation is also known as tidaling.

Other options:

Option A: Continous bubbling indicates an air leak in the drainage system, which should be corrected

Option B: Chest X-ray is useful for assessing the position of the ICD tube inside the chest, not its functioning.

Option C: Auscultation is not useful for assessing the functioning of an ICD tube.
questions.learning: Oscillation of water column in the tube Oscillation of the water column level (moving up and down during respiration) within the tube in the water seal chamber is indicative of a functioning (patent) ICD tube.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman presents with a painful, red, granular lesion on the vulva along with bilateral lymphadenopathy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A painful red granular lesion on the vulva with bilateral painful lymphadenopathy (often forming fluctuant buboes) is the classic presentation of chancroid, caused by Haemophilus ducreyi. The hallmark of this infection is that the ulcer is markedly tender, unlike syphilis. Regarding the distractors, Gonorrhea (Option B) causes urethritis or pelvic inflammatory disease but not primary genital ulcers. Granuloma Inguinale (Option C) presents with painless, beefy-red ulcers that expand slowly and, notably, lacks lymphadenopathy. Lymphogranuloma Venereum (Option D) typically features an initial painless ulcer that heals quickly, followed later by painful inguinal swelling (the "groove sign"). Because the primary lesion itself is painful and accompanied by immediate nodal involvement, chancroid is the most likely diagnosis. Therefore, H. ducreyi is the causative agent in this clinical scenario
questions.learning: A painful red granular lesion on the vulva with bilateral painful lymphadenopathy (often forming fluctuant buboes) is the classic presentation of chancroid, caused by Haemophilus ducreyi.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Regarding the facial recess and related middle ear anatomy, which of the following statements are correct? 1. The facial recess is bounded medially by the facial nerve 2. The chorda tympani forms the medial boundary of the facial recess 3. The facial recess is used as a surgical approach in cochlear implantation 4. The fossa incudis forms the superior boundary of the facial recess
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 3, 4

The facial recess is a key surgical landmark in middle ear anatomy, and understanding its boundaries and relations is essential for safe otologic procedures.

Key learning points:

•

Boundaries:

• Medial → Facial nerve
• Lateral → Chorda tympani
• Superior → Fossa incudis

•

Functional importance:

• Provides a safe access route to the middle ear cavity
• Used in posterior tympanotomy and cochlear implantation

•

Clinical significance:

• Close proximity to facial nerve → high risk of injury
• Misidentification of boundaries can lead to facial palsy
questions.learning: 1, 3, 4 The facial recess is a key surgical landmark in middle ear anatomy, and understanding its boundaries and relations is essential for safe otologic procedures.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the most common site of peripheral aneurysm?
questions.explanation: Among peripheral arterial aneurysms, the popliteal artery (Option B) is the most frequent site, accounting for approximately 70% to 80% of all cases. They are frequently bilateral and are often associated with abdominal aortic aneurysms. Femoral artery aneurysms (Option D) are the second most common peripheral site. Brachial (Option A) and radial (Option C) artery aneurysms are much rarer and are often related to trauma or iatrogenic injury (such as from cannulation) rather than primary degenerative atherosclerotic disease . Popliteal aneurysms rarely rupture; their primary danger is distal embolization or acute thrombosis, which can lead to limb-threatening ischemia. Clinical signs include a prominent pulsatile mass in the popliteal fossa. Screening with ultrasound is recommended if a large pulsatile mass is found behind the knee. Therefore, the popliteal artery remains the statistical "gold standard" answer for the most common peripheral aneurysm location
questions.learning: Among peripheral arterial aneurysms, the popliteal artery (Option B) is the most frequent site, accounting for approximately 70% to 80% of all cases. They are frequently bilateral and are often associated with abdominal aortic aneurysms.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A man was found dead due to starvation. Which of the following findings will be seen on autopsy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Distended gall bladder

In starvation, the gall bladder is distended.

In starvation, bile does not get secreted into the duodenum due to the absence of food entering the stomach and intestine. So bile gets accumulated in the gall bladder and gets distended.

Starvation:

* Feeling of intense hunger lasts for 30–48 hours.

* Person can survive for 10–12 days without food and water and for 6–8 weeks without food alone.

* Loss of 40% of body weight is usually fatal.

* Loss of 70–90% of body fat and 20% of body protein is fatal.

* There is reduction in weight and size of all organs except brain.

Other features of starvation:

* Dry, lustreless hair

* Brittle nails

* Pale skin with edema around ankles

* Loss of fat in subcutaneous tissue, in the omentum
(sparing of fat in female breast and orbit till later)

* Atrophy of muscles and darkening due to lipochrome

* The heart is atrophied with empty chambers

* Pale and collapsed lung

* Shrunken liver with necrosis

* Tissue paper-like intestinal mucosa

* Empty bladder
questions.learning: Distended gall bladder — In starvation, the gall bladder is distended. In starvation, bile does not get secreted into the duodenum due to the absence of food entering the stomach and intestine.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A pediatric patient presents with respiratory distress following a suspected foreign body inhalation. To precisely localize and potentially retrieve the object, which diagnostic procedure should be initiated first?
questions.explanation: In a stable pediatric patient with a suspected foreign body inhalation, a Chest X-ray is the essential first-line investigation. While only about 10–15% of foreign bodies are radio-opaque (e.g., coins or pins), the X-ray often reveals critical indirect signs of an airway obstruction, such as localized air trapping (emphysema), atelectasis, or a mediastinal shift. These signs help the clinician localize the object to a specific bronchus. Rigid bronchoscopy (Option A) is the gold standard for definitive management and retrieval but is an invasive procedure requiring general anesthesia; it is performed after imaging supports the diagnosis. Direct laryngoscopy (Option C) only visualizes the larynx and is not suitable for bronchial objects. Flexible endoscopy (Option D) is less useful for retrieval in children compared to the rigid type. Therefore, unless the child is in extremis and requires immediate life-saving intervention, the X-ray is the standard initial diagnostic step

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is a category C bioterrorism agent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hanta virus

Hanta virus is a category C bioterrorism agent. All the other options are category A agents.

Bioterrorism refers to the intentional release of a harmful agent by attackers to cause diseases or fatalities within the human population or impact food crops and livestock. The aim is to instil fear among civilians or influence governmental actions.

As per the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the agents associated with bioterrorism are grouped into three distinct categories, namely A, B and C. There is no designated Category D within this classification.

Emerging pathogens such as Hantavirus and Nipah are examples of category C bioterrorism agents.In the future, these pathogens might be modified to potentially spread widely. Their risk is increased by the following factors:

* Ease of production and dissemination

* High morbidity and mortality rates

* Ready availability

Hantaviruses, classified under Bunyaviridae, are rodent-borne viruses primarily transmitted through inhalation of the virus present in the dried excreta of rodents. It causes haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) or hantavirus pulmonary syndrome.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman comes to the OPD with a history of a lump in the left breast. On clinical examination, the size of the lump in the left breast is 9×10 cm with the following appearance and no axillary lymphadenopathy. The histopathology of the biopsy from the lump shows increased stromal cellularity and typical leaflike architecture. What is your likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Phyllodes tumour

The given clinical scenario and the image are suggestive of phyllodes tumour or cystosarcoma phyllodes of the breast.

Phyllodes tumour is also known as cystosarcoma phyllodes presents as a large tumour with an unevenly bosselated surface. The histopathology of the biopsy of the lump shows increased stromal cellularity, overgrowth, and typical leaflike architecture.

Phyllodes tumours usually occur in women over the age of 40 years but can appear in younger women. It is mostly benign even though it is also called cystosarcoma phyllodes or serocystic disease of Brodie. They are usually mobile over the chest wall despite their large size. Histologically, there is a wide variation with some having low malignant potential and others having a higher mitotic index.

This tumour does not infiltrate the skin though the overlying skin becomes thin and tense due to swelling. Nipple retraction is not seen in this condition. Axillary dissection is not done if malignant transformation occurs because the lymphatic spread is rare. Treatment of phyllodes tumor:

* Benign type- Enucleation or wide local excision

* Massive tumours, recurrent tumours and malignant type- Mastectomy

Other options:

Giant fibroadenomas are usually seen in the early reproductive years. These are benign, solid, encapsulated, and biphasic tumour consisting of fibroblastic stroma and epithelium-lined glands. It is a slow-growing tumour and presents as a painless lump in the breast.

Inflammatory breast cancer is the most aggressive subtype of breast cancer. Axillary nodal metastases are common, and there is a significant risk for distant metastases. Patients with inflammatory carcinoma usually have a rapid onset of disease with progression over weeks to 3 months.

The hallmark of inflammatory breast cancer is diffuse tumor involvement of the dermal lymphatic channels within the breast and overlying skin, often without an underlying tumor mass. Inflammatory breast cancer manifests clinically as erythema, edema, and warmth of the breast as a result of lymphatic obstruction.
questions.learning: Phyllodes tumour — The given clinical scenario and the image are suggestive of phyllodes tumour or cystosarcoma phyllodes of the breast. Phyllodes tumour is also known as cystosarcoma phyllodes presents as a large tumour with an unevenly bosselated surface.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A drowsy man was brought to the casualty with minimal response. He had a progressive history of weakness of the body for 2 days. A CT scan was taken which is shown below. Which vessel is likely to be thrombosed?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Middle cerebral artery

The middle cerebral artery supplies the entire motor area except for the leg area. Thus, a lesion in the middle cerebral artery causes contralateral hemiparesis, sparing the leg area.

Anterior cerebral artery:

* It is the smaller terminal branch of the internal carotid artery.

* It runs in the sagittal fissure and anastomoses with the posterior cerebral artery.

* It supplies the medial surface of the cerebral cortex and parts of lentiform, caudate nuclei, and the internal capsule.

Middle cerebral artery:

* It is the larger terminal branch of the internal carotid artery.

* It runs in the lateral sulcus.

* It supplies the entire lateral surface of the cerebral hemisphere except for a narrow strip (supplied by the anterior cerebral artery) and the occipital pole and the inferolateral surface (supplied by the posterior cerebral artery).

Posterior cerebral artery:

* It is the terminal branch of the basilar artery.

* It supplies the occipital lobe, inferolateral and medial surfaces of the temporal lobe, and parts of the brainstem.
questions.learning: Middle cerebral artery — The middle cerebral artery supplies the entire motor area except for the leg area. Thus, a lesion in the middle cerebral artery causes contralateral hemiparesis, sparing the leg area.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following types of collagens is involved in wound healing?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Type III

Type III collagen is involved in wound healing.

Collagen types I and III predominate in the skin and aponeurotic layers. In the early stages of wound healing, type III collagen is synthesized. It is replaced by type I collagen as wound healing progresses.

The tensile strength of the healing wound is directly proportional to the amount and type of collagen present. During healing, as disorganized collagen is degraded and reformed, covalent cross-links are formed that enhance tensile strength. The maximum strength of the healed wound depends upon the interconnection of collagen subunits. Approximately 80 percent of the original strength of the tissue is obtained by six weeks after surgery. Wounds slowly continue to get stronger but may never achieve 100 percent of their previous strength.
questions.learning: Type III Type III collagen is involved in wound healing. Collagen types I and III predominate in the skin and aponeurotic layers.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A girl was referred to the psychiatry department by the plastic surgeon. She had visited multiple plastic surgery departments requesting full facial reconstruction. She complains of dark blemishes and spots on her face, which are not present. She always says that she is ugly and looks constantly in the mirror and the back of the spoon and windows. Her mother assured her of no such issues, but still, she persists in getting the surgery. What should the psychiatrist do?
options: Start her on selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Start her on selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors

The given history suggests the presence of body dysmorphic disorder (BDD) in the patient, as she is preoccupied with her appearance and self-perceived flaws, despite being told otherwise by her family. The psychiatrist should start her on selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors(SSRI).

BDD is characterized by persistent preoccupations about one or more perceived defects or flaws in one’s appearance, but the defects or flaws are negligible or not even observable to others. In response to their appearance concerns, individuals with BDD demonstrate a range of mental acts:

• Comparing themselves with others
• Checking in the mirror
• Camouflaging their perceived flaws
• Avoidance- from minor social avoidance to being housebound.

The specific focus of BDD on appearance serves to differentiate it from other conditions characterized by repetitive behaviours.

The treatment for BDD typically involves a combination of SSRIs and psychotherapy. SSRIs, such as fluoxetine and clomipramine, have been shown to reduce symptoms in many patients, helping alleviate the obsessive thoughts and anxiety associated with BDD.

Psychotherapy, particularly cognitive-behavioural therapy (CBT), is crucial as it addresses the distorted self-image and underlying emotional issues. CBT helps patients reframe their thoughts about appearance and develop healthier coping strategies.

It's important to note that while surgical interventions may be sought by patients, they are often ineffective and can lead to further dissatisfaction and distress. Therefore, focusing on mental health treatment is essential. Regular follow-ups and a supportive therapeutic relationship can significantly enhance the effectiveness of treatment.

Other options:

Option A: Start on atypical antipsychotics: Antipsychotics are generally not the first-line treatment for BDD. They may be considered in cases with comorbid psychotic symptoms, but this patient does not exhibit hallucinations or delusions.

Option B: Give fitness for surgery: Giving fitness for surgery would be inappropriate and potentially harmful. Surgery is not the solution for BDD, as patients typically remain dissatisfied with the results and continue seeking more surgeries.

Option D: Initiate insight-oriented psychotherapy: While psychotherapy, particularly cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT), is effective for BDD, insight-oriented psychotherapy (focused on understanding unconscious conflicts) is less effective than targeted approaches like CBT in managing this condition.
questions.learning: Start her on selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors The given history suggests the presence of body dysmorphic disorder (BDD) in the patient, as she is preoccupied with her appearance and self-perceived flaws, despite being told otherwise by her family.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In a patient with abdominal pain and sterile pyuria, what is the finding shown in the image given?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Putty kidney

A patient with abdominal pain with sterile pyuria and the abdominal X-ray showing homogenous ground glass-like calcification is suggestive of a putty kidney.

The putty kidney is a characteristic finding of genitourinary tuberculosis (GUTB). It is caused by the dissemination of the organism through the bloodstream and is always a secondary TB (reinfection or reactivation of old TB). Genitourinary TB usually presents as sterile pyuria.

Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen is the most sensitive modality and is the preferred means of visualizing renal calcifications. Microbiological diagnosis is confirmed by at least 3 consecutive early-morning urine samples showing acid-fast bacilli using Ziehl–Neelsen (ZN) stain and subsequently cultured (gold standard).

GUTB is treated with a short course of anti-tubercular therapy (ATT). Ureteric strictures require double J stenting or percutaneous nephrostomy. Definitive treatment is after 3-6mn of ATT, where a reconstructive procedure (open surgical repair > balloon dilatation) is performed. In case the kidney is poorly functioning, a nephrectomy is done.

Option B: Nephrocalcinosis is the deposition of calcium in the kidney parenchyma or tubules, seen in hypercalcemic conditions like hyperparathyroidism.

Option C: Staghorn calculus (a triple phosphate stone) is found in urinary tract infections (UTI) by urease-producing pathogens like proteus and is not a cause of sterile pyuria.

Option D: Psoas calcification is a muscle calcification that develops after acute renal failure and rhabdomyolysis. It is not associated with sterile pyuria.
questions.learning: Putty kidney — A patient with abdominal pain with sterile pyuria and the abdominal X-ray showing homogenous ground glass-like calcification is suggestive of a putty kidney.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A young female presents with vomiting episodes for the past few days. Interpret the ABG report of pH: 7.53, pCO2 48 mm Hg and HCO3: 33 meq/L.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Metabolic alkalosis

This ABG pattern is consistent with metabolic alkalosis secondary to prolonged vomiting, leading to the loss of hydrogen ions (H⁺) and chloride (Cl⁻) from gastric secretions.

The primary disturbance is metabolic alkalosis (high HCO₃⁻ and elevated pH). This is likely caused by excessive vomiting, which leads to loss of gastric acid (HCl), increasing bicarbonate levels.

Interpretation of the ABG:

Step 1: The pH of 7.53 is above the normal limits (7.35–7.45) and thus implies the presence of alkalosis.

Step 2: Plasma HCO3- is 33 mEq/L and is higher than the normal limits (22–28 mEq/L). This implies that the alkalosis is due to an increase in the plasma HCO3- and is thus metabolic in origin. The only cause of metabolic alkalosis from the given options is vomiting.

The compensatory response is respiratory, where the body retains CO₂ (hypoventilation) to counteract the alkalosis. This explains the elevated pCO₂ 48 mmHg [normal limits (35 - 45 mmHg)]. However, compensation is incomplete, as the pH remains alkalotic.

On the contrary, normal plasma HCO3- with a decrease in pCO2 levels would point to a respiratory cause of alkalosis.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 7-year-old boy presented with a white pupillary reflex for which enucleation was done. The histopathological examination of the specimen showed Flexner Winterstein rosettes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Retinoblastoma

The most likely diagnosis with a histopathological finding of Flexner Winterstein rosettes in a 7-year-old child with a whitish pupillary reflex is retinoblastoma. Flexner Winterstein rosettes refer to an arrangement of columnar cells around a central lumen, which is highly characteristic of retinoblastoma.

Retinoblastoma is a malignant proliferation of immature retinal neural cells and is the most common intraocular malignancy in children. It is associated with mutations in the RB1 gene at chromosome 13q14. It is a tumour of a group called small round blue cell tumours because the immature retinal neural cells are seen as small round cells with large nuclei.

White pupillary reflex or leukocoria is the most common presenting feature, followed by a squint which is usually convergent. Rarely, the child may present with nystagmus and defective vision.

Image showing leukocoria of left eye

Histopathology of the tumor shows small round cells with large nuclei. Microscopic features of a well-differentiated tumor include Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes (highly specific of retinoblastoma), Homer-Wright rosettes, pseudorosettes, and fleurettes formation. Areas of necrosis and calcification can also be seen.

The histopathological image of retinoblastoma is shown below.

Treatment typically involves chemotherapy plus focal therapy. The commonly used three-drug regimen is the CVE regimen consisting of Vincristine, Carboplatin, Etoposide. Focal therapy includes cryotherapy, laser photocoagulation, thermotherapy, plaque radiotherapy, and external beam radiotherapy.

Enucleation is done when

• the tumor involves more than half of the retina
• the optic nerve is involved
• glaucoma is present and the anterior chamber is involved

In the stage of extraocular extension, the globe bursts through the sclera, usually near the limbus or near the optic disc. This is followed by rapid fungation and involvement of extraocular tissues results in marked proptosis. Distant metastasis occurs through the lymphatic spread and the direct extension by continuity to the optic nerve and brain.

Other options:

Option B - Medulloblastoma is a malignant embryonal tumor of childhood that occurs exclusively in the cerebellum. Patients usually present with headaches, ataxia, and signs of brainstem involvement.

Histologically, the tumor is very densely cellular. Individual tumor cells have scant cytoplasm and elongated or crescent-shaped hyperchromatic nuclei. Tumor cells form Homer Wright rosettes. They express neuronal markers such as synaptophysin.

Option C - Rhabdomyosarcoma is the most common soft tissue sarcoma of childhood. The child usually presents with rapidly progressive unilateral proptosis. There are 4 subtypes - embryonal, alveolar, botyroid, and pleomorphic. Cells show light microscopic features of striated muscle differentiation. Immunohistochemistry is positive for desmin.

Option D - Astrocytoma of the retina and optic nerve head is rare. It is usually asymptomatic and is most frequently seen in tuberous sclerosis. Fundus examination reveals a yellowish or white plaque, nodule, or mulberry-like lesion. These lesions are semitransparent peripherally and calcified centrally.

Image showing calcified astrocytoma:
questions.learning: Retinoblastoma — The most likely diagnosis with a histopathological finding of Flexner Winterstein rosettes in a 7-year-old child with a whitish pupillary reflex is retinoblastoma.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 28-year-old software professional presents with disturbed sleep, low mood, and stress persisting for the past three months, which he relates to ongoing workplace difficulties. He has no previous psychiatric history. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient’s presentation fits the criteria for adjustment disorder. This condition involves emotional or behavioral symptoms (low mood, stress) in response to an identifiable stressor (work pressure) beginning within three months of the stressor's onset. The distress is often disproportionate to the stressor and causes functional impairment. Generalized anxiety disorder (Option B) requires a minimum of six months of excessive worry regarding multiple domains. Acute stress disorder (Option C) follows a "traumatic" event (e.g., natural disaster) and lasts less than one month. PTSD (Option D) also requires exposure to a life-threatening trauma and specific symptoms like re-experiencing and hyperarousal, which are absent here. As the symptoms are a direct response to common workplace stress and within the 3-month window, adjustment disorder is the diagnosis
questions.learning: The patient’s presentation fits the criteria for adjustment disorder. This condition involves emotional or behavioral symptoms (low mood, stress) in response to an identifiable stressor (work pressure) beginning within three months of the stressor's onset.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 23-year-old man with epilepsy presents with pain in the right shoulder. On examination, the right upper limb is found to be abducted and externally rotated, and active movements are not possible. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient’s limb position—abducted and externally rotated—is the classic presentation of an anterior shoulder dislocation. Subglenoid dislocation is a common subtype of anterior dislocation where the humeral head rests inferior to the glenoid fossa. Regarding the distractors, posterior dislocation (Option D) is classically associated with seizures (epilepsy) but presents with adduction and internal rotation. Luxatio erecta (Option B), or inferior dislocation, is rare and presents with the arm locked in hyper-abduction over the head. Intrathoracic dislocation (Option A) is an extreme rarity where the head enters the rib cage. While the history of epilepsy often points toward a posterior dislocation, the specific physical examination findings of external rotation and abduction in this case override the history and definitively confirm an anterior (subglenoid) dislocation
questions.learning: The patient’s limb position—abducted and externally rotated—is the classic presentation of an anterior shoulder dislocation. Subglenoid dislocation is a common subtype of anterior dislocation where the humeral head rests inferior to the glenoid fossa.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old patient presents with weakness and fatigue. Laboratory investigations reveal low hemoglobin, low reticulocyte count, and normal white blood cell and platelet counts. Bone marrow examination shows a selective decrease in erythroid precursors. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This question repeats the core concept from Questions 42 and 50. The clinical finding of anemia (weakness/fatigue, low Hb) with a low reticulocyte count in the presence of normal WBC and platelet counts is the hallmark of Pure Red Cell Aplasia (PRCA). The definitive diagnostic feature is the selective reduction in erythroid precursors observed in the bone marrow analysis, while other cell lines remain healthy. Aplastic anemia (Option A) would show a decrease in all three cell lines (pancytopenia). Iron deficiency anemia (Option C) is microcytic and typically shows a low reticulocyte count but is not characterized by a total absence of erythroid precursors. Pernicious anemia (Option D), caused by B12 deficiency, is megaloblastic and also involves abnormalities in white cells and platelets. PRCA is an uncommon condition that can be associated with thymomas or autoimmune disorders
questions.learning: This question repeats the core concept from Questions 42 and 50. The clinical finding of anemia (weakness/fatigue, low Hb) with a low reticulocyte count in the presence of normal WBC and platelet counts is the hallmark of Pure Red Cell Aplasia (PRCA).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A group of students who were mainly consuming khesari dal and rice water developed weakness in their legs. On examination, their legs moved in a crossed manner while walking, and some were seen walking on their toes. Which of the following vitamin prophylaxis could have prevented this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Vitamin C

The clinical scenario of students consuming mainly khesari dal and rice water and later presenting with weakness of legs and scissor-like walking(crossed legs) gait is suggestive of neurolathyrism. Vitamin C in doses of 500-1000mg can be used for the prevention and treatment of lathyrism.

Lathyrism is a paralyzing disease of humans and animals. It is due to the consumption of Khesari dal/Lathyrus sativus or its variants such as sweet pea(Lathyrus odoratus). It is mostly consumed by agricultural labourers of poor economic status because it is relatively cheap. It can present as skeletal, vascular, or neural manifestations.

It usually affects young males aged 15-45 years and it is manifested in stages:

* Latent stage: The individual is apparently healthy, but when subjected to a physical ungainly gait. if the pulse is withdrawn from the diet, it will result in complete remission of the disease.

* No-stick stage: the patient walks with short, jerky steps without the aid of a stick.

* One-stick stage: The patient walks with a crossed gait and a tendency to walk on toes. stick is used for balance due to muscular stiffness.

* Two-stick stage: Due to excessive bending of knees and crossed legs, the patient needs two crutches for support. The gait is slow and clumsy and the patient gets tired easily after walking a short distance.

* Crawler stage: Finally, the erect posture becomes impossible as the knee joints cannot support the weight of the body. The patient is reduced to crawling by throwing his weight on his hands.

The patient is initially able to walk with short jerky steps without any aids, but the progressive spastic paralysis causes a crossed gait, and the patient has to use sticks to maintain his balance. Eventually, the knee joints are unable to support the weight of the body and the patient cannot stand erect at all. Long-term consumption of khesari dal leads to neurolathyrism. It is characterized by gradual spastic paralysis of the lower limbs.

The interventions that can be used to prevent lathyrism include:

* Vitamin C prophylaxis.

* Limiting the proportion of the dal to less than a quarter of the total cereals and pulses consumed in a day.

* Removal of the toxin by parboiling and steeping method.
questions.learning: Vitamin C — The clinical scenario of students consuming mainly khesari dal and rice water and later presenting with weakness of legs and scissor-like walking(crossed legs) gait is suggestive of neurolathyrism.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following develops from the dorsal mesogastrium?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Spleen

The spleen develops from the mesoderm in the dorsal mesogastrium.

The mesenchymal cells in the dorsal mesogastrium form small lobular masses of splenic tissue called spleniculi. Later, these lobules fuse to form a single mass of spleen. The capsule, septa, and connective tissue framework, including reticular fibers, develop from mesoderm. The mesenchymal cells also differentiate into lymphoblasts and other blood-forming cells.

When the spleen develops, the dorsal mesogastrium gets divided into an anterior segment called gastrosplenic ligament that extends from the spleen to stomach, and a posterior part called the lienorenal ligament that extends from the spleen to the left kidney.
questions.learning: Spleen — The spleen develops from the mesoderm in the dorsal mesogastrium. The mesenchymal cells in the dorsal mesogastrium form small lobular masses of splenic tissue called spleniculi.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The duration for which copper T 380 A remains effective is referred to as its shelf life.
questions.explanation: The Copper T 380 A (CuT 380A) is one of the most effective and widely used long-acting reversible contraceptives (LARC). The question asks for its effective duration, often clinically termed its lifespan rather than just "shelf life" (which technically refers to storage time). The Copper T 380 A is FDA-approved for 10 years of continuous protection against pregnancy. Option A (3 years) corresponds to older CuT 200 models. Option B (5 years) is the typical duration for the levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system (LNG-IUS) like Mirena or the CuT 375. Option C (7 years) is not a standard duration for most commonly available IUDs. The CuT 380 A contains a larger amount of copper (380 ) than previous models, allowing for its significantly extended duration of action. Therefore, it is a highly cost-effective option for long-term birth control, requiring replacement only once every decade

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 45-year-old man presents with severe eye pain following an injury involving vegetative material. Examination and microscopy reveal septate hyphae with acute-angle branching. Which organism is most likely responsible for this ocular infection?
questions.explanation: A history of ocular trauma with vegetative matter (such as a leaf, twig, or branch) is a classic red-flag history for fungal corneal ulcer (mycotic keratitis). The definitive laboratory finding of septate hyphae branching at acute angles (≈45°) is characteristic of filamentous fungi, most commonly Aspergillus or Fusarium species. Bacterial corneal ulcers (Option C) usually present with an acute onset, marked purulent discharge, and a wet-looking infiltrate. Viral keratitis (Option B), most commonly due to herpes simplex virus, typically shows dendritic or geographic ulcers on fluorescein staining. Acanthamoeba keratitis (Option D) is strongly associated with contact lens use, severe pain out of proportion to clinical findings, and a characteristic ring-shaped stromal infiltrate. Fungal corneal ulcers classically have feathery margins, satellite lesions, and a dry, grayish-white infiltrate. Management is an ophthalmic emergency and requires prompt initiation of topical antifungal therapy, most commonly natamycin 5%. In cases with deep stromal involvement or poor response to medical treatment, therapeutic penetrating keratoplasty may be required to prevent corneal perforation and preserve vision
questions.learning: A history of ocular trauma with vegetative matter (such as a leaf, twig, or branch) is a classic red-flag history for fungal corneal ulcer (mycotic keratitis).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 50-year-old woman presents with bone pain for several months. A skull X-ray is provided. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The skull X-ray demonstrates a thickened calvarium with a characteristic "cotton wool" appearance, where areas of sclerotic (dense) bone alternate with areas of lysis. This finding, combined with a history of chronic bone pain in an older adult, is classic for Paget's disease of bone (osteitis deformans). Paget's disease involves disordered bone remodeling with excessive resorption followed by the disorganized formation of new bone. Osteosarcoma (Option A) and Ewing's sarcoma (Option D) are highly malignant tumors that typically affect children and adolescents and show aggressive bone destruction. Osteochondroma (Option B) is a benign bony outgrowth usually found near joints, not as a diffuse skull condition. Biochemically, patients with Paget's disease often show a markedly elevated serum alkaline phosphatase level with normal calcium and phosphate. Treatment focuses on bisphosphonates to inhibit the abnormal bone remodeling
questions.learning: The skull X-ray demonstrates a thickened calvarium with a characteristic "cotton wool" appearance, where areas of sclerotic (dense) bone alternate with areas of lysis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is the bleeding vessel in extradural hemorrhage?
questions.explanation: An extradural (or epidural) hemorrhage (EDH) occurs between the skull and the dura mater. The most common cause is a fracture of the temporal bone, which results in the rupture of the middle meningeal artery. This arterial bleeding causes the rapid accumulation of blood and the formation of a biconvex (lens-shaped) hematoma on CT scans. Bridging veins (Option B) are the vessels responsible for subdural hemorrhages, which typically occur in elderly or alcoholic patients following minor trauma. The Circle of Willis (Option C) and its branches, like the anterior cerebral artery (Option D), are common sites for aneurysms; their rupture results in subarachnoid hemorrhage, classically presenting with a "thunderclap" headache. Clinically, EDH is famous for the "lucid interval," where a patient initially regains consciousness after trauma before rapidly deteriorating as the hematoma expands and increases intracranial pressure. Urgent neurosurgical evacuation is required to prevent death from brain herniation
questions.learning: An extradural (or epidural) hemorrhage (EDH) occurs between the skull and the dura mater. The most common cause is a fracture of the temporal bone, which results in the rupture of the middle meningeal artery.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 3-year-old boy has been observed by his parents to be increasingly clumsy for the past 6 months. On physical examination, there is leukocoria with an absence of the red reflex in the left eye. A diagnosis was made and enucleation was done. The specimen is shown below. The microscopic appearance shows Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Retinoblastoma

The histology, clinical history, and gross specimen point toward a diagnosis of retinoblastoma.

Retinoblastoma is the most common intraocular malignancy in children associated with mutations in the RB1 gene at chromosome 13q14.

It most commonly presents with leukocoria followed by a squint which is usually convergent. Rarely, the child may present with nystagmus and defective vision.

Signs:

* An intraretinal tumor is a homogeneous, dome-shaped white lesion that becomes irregular, often with white flecks of calcification.

* An endophytic tumor projects into the vitreous as a white mass that may "seed" into the gel.

* An exophytic tumor forms multilobular subretinal white masses and causes an overlying retinal detachment.

Investigations:

* Red reflex testing with a direct ophthalmoscope is a simple screening test for leukocoria.

* Dilated fundus examination using indirect ophthalmoscope

* MRI of the orbit + brain is the investigation of choice.

Histopathology of the tumor shows small round cells with large nuclei. Microscopic features of a well-differentiated tumor include Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes (highly specific of retinoblastoma), Homer-Wright rosettes, pseudorosettes, and fleurettes formation. Areas of necrosis and calcification can also be seen.

Treatment typically involves chemotherapy plus focal therapy.Vincristine, Carboplatin, Etoposide are the choice of drugs for chemotherapy. Focal therapy includes cryotherapy, laser photocoagulation, thermotherapy, plaque radiotherapy, and external beam radiotherapy.

Enucleation is done when the tumor involves more than half of the retina, optic nerve involvement, glaucoma, and anterior chamber involvement.
questions.learning: Retinoblastoma — The histology, clinical history, and gross specimen point toward a diagnosis of retinoblastoma. Retinoblastoma is the most common intraocular malignancy in children associated with mutations in the RB1 gene at chromosome 13q14.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs is used for the treatment of motion sickness?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Promethazine

Promethazine is used for motion sickness. It is an antihistaminic agent that acts as an antagonist of H1 receptors. It also has central anticholinergic activity that is responsible for its antiemetic action.
questions.learning: Promethazine Promethazine is used for motion sickness. It is an antihistaminic agent that acts as an antagonist of H1 receptors.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following vaccines is not recommended after 65 years?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Human papilloma virus

Human papillomavirus vaccine is not recommended after 65 years.

In otherwise healthy elderly patients, the recommended vaccines are:

• Inactivated or recombinant influenza vaccine, 1 dose annually
• Td or Tdap booster, every 10 years
• Zoster recombinant vaccine
• Pneumococcal vaccine
• COVID-19 vaccine

The zoster recombinant vaccine is not indicated for the prevention of varicella. This vaccine is given to prevent episodes of herpes zoster and post-herpetic neuralgia. It is indicated regardless of a previous episode of Zoster.

All adults ≥65 years of age should also receive pneumococcal vaccination. This is in the form of pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV) first, followed by pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV23) after an interval.
questions.learning: Human papilloma virus Human papillomavirus vaccine is not recommended after 65 years. In otherwise healthy elderly patients, the recommended vaccines are: • Inactivated or recombinant influenza vaccine, 1 dose annually • Td or Tdap booster, every 10 years…

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a town, there are 2500 live births within 6 months. During the same period, 5 women died due to peripartum infection, 5 women died due to electrocution, 2 died due to obstructed labour and 3 died due to postpartum haemorrhage. What is the maternal mortality ratio?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 400 per 100000 live births

MMR = Number of maternal deaths in a period x 100,000 (or 1000)/Number of live births in the same period

In this scenario, only 10 women died due to causes related to pregnancy (5-peripartum infection,2- obstructed labour and 3-postpartum haemorrhage). Only they can be included in the statistics.

So, MMR here = 10 x 100000/2500 = 400 per 100,000 live births.
