questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: An infant presents with hepatosplenomegaly and thrombocytopenia. Neuroimaging with CT shows periventricular calcifications. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Congenital cytomegalovirus infection

The most likely diagnosis in this infant is congenital cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection.

The clinical manifestations are hepatosplenomegaly, petechial rashes, jaundice, chorioretinitis, and microcephaly. Head neuroimaging shows intracranial periventricular calcifications. One of the long-term sequelae is sensorineural hearing loss. Diagnosis is made by isolating the virus from the urine or blood by polymerase chain reaction (PCR).

There is no definitive treatment for congenital CMV infection. Treatment with ganciclovir is indicated only in patients with progressive neurologic disease and deafness. The images below show periventricular calcifications and a blueberry muffin baby.

Other options:

Option A - Congenital rubella syndrome is due to the rubella virus. The classical triad of congenital rubella syndrome is deafness, cataract, and congenital heart disease. Patent ductus arteriosus is a common cardiac defect. Eye findings also include salt and pepper retinopathy as shown below.

Option B - Herpes simplex infection in neonates presents with skin vesicles, eye findings (chorioretinitis, keratoconjunctivitis), and microcephaly/hydranencephaly. It can also present as localized skin, eye, and mouth disease, encephalitis, or disseminated disease with a sepsis-like presentation.

Option C - Congenital toxoplasmosis is due to Toxoplasma gondii. A classic triad of chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and intracerebral calcifications is seen. Blueberry muffin baby appearance is also seen in this. Calcifications occur randomly throughout the brain in congenital toxoplasmosis while periventricular calcification is characteristic of congenital CMV infection.
questions.learning: Congenital cytomegalovirus infection — The most likely diagnosis in this infant is congenital cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection. The clinical manifestations are hepatosplenomegaly, petechial rashes, jaundice, chorioretinitis, and microcephaly.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presented with sudden sensorineural hearing loss (SSNHL). Which of the following regimens is the most effective?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Oral prednisolone

Sudden sensorineural hearing loss (SSNHL) is an otologic emergency defined as a sensorineural hearing loss of ≥30 dB affecting at least three consecutive frequencies within 72 hours. Early initiation of corticosteroid therapy (preferably within 2 weeks of symptom onset) offers the best chance of hearing recovery. Oral prednisolone is the first-line treatment for most patients.

Why not the other options?

• B. Steroid + high-dose aspirin: Aspirin is ototoxic at high doses and can worsen hearing loss.
• C. Gentamicin + steroid: Gentamicin is ototoxic and is used for conditions such as Ménière disease, not SSNHL.
• D. Intratympanic steroid injection: Primarily used as salvage therapy when oral steroids are contraindicated or when there is incomplete recovery after systemic corticosteroids.
questions.learning: Oral prednisolone Sudden sensorineural hearing loss (SSNHL) is an otologic emergency defined as a sensorineural hearing loss of ≥30 dB affecting at least three consecutive frequencies within 72 hours.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In a 13-year-old with acute flaccid paralysis, the pediatrics resident orders an RT-PCR on a CSF sample to identify the causative virus. Which of the following describes the enzyme correctly?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. RNA-dependent DNA polymerase

Reverse transcriptase has RNA-dependent DNA polymerase activity and it uses RNA as a template and then synthesizes a single-stranded DNA by reverse transcription of RNA, and finally leads to the formation of double-stranded DNA.

The given case scenario is suggestive of paralytic poliomyelitis caused by the poliovirus. Viral RNA is demonstrable in CSF by reverse transcriptase PCR (RT-PCR).

Note: In RT-PCR, reverse transcriptase synthesizes DNA from RNA which is used as a template for PCR. It is used in detection of viruses from nasopharyngeal swabs (SARS-CoV2, H1N1). In real-time PCR, fluorescent dyes or DNA probes are used to quantify the pathogen DNA load in the specimen. It's used to quantify viral loads in HIV, hepatitis B, etc., and is also called quantitative PCR (qPCR).
questions.learning: RNA-dependent DNA polymerase Reverse transcriptase has RNA-dependent DNA polymerase activity and it uses RNA as a template and then synthesizes a single-stranded DNA by reverse transcription of RNA, and finally leads to the formation of double-stranded DNA.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: The radiological imaging of choice for pheochromocytoma is ___
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. MRI

MRI is the investigation of choice for localizing the tumor in pheochromocytoma.

Pheochromocytoma is a catecholamine-secreting tumor derived from the chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla.

Clinical features of pheochromocytoma are due to the autonomic effects of excess epinephrine and norepinephrine.

* Weight loss is due to the increase in catecholamines which increase basal metabolism.

* Pallor is due to alpha 1-mediated vasoconstriction.

* Abdominal pain with nausea and vomiting is commonly seen.

Diagnosis of pheochromocytoma requires biochemical testing followed by imaging.

* Urinary and plasma levels of catecholamines and metanephrines

* MRI is the investigation of choice for localizing the tumor

* MIBG Scintigraphy and PET Scans like Ga- DOTATE, DOPA- or FDG- PET can be used for extra-adrenal tumors and metastases

Treatment of pheochromocytoma:

Surgical resection of the tumor is the definitive treatment. Preoperatively, an alpha-receptor blocker (phenoxybenzamine) is given to control the effects produced by excess catecholamines. Beta-blockers are administered to manage tachycardia once sufficient alpha blockade has been established.This is to prevent unrestricted alpha-mediated vasoconstriction.

Following surgery, yearly follow-ups lifelong should be done.
questions.learning: MRI MRI is the investigation of choice for localizing the tumor in pheochromocytoma. Pheochromocytoma is a catecholamine-secreting tumor derived from the chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which health program does the Danish International Developmental Agency support in India?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Blindness

The Danish International Development Agency (DANIDA) assists in the development of services under the National Blindness Control Program.

DANIDA (Danish International Development Agency) is the development cooperation arm of the Danish government, working to support sustainable development, poverty reduction, and humanitarian assistance worldwide.

It primarily focuses on sectors such as health, education, human rights, climate change, and economic growth in developing countries. DANIDA collaborates with governments, NGOs, and international organizations to implement projects that enhance social and economic progress. Its initiatives emphasize capacity building, infrastructure development, and improving healthcare access, particularly in low-income nations.

Through strategic partnerships and funding, DANIDA plays a crucial role in promoting global development and achieving the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Koebner phenomenon is seen in which one of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Psoriasis

Koebner phenomenon (Isomorphic response) refers to the development of characteristic skin lesions at sites of skin trauma in patients with certain dermatological diseases. Trauma may include scratching, surgical incisions, burns, tattoos, or pressure.

Psoriasis is the classical disease associated with the Koebner phenomenon. In psoriasis, new psoriatic plaques develop 7–14 days after skin injury.

Why not the other options?

• B. Acne vulgaris: Does not exhibit the Koebner phenomenon.
• C. Behçet’s disease: Characteristically shows the Pathergy phenomenon, in which a sterile pustule or papule develops after a needle prick, not the Koebner phenomenon.
• D. Leprosy: Does not classically demonstrate the Koebner phenomenon.
questions.learning: Psoriasis Koebner phenomenon (Isomorphic response) refers to the development of characteristic skin lesions at sites of skin trauma in patients with certain dermatological diseases.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following is incorrect regarding High-Quality CPR?
options: Chest compression to Rescue breath ratio is 30:2
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Depth of compression must be 3-4cm

High-quality adult CPR requires compression depth of at least 5 cm (about 2 inches) to generate adequate cardiac output. Recommended rate is 100–120/min with complete chest recoil between compressions.

| Parameter | Recommended Value

| --------- | -----------------

| Compression rate | 100–120/min

| Compression depth | 5–6 cm (2–2.4 inches)

| Compression : ventilation | 30 : 2

| Chest recoil | Must be complete

| Interruptions | <10 seconds

During chest recoil: Negative intrathoracic pressure develops

This allows:

• Venous blood to return to the heart
• Cardiac chambers to refill

If recoil is incomplete:

• Cardiac output decreases
• Coronary perfusion falls

The standard compression-to-ventilation ratio is 30:2 for single rescuer CPR.

Thus, a depth of 3–4 cm is inadequate, making option D incorrect.
questions.learning: Depth of compression must be 3-4cm High-quality adult CPR requires compression depth of at least 5 cm (about 2 inches) to generate adequate cardiac output.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the FIGO stage of endometrial carcinoma when the disease has extended to involve the vagina?
questions.explanation: The FIGO staging for endometrial carcinoma defines Stage III as local and/or regional spread of the tumor. Specifically, Stage IIIb (Option B) refers to tumors that have spread to the vagina and/or the parametrium. Stage IIIa (Option A) involves the tumor spreading to the serosa of the corpus uteri and/or the adnexa (ovaries/tubes). Stage IIIc (Option C) indicates spread to the pelvic and/or para-aortic lymph nodes. Stage IVa (Option D) is more advanced and involves the invasion of the bladder and/or bowel mucosa . Accurate staging is essential for determining the prognosis and the need for adjuvant therapies such as radiation or chemotherapy. Because vaginal involvement is the specific criteria for the "b" sub-category of Stage III, Stage IIIb is the correct diagnostic stage. Management of Stage IIIb disease often requires a combination of surgery and radiation therapy
questions.learning: The FIGO staging for endometrial carcinoma defines Stage III as local and/or regional spread of the tumor. Specifically, Stage IIIb (Option B) refers to tumors that have spread to the vagina and/or the parametrium.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text:
Arrange the following anesthetic agents on the basis of their potency.

Nitrous oxide

Halothane

Isoflurane

Methoxyflurane
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Methoxyflurane> Halothane> Isoflurane> Nitrous oxide

The potency of the inhaled anesthetics given above can be arranged as methoxyflurane> halothane> isoflurane> nitrous oxide. It is due to the change in the agents' minimum alveolar concentration (MAC).

The minimum alveolar concentration (MAC) of an inhaled anesthetic is the lowest concentration required to prevent movement in response to a defined noxious stimulus in 50% of subjects. It is a measure of the potency of inhalational anesthetics. So, the lower the MAC value, the lower the concentration of anesthetic drug required, implying the drug is more potent.

MAC values (expressed as a '%' of 1 atmosphere) of some anesthetic agents:

• Nitrous oxide with a MAC value of 104 is the least potent inhaled anesthetic
• Methoxyflurane – MAC- 0.2 (most potent)
• Desflurane: 6.0
• Sevoflurane– 2.05
• Isoflurane – 1.28
• Halothane – 0.75
questions.learning: Methoxyflurane> Halothane> Isoflurane> Nitrous oxide The potency of the inhaled anesthetics given above can be arranged as methoxyflurane> halothane> isoflurane> nitrous oxide.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 35-year-old male presents with recurrent gastric ulcers and a nodule in the medial wall of the second part of the duodenum. What is the next step in the management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Serum gastrin levels

Recurrent gastric ulcers and a nodule in the medial wall of the 2nd part of the duodenum suggest Zollinger-Ellison syndrome occurs due to a gastrin-secreting tumor (gastrinoma).

• Most gastrinomas occur in the duodenum or pancreas, especially within the gastrinoma triangle (pancreas–duodenum region).
• So the first investigation —> check serum gastrin levels
• Initial test: Fasting serum gastrin (stop PPIs if possible).
• Diagnostic finding: Very high gastrin (>1000 pg/mL) with gastric pH <2.
• If gastrin is moderately elevated (100–1000 pg/mL), do the Secretin stimulation test → rise in gastrin ≥120 pg/mL confirms ZES.
• Localize tumor with Ga-68 DOTATATE PET/CT, CT/MRI, or EUS.
• Screen for Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 1 association.
questions.learning: Serum gastrin levels Recurrent gastric ulcers and a nodule in the medial wall of the 2nd part of the duodenum suggest Zollinger-Ellison syndrome occurs due to a gastrin-secreting tumor (gastrinoma). • Most gastrinomas occur in the duodenum or pancreas,…

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 10-year-old male child came to the casualty with difficulty in walking and pain in the perianal region. On subjecting the specimen from the perianal region to a test, it produces yellow needle-shaped rhombic crystals with picric acid. What is the test done?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Barberio test

The test done in the scenario is the Barberio test.

Barberio is used to detect seminal fluid. When a saturated aqueous or alcoholic solution of picric acid is added to the spermatic fluid, yellow needle-shaped rhombic crystals of spermine picrate are produced.

Other options:

Option B: Florence test is used to detect semen. If semen is present, dark brown rhombic or needle-shaped crystals of choline iodide appear immediately

Option C: The Teichmann test (hemin crystal test) is used to detect bloodstains. If bloodstain is present, faint yellowish-red to brownish-black rhombic crystals of hemin or hematin chloride appear. When hydrogen peroxide is added, the hematin crystals give bubbles of gas.

Option D: The acid phosphatase test is a quantitative test for the presence of acid phosphatase enzyme in the semen. High levels of acid phosphatase from prostatic secretions are present in seminal stains (Normal vaginal secretions have low levels of acid phosphatase). Positive reactions are found till 36 hours after which the enzyme levels fall and disappear within 72 hours. In the absence of demonstrable sperm or aspermia, this test can be considered conclusive.
questions.learning: Barberio test — The test done in the scenario is the Barberio test. Barberio is used to detect seminal fluid.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 28-year-old married woman who is anxious to conceive presents with copious vaginal discharge, without any itching. Her last menstrual period was 13 days ago. What is the cause of her vaginal discharge?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Physiological

The given clinical scenario of a young woman with copious, non-pruritic (without itching) vaginal discharge occurring 13 days after menstrual period (period of ovulation) is most likely to be leucorrhoea (physiological).

The term leucorrhoea can be used in conditions where normal vaginal secretion is increased in amount. An increase in this normal vaginal secretion develops physiologically:

• At puberty
• At ovulation
• During pregnancy
• During the premenstrual phase, occasionally

It may be cervical or vaginal in origin. A speculum examination of the vagina can distinguish between the two. If the discharge is cervical in origin, an excessive mucoid discharge will be visible at the external os.

Normal discharge appears clear or white, without any odor or itching, and will have a pH of 3.8-4.2.

Other options:

Option A: Candidiasis is caused by infection with Candida albicans and presents with pruritus, burning, and dysuria with vulvar erythema, edema, and excoriations. A curdy white discharge will be present.

Option B: Bacterial vaginosis is caused by an alteration in the normal vaginal flora and presents without itching and a malodorous grey-white discharge. It is diagnosed using Amsel's criteria, where at least three of the four following criteria should be present to confirm the diagnosis:

• Homogenous vaginal discharge
• Vaginal pH > 4.5
• Amine-like odor on adding KOH (Whiff test positive)
• Clue cells (>20% of cells)

Option C: Trichomoniasis is caused by Trichomonas vaginalis and presents with a copious, frothy, offensive yellow-green discharge with vaginal soreness or irritation and urinary frequency. On examination, the vagina looks red and inflamed. The inflamed cervix looks like a strawberry with punctate hemorrhagic spots.
questions.learning: Physiological — The given clinical scenario of a young woman with copious, non-pruritic (without itching) vaginal discharge occurring 13 days after menstrual period (period of ovulation) is most likely to be leucorrhoea (physiological).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A patient with 12 weeks amenorrhea presents with vaginal bleeding. On examination, the cervical os is open and the uterus is of 14 weeks size. USG shows a snowstorm appearance. The next best step in the management is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Suction and evacuation

The clinical scenario of vaginal bleeding, an enlarged uterus exceeding the corresponding period of amenorrhea, and a snowstorm appearance on USG strongly indicates a diagnosis of a hydatidiform mole. Suction and evacuation is the next best step in the management of this patient.

Hydatidiform mole is an abnormal condition of the placenta, characterized by partly degenerative and partly proliferative changes in the chorionic villi. It may be either partial or complete.

The patient presents with a characteristic history of abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding or spotting, and vomiting during the first trimester. Also, there may be a history of passing grape-like vesicles vaginally. On examination, the size of the uterus is larger for gestational age and the fetal heart sounds are absent.

A USG scan shows a snowstorm appearance which is characteristic of a complete mole.

Suction and evacuation is the treatment of choice. Hysterectomy (option D) is done only if there is uncontrolled hemorrhage or perforation during surgical evacuation or if the age of the patient is above 35 years and has completed her family.

Serum hCG levels (option B) are checked within 48 hours of evacuation and are used as a baseline for future comparisons. It is then checked every week till it normalizes, which usually takes around 4 to 8 weeks. After the hCG values return to normal, a regular follow-up is done monthly for 6 months.
questions.learning: Suction and evacuation — The clinical scenario of vaginal bleeding, an enlarged uterus exceeding the corresponding period of amenorrhea, and a snowstorm appearance on USG strongly indicates a diagnosis of a hydatidiform mole.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In what amino acid form is ammonia transported from the brain to the liver for detoxification?
questions.explanation: Ammonia is a toxic byproduct of nitrogen metabolism, particularly dangerous to the central nervous system. In the brain, excess ammonia is detoxified by being combined with glutamate to form Glutamine, a reaction catalyzed by the enzyme glutamine synthetase. Glutamine is a non-toxic, neutral amino acid that can safely circulate in the blood to be transported to the liver (and kidneys). Once in the liver, glutamine is broken back down into glutamate and ammonia by glutaminase, and the ammonia is then converted into urea for excretion. Glutamate (Option A) itself cannot cross the blood-brain barrier effectively for transport. Alanine (Option B) is the primary form of ammonia transport from skeletal muscle to the liver (via the Cahill cycle). Glycine (Option C) is involved in various metabolic pathways but not primary systemic ammonia transport. The "glutamine shuttle" is essential for preventing hyperammonemia, which can lead to cerebral edema, encephalopathy, and potentially fatal brain damage in liver failure
questions.learning: Ammonia is a toxic byproduct of nitrogen metabolism, particularly dangerous to the central nervous system. In the brain, excess ammonia is detoxified by being combined with glutamate to form Glutamine, a reaction catalyzed by the enzyme glutamine synthetase.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Following a road traffic accident, a 30-year-old man presents to the emergency department with maxillofacial trauma and inability to open the mouth. To establish an airway, an emergency laryngotomy is performed. Where is the opening made?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cricothyroid membrane

In laryngotomy, an opening is made on the cricothyroid membrane.

Laryngotomy is also called cricothyrotomy or mini-tracheostomy. It is done as an emergency life-saving procedure to buy some time to allow a patient to be carried to the operation theatre. Once stable, it is replaced by intubation or tracheostomy.

Most of the laryngeal foreign bodies are arrested above the vocal cords, i.e. above the middle of the thyroid cartilage. Thus, an effective airway can be provided by piercing the cricothyroid membrane.
questions.learning: Cricothyroid membrane — In laryngotomy, an opening is made on the cricothyroid membrane. Laryngotomy is also called cricothyrotomy or mini-tracheostomy.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A man falls into a deep sleep with one arm under his head. Upon waking, he is unable to move the arm, though he still feels tingling and pain. The reason for the loss of motor function while maintaining pain sensation is?
options: B fibers are more susceptible to pressure than A fibers
A fibers are more sensitive to pressure than C fibers
C fibers are more sensitive to pressure than A fibers
Motor nerves are more affected by sleep than sensory nerves
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. A fibers are more sensitive to pressure than C fibers

In the above scenario, the patient has developed paresis (partial paralysis), but the pain sensation is intact (no numbness). This is because A fibers that carry motor, touch, and pressure sensations are more susceptible to pressure changes/compression than C fibers that carry pain sensations.

The compression of a large-diameter nerve fiber leads to a reversible physiologic conduction block, or neuropraxia. The susceptibility of the nerve fibers to pressure is A>B>C. This is responsible for Saturday night or Sunday morning paralysis.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman presents to you with hair loss for the past three months. She tested positive for COVID-19 eight months ago. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Telogen effluvium

The most likely diagnosis based on the clinical scenario is telogen effluvium.

The hair follicle goes through three phases known as the hair cycle:

• Anagen: Phase of active hair growth
• Catagen: Involutionary phase
• Telogen: Time period between catagen and next anagen phase

Telogen effluvium is a type of nonscarring alopecia that is marked by diffuse shedding of normal hair. This occurs due to premature termination of the anagen phase of the hair cycle.  It can be either acute or chronic.

Acute telogen effluvium occurs 2-3 months after a stressful event such as high fever, surgery, starvation, and hemorrhage. Hormonal fluctuations during the postpartum period can trigger it (telogen gravidarum). Telogen effluvium can result in a diffuse reduction in hair density but never total baldness. It generally resolves spontaneously.

Chronic telogen effluvium is used to describe the diffuse shedding of telogen hair for more than 6 months. Common causes include thyroid disorders, iron-deficiency anemia, and malnutrition.

Other options:

Option A - Tinea capitis is used to describe an infection of the scalp by the dermatophyte group of fungi. The most common pathogenic species are Trichophyton tonsurans and Trichophyton violaceum. The presentation can vary from hair breakage associated with scaling to widespread inflammatory mass on the scalp.

Clinical variants of tinea capitis:

• Endothrix - A non-inflammatory type in which multiple black dots are present within the areas of alopecia
• Ectothrix - A mild inflammatory type in which single or multiple scaly patches with hair loss are seen
• Kerion - A severe inflammatory type that presents with an inflammatory mass with thick crusting and matting of hair with pus and sinus formation
• Favus - Characterized by the presence of yellowish, cup‐shaped crusts known as scutula that develop around hair follicles

Observation under KOH mount is used for diagnosis.

Option C - Trichotillomania (trichotillosis) is considered an obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) spectrum disorder, marked by gratification from pulling one's own hair. It could be associated with underlying anxieties or depression. The vertex region of the scalp is most commonly involved. Scalp histology will show perifollicular hemorrhages and intrafollicular pigment casts.

Option D - Androgenic hair loss is used to describe a progressive decrease in hair fiber production. Dihydrotestosterone, an androgenic metabolite, is implicated in the etiology. Female-pattern hair loss involves the mid-frontal scalp diffusely. There is no or minimal involvement of the temporal region.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Calculate the net filtration pressure across the GBM for a patient with Glomerular ultrafiltration coefficient = 6 Glomerular hydrostatic pressure =45 Glomerular capillary oncotic pressure =20 Bowman’s capsule hydrostatic pressure =10 Bowman’s capsule oncotic pressure =0
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 15 mmHg

Net filtration pressure = Hydrostatic pressure in the glomerular capillaries - Pressure in Bowman's capsule - Oncotic pressure in the glomerular capillaries.

Net filtration pressure= [PG -PB- πG+ πB]

Therefore,

Net filtration pressure      = (45-10-20+0)

= 25-10

= 15 mmHg

Note:

Here, just the net filtration pressure is asked and not the GFR.

GFR= Kf [PG -PB- πG+ πB]
questions.learning: 15 mmHg Net filtration pressure = Hydrostatic pressure in the glomerular capillaries - Pressure in Bowman's capsule - Oncotic pressure in the glomerular capillaries.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following compounds is predominantly responsible for the disinfecting property of bleaching powder?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hypochlorous acid

The disinfectant property of bleaching powder is predominantly due to the action of hypochlorous acid. It is 70-80 times more effective than hypochlorite ions.

Bleaching powder, also known as chlorinated lime (CaOCl2), has 33 per cent of chlorine in it. When chlorine is added to water, there is the formation of hydrochloric and hypochlorous acids. The hydrochloric acid is neutralized by the alkalinity of the water. The hypochlorous acid ionizes to form hydrogen ions and hypochlorite ions, as follows:

H2O + Cl2 → HCl + HOCl

HOCl → H + OCl
questions.learning: Hypochlorous acid — The disinfectant property of bleaching powder is predominantly due to the action of hypochlorous acid. It is 70-80 times more effective than hypochlorite ions.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 50-year-old man with a history of repeated pain over the medial canthus and chronic use of nasal decongestants presents to the OPD with high-grade fever, chills, headache, and bilateral proptosis. On eliciting further history, it was confirmed that proptosis began in the right eye, and a few days later, the left eye was also affected. Fundoscopy reveals papilloedema. On examination, damage to the abducens nerve was noted. Which of the following ocular movements will be impaired?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Lateral

The given clinical scenario, with recurrent episodes of headache and pain over the medial canthus and repeated use of nasal decongestants, suggests that the patient was suffering from sinusitis, which has most likely resulted in cavernous sinus thrombosis, and the injury of the abducens nerve will affect the lateral ocular movement as it supplies the lateral rectus muscle of the eye.

Cavernous sinus syndrome (CSS) is a rare condition characterized by ophthalmoplegia, proptosis, ocular and conjunctival congestion, trigeminal sensory loss, and Horner’s syndrome. These signs and symptoms result from the involvement of the cranial nerves passing through the cavernous sinus. The cavernous sinus syndrome affects III, IV, V, and VI cranial nerves.

In cavernous sinus thrombosis, proptosis is initially unilateral but soon becomes bilateral due to the spread of infection to the contralateral sinus through the intercavernous communication. Also, cavernous sinus thrombosis presents with high-grade fever with chills, rigor, and headache.
On the other hand, orbital cellulitis and panophthalmitis are unilateral conditions

The cavernous sinuses are two large venous plexuses that lie on either side of the body of the sphenoid bone, extending from the superior orbital fissure to the apex of the petrous temporal bone.

Structures related to the lateral wall of the cavernous sinuses are the oculomotor nerve, trochlear nerve and the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve. Within the cavernous sinus are the abducens nerve and the cavernous part of the internal carotid artery.

Image showing cavernous sinus and the structures related to it.

Orbital apex syndrome is a condition similar to cavernous sinus syndrome with retro-orbital pain and involvement of 2,3,4,5 and 6 cranial nerves. The differentiating feature is the optic nerve involvement leading to early visual loss and afferent pupillary defect.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What is the definition of Electron Volt (EV)?
options: The speed of an electron in a magnetic field
The force acting on an electron in an electric field
The energy gained by an electron when accelerated through a potential difference of one volt.
The kinetic energy of an electron at rest in a vacuum
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. The energy gained by an electron when accelerated through a potential difference of one volt.

An electronvolt (eV) is defined as the energy required to accelerate a single electron at rest through an electron potential difference of one volt in a vacuum. This is different from the electrical potential difference applied to the X-ray tube in terms of kilovolts (kV). However, the kV applied to an X-ray tube is approximately equal to the maximum photon energy achievable by a photon (keVmax).
questions.learning: The energy gained by an electron when accelerated through a potential difference of one volt. An electronvolt (eV) is defined as the energy required to accelerate a single electron at rest through an electron potential difference of one volt in a vacuum.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A lady presents with abdominal pain. USG reveals multiple gall stones with no wall thickening. CBD diameter is 12 mm and serum bilirubin was 0.8. Alkaline phosphatase is 380 and GGT is raised by 5 times. What is the next best step of management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. MRCP

In this clinical scenario, a patient with gallstones, a dilated common bile duct, and an elevated alkaline phosphatase level raises suspicion for common bile duct stones. The next best step would be to perform magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) to confirm their presence.

A dilated common bile duct (>8 mm) detected on ultrasound in a patient with gallstones, jaundice, biliary pain and an abnormal liver function panel (elevated bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and transaminases; but these can be normal in some cases) strongly indicates the presence of common bile duct stones (choledocholithiasis).

If there is uncertainty regarding the presence of bile duct stones, as in this case where bilirubin levels are normal, MRCP offers precise anatomical visualization and exhibits high sensitivity and specificity for diagnosing choledocholithiasis.

While endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) is also highly effective in diagnosing choledocholithiasis, due to its invasive nature and the risks associated with the procedure, it is rarely used as a purely diagnostic modality. Instead, it is reserved for cases in which a therapeutic intervention, such as stone extraction or sphincterotomy, is planned.

Treatment options:

• ERCP along with sphincterotomy and stone removal.
• Laparoscopic common bile duct exploration
• Open common bile duct exploration is only done when endoscopic and laparoscopic methods are not feasible or when concomitant biliary drainage is needed.
questions.learning: MRCP — In this clinical scenario, a patient with gallstones, a dilated common bile duct, and an elevated alkaline phosphatase level raises suspicion for common bile duct stones.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following enzymes are involved in gluconeogenesis? A. Pyruvate carboxylase B. Phosphoenol pyruvate kinase C. Hexokinase D. Pyruvate kinase E. Glucose 6 phosphatase
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. A and E only

Among the given options, A and E are correct. Pyruvate carboxylase and Glucose-6-phosphatase are enzymes used in gluconeogenesis.

Glycolysis and gluconeogenesis are 2 metabolic pathways in opposite directions (glucose being the substrate and product respectively). But a few reactions are not reversible in glycolysis. So a different pathway is used or a different enzyme is used by the body to make the reactions feasible.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following vaccines is C/I in pregnancy?
questions.explanation: Live attenuated vaccines, such as the Varicella vaccine, are strictly contraindicated during pregnancy due to the potential risk of fetal infection and congenital varicella syndrome. Other live vaccines to avoid include MMR and Yellow Fever. In contrast, inactivated influenza (Option A) is recommended to protect both mother and newborn. Rabies vaccine (Option C) is safe and mandatory for post-exposure prophylaxis as the disease is fatal. TDaP (Option D) is recommended during the third trimester to provide passive immunity to the infant against pertussis. Therefore, while killed vaccines and toxoids are generally safe, live viral vaccines like varicella pose a theoretical risk to fetal development and must be administered either before conception or postpartum
questions.learning: Live attenuated vaccines, such as the Varicella vaccine, are strictly contraindicated during pregnancy due to the potential risk of fetal infection and congenital varicella syndrome.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which anticoagulant is used in the test tube for estimating Hba1c?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. EDTA

EDTA is used in test tubes as an anticoagulant for estimating HbA1C.

EDTA (ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid) is used for estimating HbA1c because it prevents clotting and preserves the integrity of the red blood cells for accurate measurement of glycated hemoglobin. It is a chelating agent, that works by binding to calcium ions in the blood.

Other Options:

Option A: Warfarin is an oral anticoagulant. It is not used in blood collection tubes. It is a therapeutic anticoagulant, not suitable for preserving blood samples for laboratory testing, such as HbA1c.

Option B: Sodium Fluoride is used in grey-top tubes for blood glucose testing. It is specific for glucose preservation, not for HbA1c estimation, as it does not effectively prevent clotting or preserve red blood cells.

Option D: Heparin is used in green-top tubes to collect plasma samples. It can interfere with some analytical methods for measuring glycated hemoglobin and does not preserve red blood cells effectively for this purpose.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: After undergoing a vasectomy, for how long is a patient advised to continue using alternative contraceptive methods??
questions.explanation: Sterility is not achieved immediately after a vasectomy because viable sperm remain in the distal portion of the vas deferens. Patients are advised to use alternative contraception for approximately 3 months or until they have had at least 20 ejaculations. Confirmation of sterility is mandatory through semen analysis, which must show azoospermia in two consecutive samples. Option A (1 month) and Option B (2 months) are insufficient timeframes, as studies show that while 80% of men are sterile by 6 weeks, nearly 10% still have sperm present at 10 weeks. Option D (6 months) is longer than the standard clinical recommendation for initial follow-up. Failure to adhere to this waiting period is a common cause of "failed" vasectomy and unintended pregnancy. Therefore, the 3-month guideline provides a safe buffer for the physiological clearance of stored sperm
questions.learning: Sterility is not achieved immediately after a vasectomy because viable sperm remain in the distal portion of the vas deferens. Patients are advised to use alternative contraception for approximately 3 months or until they have had at least 20 ejaculations.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Following a surgical procedure, a patient develops a characteristic clinical sign. Injury to which specific nerve is most likely responsible for this finding?
questions.explanation: The image depicts the classic “hand of benediction”, seen when a patient with median nerve injury attempts to make a fist. In this condition, the index and middle fingers fail to flex, while the ring and little fingers flex normally due to intact ulnar nerve function. This occurs because the median nerve supplies the flexor digitorum superficialis and the lateral half of flexor digitorum profundus, which are responsible for flexion of the index and middle fingers. This deformity is typically observed in proximal median nerve injuries, such as those occurring at the elbow or during surgical procedures. Other options are incorrect: (A) Radial nerve injury causes wrist drop, not finger flexion defects. (C) Ulnar nerve injury leads to clawing of the ring and little fingers at rest, not inability to flex the index and middle fingers. (D) Long thoracic nerve injury causes winged scapula, unrelated to hand movements. Thus, the inability to flex the lateral two digits confirms a median nerve injury

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: In a 70-year-old patient with schizophrenia who is being treated for drug-induced Parkinsonism, which medication is most likely responsible for anticholinergic side effects such as constipation, blurred vision, and dry mouth?
questions.explanation: Drug-induced Parkinsonism is a common side effect of traditional antipsychotic medications used for schizophrenia. To manage these motor symptoms, clinicians often prescribe anticholinergic medications like Benzhexol (Trihexyphenidyl) (Option C). These drugs block acetylcholine to restore the dopamine-acetylcholine balance in the basal ganglia. However, they cause significant systemic anticholinergic side effects, including dry mouth (xerostomia), blurred vision (due to mydriasis/cycloplegia), and constipation. Lithium (Option A) causes polyuria and tremors. Pramipexole (Option B), a dopamine agonist, causes nausea and orthostatic hypotension. Selegiline (Option D), an MAO-B inhibitor, is less associated with this classic anticholinergic triad. Therefore, given the specific combination of symptoms—dry mouth, constipation, and blurred vision—Benzhexol is the definitive medication responsible for the patient's distress. These side effects are particularly bothersome in elderly patients and can exacerbate pre-existing glaucoma or urinary retention. **************
questions.learning: Drug-induced Parkinsonism is a common side effect of traditional antipsychotic medications used for schizophrenia. To manage these motor symptoms, clinicians often prescribe anticholinergic medications like Benzhexol (Trihexyphenidyl) (Option C).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 7-year-old boy weighing 30 Kgs has been posted for surgical resection of a tumor. What is the daily maintenance fluid required for this child while he’s NPO?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1700 mL

The daily maintenance fluid required for a child weighing 30 Kg is 1700 ml.

Bodyweight method for calculating the daily maintenance fluid volume (also known as Holliday-Segar method) is used.

Bodyweight
Fluid required per day

0–10 Kg
100 mL/Kg

11–20 Kg
1000 mL + 50 mL/Kg for each Kg >10 Kg

>20 Kg
1500 mL + 20 mL/Kg for each Kg >20 kg

Calculation:

In the question, the weight of the child is given as 30 Kgs.

So, the formula for >20 Kg is used.

1500 mL + (20 mL x weight more than 20 Kgs)

Since the child weight is 30 Kgs, he/she is 10 Kgs more.

Therefore, fluid required is

= 1500 mL + (20 mL x 10)

= 1500 mL + 200 mL

= 1700 mL.
questions.learning: 1700 mL The daily maintenance fluid required for a child weighing 30 Kg is 1700 ml. Bodyweight method for calculating the daily maintenance fluid volume (also known as Holliday-Segar method) is used.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: You are shown several vaccine vials with different Vaccine Vial Monitor (VVM) stages. Based on the condition of the VVMs shown in the image, which of the following vaccine vials is suitable for use?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 only

A Vaccine Vial Monitor (VVM) indicates cumulative heat exposure of a vaccine.

A vial is usable only when the inner square is lighter than the outer circle (VVM stages 1 and 2).

Once the inner square becomes equal to or darker than the outer circle (stages 3 and 4), the vaccine has lost potency and must be discarded.

Therefore, only vials 1 and 2 are suitable for use.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is the classical triad of acute cholangitis?
questions.explanation: The classical clinical triad for acute cholangitis is known as Charcot's triad, which consists of right upper quadrant pain, jaundice, and fever. This condition usually results from an obstruction in the biliary tree (often by stones) leading to a secondary bacterial infection. Regarding the distractors, shock (Option B) is not part of Charcot's triad but is a component of Reynolds' pentad, which also includes altered mental status and indicates severe, life-threatening obstructive suppurative cholangitis. While increased white blood cells (↑WBC) and elevated bilirubin (Options C and D) are common laboratory findings in this disease, they are not formal components of the recognized clinical triad. Early recognition of Charcot's triad is essential for initiating prompt antibiotic therapy and biliary decompression to prevent sepsis. Therefore, pain, jaundice, and fever are the defining features. is definitive for BCC

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A child presents with a fever and a rash. Urine examination showed cells with owl's eye appearance. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cytomegalovirus

The most likely causative agent is cytomegalovirus (CMV) based on the clinical symptoms and the presence of the owl's eye appearance on urinary examination.

CMV is the largest virus in the herpes family of viruses. It causes the following conditions:

• Immunocompetent individuals - asymptomatic or mononucleosis-like infection such as fever and rash
• Neonates - devastating systemic infections
• Immunosuppressed individuals - serious, life-threatening, disseminated CMV infections of the lungs (pneumonitis) and gastrointestinal tract (colitis)

CMV spreads through contact with salivary secretions and sexual contact, blood transfusion, and organ transplantation.

Laboratory diagnosis is by recovery of the virus from urine, saliva, or other bodily fluids into human fibroblast cells. Antibody demonstration using ELISA is used for diagnosis of primary infection.

A cytomegalic pneumocyte containing characteristic intranuclear basophilic inclusion surrounded by a clear halo known as an owl’s eye appearance.

Other options:

Option B: Epstein Barr virus: Conditions associated with EBV infection are

• Glandular fever (infectious mononucleosis): fever, pharyngitis, and posterior cervical lymphadenopathy
• Hodgkin lymphoma
• Non-Hodgkin lymphoma
• Burkitt's lymphoma
• Nasopharyngeal carcinoma
• EBV‐associated lymphoproliferative disease

Option C: Herpes simplex virus causes cutaneous infections like herpes labialis caused by viral reactivation in febrile patients. It presents as blisters around the mouth, cheeks, and forehead. Gingivostomatitis and pharyngitis are the most frequent manifestations of primary herpes infections. HSV esophagitis presents as dysphagia, sub-sternal pain, and weight loss.

Option D: Acute congenital toxoplasmosis may manifest as fever, jaundice, petechial rashes, microphthalmia, cataract, glaucoma, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, myocarditis, cerebral calcifications, and chorioretinitis.

Most infections in adults who are immunocompetent are usually asymptomatic. Active progression of infection is more likely in immunocompromised individuals.
questions.learning: Cytomegalovirus — The most likely causative agent is cytomegalovirus (CMV) based on the clinical symptoms and the presence of the owl's eye appearance on urinary examination.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Cilnidipine does not cause reflex tachycardia because it blocks:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. N-type calcium channels

Cilnidipine blocks:

• L-type calcium channels → vasodilation
• N-type calcium channels → ↓ sympathetic neurotransmitter release

Why less reflex tachycardia?

N-type blockade reduces norepinephrine release from sympathetic nerve terminals.

Thus:

• Vasodilation occurs
• Reflex sympathetic activation is suppressed

High-yield comparison:

| Drug | Special feature

| ---- | ---------------

| Amlodipine | L-type blocker

| Cilnidipine | L + N type blocker

• Fourth degree- the external anal sphincter is torn and anal mucosa is also involved

A central tear of the perineum is when the head penetrates first through the posterior vaginal wall, then through the perineal body and appears through the skin of the perineum. It usually occurs in patients with a contracted outlet.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following poison can be found even in skeletonised remains of the body?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Arsenic

Arsenic can be found even in skeletonized remains of the body.

It becomes fixed in the cancellous tissues of the long bones by the conversion of phosphates to arsenates. The elimination of arsenic in this form is much slower and can be detected in the bones for several years after death.

Heavy metals such as lead, copper, mercury, including metalloids like arsenic and antimony, may be found in bones for a prolonged period in cases of chronic poisoning. They are also deposited in hair, nails, etc. For these reasons, when heavy metal poisoning is suspected, these specimens are collected in addition to the routine viscera and body fluids.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is the preferred treatment for Plasmodium falciparum malaria?
questions.explanation: Due to widespread resistance, chloroquine (Option A) is no longer effective for most cases of P. falciparum. The current global and WHO standard for treating uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria is Artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT). This involves pairing a rapid-acting artemisinin derivative (like artemether) with a longer-acting partner drug (like lumefantrine). This dual approach ensures rapid clearance of parasites and prevents the development of further resistance. Primaquine (Option C) is primarily used to clear the dormant liver stages (hypnozoites) of P. vivax and P. ovale and should be avoided in P. falciparum unless as a single dose to reduce gametocyte transmission. Doxycycline (Option D) is used for malaria prophylaxis or as an adjunct in severe cases, but not as the primary treatment for uncomplicated falciparum malaria. Prompt diagnosis with a rapid test or microscopy and immediate initiation of ACT are life-saving, as falciparum malaria can rapidly progress to severe, fatal complications if left untreated
questions.learning: Due to widespread resistance, chloroquine (Option A) is no longer effective for most cases of P. falciparum. The current global and WHO standard for treating uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria is Artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A government plans to outline tobacco control laws. What is the level of prevention here?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Primary prevention

Creating tobacco control laws is a method of primary prevention.

Making tobacco control laws targets smokers who are already exposed to risk of smoking, who have not yet developed any disease. This aims to reduce smoking which is essentially a reduction of risk factor which is a primary prevention stratergy.

Primary prevention is defined as an action taken prior to the onset of disease, whose aim is to prevent the disease from occuring. Its target population is healthy individuals. It commonly institutes activities that limit risk exposure or increase the immunity of individuals at risk to prevent a disease from progressing in a susceptible individual. They approaches can be as follows:

* Population (mass) strategy where the target group is the whole population

* A high-risk strategy where the target group is limited to the people who are most at risk of developing a particular disease.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Identify the type of fingerprint pattern depicted in the image below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Whorls

Understand the basic fingerprint (dermatoglyphic) patterns used in forensic identification. A whorl is characterized by concentric or spiral ridges with two triradii (deltas) and is the second most common fingerprint pattern after loops. Fingerprints are unique, permanent, and remain unchanged throughout life, making them a reliable method of personal identification.

Why not the other options?

• A. Loops: The most common pattern (60–70%), with ridges entering from one side, looping around, and exiting the same side; one delta is present.
• C. Arches: The least common pattern (5–10%), with ridges passing from one side to the other without looping; no delta is present.
• D. Composite: A mixed pattern containing features of two or more basic patterns (e.g., central pocket loop, double loop, accidental); not seen in this image.

| Fingerprint Pattern | Key Feature | No. of Deltas

| ------------------- | ----------- | -------------

| Loop | Ridges loop back to the same side | 1

| Whorl | Circular/spiral concentric ridges | 2

| Arch | Ridges pass straight across | 0

| Composite | Combination of basic patterns | Usually 2 or more

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The image below shows a pressure sore. Which stage does this belong to ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Stage 4

The given image shows a pressure sore with extensive tissue destruction, including damage to the muscle layer and thus it belongs to stage 4.

Pressure sores also referred known as bed sores, pressure ulcers and decubitus ulcers are ulcers that occur due to prolonged pressure on certain sites thereby leading to tissue necrosis. The commonest sites involved are ischium, greater trochanter, sacrum, heel, malleolus (lateral >medial), and occiput. Paraplegic patients, elderly patients, and severely ill patients are at a higher risk of developing pressure sores.

They are staged as:

• Stage 1 - Erythema with no blanching and no breach in the epidermis.
• Stage 2- Partial-thickness skin loss with epidermal and dermal involvement.
• Stage 3- Full-thickness skin loss with intact fascia but the involvement of the subcutaneous tissue.
• Stage 4- Full-thickness skin loss extending to the fascia with massive tissue destruction and involvement of muscle, bone, tendon, or joint.

Management is primarily proper skin care with pressure dispersion cushions, air-fluidized beds, and urinary or fecal diversion if required. Patients who are bed-bound should be turned once in 2 hours. Those in a wheelchair should lift themselves off the seat for 10 seconds every 10 minutes.

Surgery is the last resort and is done after a proper initial debridement and vacuum-assisted closure. Vacuum-assisted closure is a wound closure technique in which negative pressure is applied to the wound which leads to a decrease in edema. This hastens the debridement and formation of granulation tissue. Skin flaps with a muscle are also used for closure.

questions.text: A diabetic, hypertensive, and post-MI patient on atorvastatin, metoprolol, and aspirin has lipid profile results of total cholesterol: 238 mg/dL, triglycerides: 125 mg/dL, HDL: 50 mg/dL, and LDL: 160 mg/dL. Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 4

This is a very high–risk ASCVD patient (diabetes, hypertension, post-MI) with persistently elevated LDL despite statin therapy. Target LDL according to major guidelines: <55 mg/dL

But his LDL is: 160 mg/dL

So intensification of lipid therapy is required.

Ezetimibe, bempedoic acid, and PCSK9 inhibitors (evolocumab) are appropriate add-on agents to further lower LDL.

| Bempedoic acid | ATP citrate lyase

| Ezetimibe | Intestinal cholesterol absorption

| PCSK9 inhibitors (Evolocumab) | LDL receptor degradation

Triglycerides are normal, so gemfibrozil is not indicated.

Thus, the correct combination is 1, 2, and 4.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A newborn admitted to the NICU is diagnosed with a patent ductus arteriosus (PDA). To promote pharmacological closure of the ductus arteriosus, which drug is most commonly used?
questions.explanation: In the neonatal period, the closure of the ductus arteriosus is triggered by a rise in oxygen and a fall in circulating prostaglandins. If the ductus remains patent (PDA), causing significant hemodynamic shifts, pharmacological closure is attempted using non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). Indomethacin is the most commonly used agent for this purpose as it is a potent inhibitor of prostaglandin synthesis. Ibuprofen is also frequently used. Magnesium sulfate (Option A) is used for neuroprotection or seizure prophylaxis, not PDA closure. Alprostadil (Option B), a synthetic prostaglandin , is used for the opposite purpose: to keep the ductus arteriosus open in infants with ductal-dependent congenital heart defects. Aspirin (Option D), while an NSAID, is not used in neonates due to the risk of Reye's syndrome and lower efficacy for this specific indication. Indomethacin therapy requires careful monitoring of renal function and platelet counts, as it can decrease renal perfusion and impair platelet aggregation
questions.learning: In the neonatal period, the closure of the ductus arteriosus is triggered by a rise in oxygen and a fall in circulating prostaglandins. If the ductus remains patent (PDA), causing significant hemodynamic shifts, pharmacological closure is attempted using…

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presents to the outpatient department with complaints of numbness over the mandibular region. Injury to which of the following nerves best explains this finding?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Inferior alveolar nerve

The inferior alveolar nerve, a branch of the mandibular division (V3) of the trigeminal nerve, provides sensory innervation to the mandibular teeth and, through its terminal mental nerve, supplies sensation to the chin, lower lip, and skin over the mandibular region. Injury to this nerve causes numbness of the lower lip, chin, and mandibular area.

Why not the other options?

• A. Auriculotemporal nerve: Supplies sensation to the temporal region, external ear, and TMJ.
• B. Masseteric nerve: A motor nerve supplying the masseter muscle.
• D. Lingual nerve: Provides general sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and floor of the mouth, not the skin over the mandible.
questions.learning: Inferior alveolar nerve — The inferior alveolar nerve, a branch of the mandibular division (V3) of the trigeminal nerve, provides sensory innervation to the mandibular teeth and, through its terminal mental nerve, supplies sensation to the chin, lower lip,…

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 48-year-old man presents with chronic gait imbalance, numbness in the feet, and generalized muscle weakness. He reports long-term self-administration of high-dose multivitamins for over a year. Based on his symptoms and history, which vitamin toxicity is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: While most B-vitamins are water-soluble and safely excreted, Vitamin B6 (Pyridoxine) is unique because chronic megadosing (typically) can lead to severe sensory neuropathy. This toxicity characteristically manifests as foot numbness, "pins and needles" sensations, and significant imbalance (sensory ataxia) due to damage to the dorsal root ganglia. This perfectly matches the patient's symptoms of imbalance and numbness. Vitamin D toxicity (Option A) causes hypercalcemia, leading to kidney stones and confusion. Vitamin C toxicity (Option C) is rare but may cause diarrhea or kidney stones. Vitamin A toxicity (Option D) causes headache, bone pain, and skin changes. The paradoxical nature of B6 is a classic board exam topic: while it is used to treat certain neuropathies (like those from isoniazid), excessive intake is a well-documented cause of nerve damage. Therefore, the combination of sensory deficits and a history of multivitamin megadosing identifies B6 as the toxic agent
questions.learning: While most B-vitamins are water-soluble and safely excreted, Vitamin B6 (Pyridoxine) is unique because chronic megadosing (typically) can lead to severe sensory neuropathy.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs can cause gynecomastia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Spironolactone

Gynecomastia can occur as an adverse effect of spironolactone.

Spironolactone results in gynecomastia by:

* Reduced production of testosterone

* More testosterone being converted to oestradiol

* Displacing estradiol from plasma-protein binding sites

* Blocking androgen receptors

* Blocking progesterone receptors

Other drugs causing gynecomastia are:

Drugs causing gynecomastia:

* Alcohol, marijuana, heroin

* Antiretroviral therapy

* Anabolic steroids

* Digoxin

* Risperidone

* Ketoconazole

* Spironolactone

* α-methyldopa

* Bromocriptine

* Cimetidine

* Phenytoin therapy

* Androgens- testosterone and its esters (except dihydrotestosterone)

Note:

Clomiphene and tamoxifen are used mainly in reducing male gynecomastia.
questions.learning: Spironolactone Gynecomastia can occur as an adverse effect of spironolactone. Spironolactone results in gynecomastia by: * Reduced production of testosterone * More testosterone being converted to oestradiol * Displacing estradiol from plasma-protein…

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient presents with shortness of breath and fatigue. On examination, distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds are noted. A chest X-ray is provided. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with shortness of breath, fatigue, distended neck veins, and muffled heart sounds, which strongly suggest chronic cardiac compression. These findings are classical for constrictive pericarditis, where the pericardium becomes thickened, fibrotic, and sometimes calcified, restricting normal cardiac filling. The chest X-ray in such cases often shows pericardial calcification, which appears as curvilinear radio-opaque shadows around the cardiac silhouette. This radiological feature is highly suggestive of constrictive pericarditis and helps differentiate it from other causes of heart failure. Why other options are wrong: (B) Bronchial asthma : Presents with wheezing and hyperinflated lungs, not JVD or muffled heart sounds (C) Acute pericarditis : Causes chest pain and pericardial effusion but not calcification (D) Atrial myxoma : May cause obstruction but does not show pericardial calcification on X-ray
questions.learning: The patient presents with shortness of breath, fatigue, distended neck veins, and muffled heart sounds, which strongly suggest chronic cardiac compression.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is the surest sign of wound dehiscence?
questions.explanation: Abdominal wound dehiscence, or "burst abdomen," is a serious surgical complication where the fascial closure fails. As discussed in Q.199, the surest clinical sign of impending or actual dehiscence is the sudden, profuse discharge of pinkish, serosanguinous fluid from the wound. This "salmon-pink" drainage represents peritoneal fluid leaking through a compromised fascial layer and is often described by patients as a feeling that "something gave way" during coughing or straining. Infection (Option B) is a risk factor for dehiscence but not a diagnostic sign of the dehiscence itself. Hypotension (Option C) and rebound tenderness (Option D) are signs of systemic sepsis or peritonitis, which can complicate but do not define the mechanical failure of the wound. Recognizing serosanguinous discharge is vital, as it often precedes the physical evisceration of bowel loops. Treatment involves immediate protection of the wound with sterile saline-soaked dressings followed by an urgent return to the operating room for a formal re-closure, typically using non-absorbable tension sutures
questions.learning: Abdominal wound dehiscence, or "burst abdomen," is a serious surgical complication where the fascial closure fails. As discussed in Q.199, the surest clinical sign of impending or actual dehiscence is the sudden, profuse discharge of pinkish,…

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 14-year-old male presented with recurrent epistaxis. There is no history of trauma associated with it. He also complained of nasal obstruction and rhinorrhea. On examination, there is a firm purplish mass on the posterior nasopharynx. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma

The most probable diagnosis is Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma.

Adolescent male presenting with recurrent epistaxis, nasal obstruction, and purplish mass on the posterior nasopharynx points towards angiofibroma. The consistency of the tumor is firm but the digital palpation should never be done until at the time of operation, because of the risk of profuse bleeding.

Computed tomography (CT) scan of the head with contrast enhancement is now the investigation of choice. Anterior bowing of the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus often called antral sign or Holman-Miller sign, is pathognomonic of angiofibroma.

Surgical excision is the treatment of choice though radiotherapy and chemotherapy monotherapy or in combination have also been used.
questions.learning: Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma — The most probable diagnosis is Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma. Adolescent male presenting with recurrent epistaxis, nasal obstruction, and purplish mass on the posterior nasopharynx points towards angiofibroma.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 26-year-old man involved in a road traffic accident presents with acute respiratory distress. On examination, he has hypotension, weak peripheral pulses, raised jugular venous pressure without a Y descent, and muffled heart sounds. Based on these clinical findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with the classic Beck’s triad following trauma: hypotension, muffled heart sounds, and elevated jugular venous pressure (JVP). These findings are characteristic of cardiac tamponade, a life-threatening condition in which blood accumulates rapidly in the pericardial sac, impairing ventricular filling and reducing cardiac output. A key diagnostic clue is the elevated JVP with an absent Y descent, which occurs because increased intrapericardial pressure prevents rapid atrial emptying into the ventricle during early diastole. Constrictive pericarditis (Option A) may also present with raised JVP but is distinguished by a prominent Y descent (Friedreich sign). Acute pericarditis (Option C) typically causes sharp pleuritic chest pain and a pericardial friction rub rather than obstructive shock. Cardiac failure (Option D) commonly presents with pulmonary edema and basal crackles, which are often absent in acute tamponade. Therefore, the history of trauma combined with Beck’s triad confirms cardiac tamponade, which requires urgent pericardiocentesis

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 21-year-old woman is referred from a PHC to the emergency department with altered sensorium, high-grade fever, severe lower abdominal pain, and foul-smelling vaginal discharge. Her friend reports a history of an unsafe abortion performed one week ago. On examination, there is marked uterine tenderness and features of septic shock with blood pressure 80/60 mmHg, pulse 140/min, and respiratory rate 36/min. Blood culture grows a gram-positive aerobic organism. Which pathogen is most likely responsible for this clinical presentation?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with septic abortion, a severe intrauterine infection typically following instrumentation or unsafe procedures. She is in septic shock with multi-organ signs. The critical diagnostic clue provided is the blood culture result: a gram-positive, aerobic bacterium. Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A Strep) is a classic aerobic pathogen responsible for post-abortal and puerperal sepsis. Clostridium perfringens (Option A) and Clostridium welchii (Option C) are also common in septic abortions but are strictly anaerobic, which contradicts the culture result. Escherichia coli (Option D) is a major cause of sepsis but is a gram-negative rod. S. pyogenes can cause a rapidly progressing toxic shock-like syndrome with high mortality. Therefore, given the specific microbiology provided, Streptococcus pyogenes is the definitive answer
questions.learning: The patient presents with septic abortion, a severe intrauterine infection typically following instrumentation or unsafe procedures. She is in septic shock with multi-organ signs.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The most sensitive index of recent transmission of malaria is _________
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Infant parasite rate

The infant parasite rate provides the most sensitive index for recent transmission of malaria in a locality.

Infant Parasite Rate is defined as the percentage of infants showing malarial parasites in their blood films.
questions.learning: Infant parasite rate — The infant parasite rate provides the most sensitive index for recent transmission of malaria in a locality. Infant Parasite Rate is defined as the percentage of infants showing malarial parasites in their blood films.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Mark the correct statement regarding inflammatory bowel disease.
options: Skip lesions are present in Crohn's disease
Mucosal layers are involved in Crohn's while transmural involvement seen in ulcerative colitis
Inflammatory bowel disease has a strong genetic predisposition
Crohn's is curable through surgical resection of the affected segment
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Skip lesions are present in Crohn's disease

The correct statement regarding inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is that skip lesions are present in Crohn's disease.

Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a chronic inflammatory condition of the gastrointestinal tract and is mainly idiopathic. It includes ulcerative colitis (UC) and Crohn's disease (CD). Genetic predisposition has been identified for IBD. But its association is weak for both CD and UC (option C)

Ulcerative colitis mainly involves the mucosa of the rectum (Option B) and extends proximally to the colon. Microscopically, crypt architecture is distorted. Neutrophils invade the epithelium and the crypts leading to cryptitis and crypt abscess. Clinically, UC presents with diarrhea, rectal bleeding, tenesmus, and abdominal cramps.

Crohn's disease can affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract from the mouth to the anus but mostly involves the terminal ileum. It is characterized by transmural inflammation. The characteristic lesions include cobblestone appearance, skip lesions, and transmural inflammation (Option B). CD presents as ileocolitis characterized by right lower quadrant pain, palpable mass, fever, and leukocytosis. Bowel obstruction can also be seen. They also present as jejunocolitis characterized by malabsorption and steatorrhea.

Management can be:

• Medical management with sulfasalazine, glucocorticoids, and immunosuppressants like azathioprine and mercaptopurine are useful
• Surgical management is indicated in ulcerative colitis. It does not cure Crohn's disease (Option D)
questions.learning: Skip lesions are present in Crohn's disease — The correct statement regarding inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is that skip lesions are present in Crohn's disease.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 29-year-old male diagnosed with schizophrenia has been stable on risperidone for the past few months. Recently, he began experiencing dystonia, for which he was started on benztropine 2 mg twice daily by his psychiatrist. A week later, he presents to the emergency department with complaints of dry mouth, blurred vision, confusion and urinary retention. On examination, he is disoriented, tachycardic, and febrile. Pupils are dilated and bowel sounds are absent. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?
options: Discontinue risperidone and initiate lorazepam for possible neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS)
Administer intravenous dantrolene and initiate cooling measures for suspected serotonin syndrome
Start physostigmine with continuous cardiac monitoring for anticholinergic toxicity due to benztropine overdose
Administer activated charcoal and IV fluids; observe the patient as symptoms are likely self-limiting
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Start physostigmine with continuous cardiac monitoring for anticholinergic toxicity due to benztropine overdose

Key clues:

• Dry mouth
• Blurred vision
• Confusion
• Urinary retention
• Dilated pupils
• Absent bowel sounds
• Tachycardia

This is classic ANTICHOLINERGIC TOXICITY

Drug added: Benztropine

• Used for:

• Drug-induced dystonia (from antipsychotics)

Mechanism:

• Central + peripheral muscarinic receptor blockade

Benztropine → muscarinic blockade

↓

Anticholinergic toxicity

↓

Give physostigmine

↓

↑ Acetylcholine

↓

Restores parasympathetic activity

Dry mouth, mydriasis, confusion, urinary retention, tachycardia, and absent bowel sounds indicate severe anticholinergic toxicity from benztropine. Physostigmine is a centrally acting acetylcholinesterase inhibitor that reverses both CNS and peripheral effects. It must be given with cardiac monitoring due to arrhythmia risk. This is the antidote for life-threatening anticholinergic delirium.

| Feature | Anticholinergic | NMS | Serotonin syndrome

| ------- | --------------- | --- | ------------------

| Skin | Dry | Sweaty | Sweaty

| Pupils | Dilated | Normal | Dilated

| Bowel sounds | ↓ | Normal | ↑

| Reflexes | Normal | ↓ | ↑ (clonus)

| CNS | Delirium | Rigidity | Agitation
questions.learning: Start physostigmine with continuous cardiac monitoring for anticholinergic toxicity due to benztropine overdose Key clues: • Dry mouth • Blurred vision • Confusion • Urinary retention • Dilated pupils • Absent bowel sounds • Tachycardia This is classic…

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is a technology-based surveillance system used for tuberculosis (TB) control in India?
questions.explanation: Nikshay is the unified ICT (Information and Communication Technology) platform for tuberculosis (TB) surveillance and case management under India's National TB Elimination Programme (NTEP). It allows health officials to track TB patients from diagnosis through treatment completion across both public and private sectors. The platform facilitates real-time notification, monitors treatment adherence, and manages Direct Benefit Transfers (DBT) to patients for nutritional support. Nischay (Option B) is a brand of home pregnancy test kits and not related to TB. Dots99 (Option C) refers to a specific adherence monitoring tool using toll-free missed calls on medication packaging but is not the overarching surveillance system. DOTS (Option D) stands for "Directly Observed Treatment, Short-course," which is the standardized clinical management strategy rather than a digital surveillance application. Nikshay's comprehensive database is vital for evaluating program performance and achieving the national goal of eliminating TB by 2025 through data-driven public health actions
questions.learning: Nikshay is the unified ICT (Information and Communication Technology) platform for tuberculosis (TB) surveillance and case management under India's National TB Elimination Programme (NTEP).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 30 year old female came for routine PAP smear testing. The report came as carcinoma in situ. What is the next step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Colposcopy and biopsy

Carcinoma in situ is classified as Cervical Intraepithelial Neoplasia-III and the next step in management for such lesions is Colposcopy and biopsy.
questions.learning: Colposcopy and biopsy Carcinoma in situ is classified as Cervical Intraepithelial Neoplasia-III and the next step in management for such lesions is Colposcopy and biopsy.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following structures is the arrow pointing to?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Posterior end of rib

The structure pointed by the arrow mark in the given chest X-ray PA view is the posterior end of the rib.

In the chest X-ray PA view, ribs appear as light grey strips. The anterior part of the rib is more oblique and the medial part cannot be demonstrable as it ends with costal cartilage. The posterior part of the rib is more horizontal, hyperdense and the attachment of the rib with the vertebra can be easily made out.

Normal Chest X-ray Rib Identification

The anterior(yellow) and posterior(red) ribs are highlighted in the image given below.
