questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: OCPs can be given in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation: Oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) are safe for use in women with HIV infection. While clinicians must monitor for potential drug-drug interactions with certain antiretroviral therapies, HIV itself is not a contraindication to their use. In contrast, moderate to severe Hypertension (HTN) (Option A) is a contraindication because estrogen increases the risk of stroke and myocardial infarction. Diabetes Mellitus (DM) (Option B) with vascular complications or a duration of >20 years is a contraindication due to heightened cardiovascular risk. Hyperlipidemia (Option D) is also a contraindication as OCPs can further alter lipid profiles and increase the risk of arterial thrombosis. Therefore, among the choices provided, HIV is the only condition where OCP use is generally acceptable
questions.learning: Oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) are safe for use in women with HIV infection. While clinicians must monitor for potential drug-drug interactions with certain antiretroviral therapies, HIV itself is not a contraindication to their use.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 25-year-old woman reports episodes of palpitations and dizziness, particularly following physical activity such as playing tennis. She has experienced these symptoms multiple times over the last two years. ECG is taken and it is shown. Based on her presentation and the accompanying ECG findings, which of the following diagnoses is most likely?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Arrhythmogenic right ventricular dysplasia

Arrhythmogenic Right Ventricular Dysplasia/Cardiomyopathy is a genetic cardiomyopathy where the right ventricular myocardium is replaced by fibrofatty tissue.

This leads to:

• Ventricular arrhythmias
• Palpitations
• Syncope
• Sudden cardiac death in young individuals

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY- Mutation occurs in desmosomal proteins, which normally maintain cell-to-cell adhesion between cardiomyocytes.

Common genes involved:

| Gene | Protein

| ---- | -------

| PKP2 | Plakophilin

| DSP | Desmoplakin

| DSG2 | Desmoglein

Loss of adhesion → myocyte death → fibrofatty replacement. Commonly affected areas:

Triangle of dysplasia

• RV inflow tract
• RV outflow tract
• RV apex

Young patient with exercise-induced palpitations and syncope suggests a malignant ventricular arrhythmia. ECG shows features consistent with ARVD—classically epsilon waves, T-wave inversion in right precordial leads (V1–V3). ARVD is due to fibrofatty replacement of right ventricular myocardium, predisposing to VT during exertion.

Brugada is febrile/drug-related, HOCM shows LVH with systolic murmur, and Uhl anomaly is rare and neonatal.

ECG of a patient with ARVC/D showing the presence of an epsilon wave (electric potentials after the end of the QRS complex) (red arrows) and T-wave inversion in V1-V5.

Treatment focuses on preventing fatal arrhythmias.

Options include:

| Treatment | Role

| --------- | ----

| Beta blockers | Reduce arrhythmias

| Amiodarone | Antiarrhythmic therapy

| ICD implantation | Prevent sudden death

| Exercise restriction | Reduce arrhythmia risk

A) Brugada syndrome

ECG shows: Coved ST elevation in V1–V3

Associated with sodium channel mutations, not fibrofatty RV replacement.

B) Uhl anomaly

Rare congenital condition with absence of RV myocardium ("paper-thin RV").

Usually presents in childhood, not adulthood.

C) Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy

Features include:

• LV hypertrophy
• Systolic murmur
• Sudden death in athletes

But ECG findings differ and RV fibrofatty replacement is absent.
questions.learning: Arrhythmogenic right ventricular dysplasia Arrhythmogenic Right Ventricular Dysplasia/Cardiomyopathy is a genetic cardiomyopathy where the right ventricular myocardium is replaced by fibrofatty tissue.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 64-year-old man presents with episodes of palpitations and syncope. He has a past history of an inferior-wall myocardial infarction one year ago. A Holter monitoring study has been performed, and the 24-hour ECG tracing is shown. Based on these findings, what is the most appropriate long-term management for this patient?
questions.explanation: The patient’s history of inferior-wall myocardial infarction followed by symptoms of palpitations and syncope suggests a significant conduction system disorder. The Holter ECG strip likely reveals a high-grade or complete (third-degree) atrioventricular (AV) block, given the heart rate (HR 45) and clinical symptoms. For symptomatic bradycardia due to advanced AV block, the gold standard for long-term management is the insertion of a permanent pacemaker. Amiodarone (Option A) is an antiarrhythmic used for tachycardias and would worsen bradycardia. Atropine (Option B) and isoproterenol (Option D) are used for temporary, acute management of bradycardia but are not definitive long-term solutions. The presence of syncope in a patient with a prior MI and severe bradycardia indicates a high risk of sudden cardiac death, necessitating permanent cardiac pacing
questions.learning: The patient’s history of inferior-wall myocardial infarction followed by symptoms of palpitations and syncope suggests a significant conduction system disorder.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: In the evaluation of a female patient with unexplained urinary leakage, a diagnostic test using methylene blue along with a three-swab technique is performed to determine the source of the leak. During the procedure, the middle swab becomes stained with the dye. What is the most likely diagnosis based on this finding?
questions.explanation: The 3-swab test (Moir's test) is used to differentiate between various types of urinary fistulae. Methylene blue dye is instilled into the bladder, and three cotton swabs are placed in the vagina at different levels. If the middle swab (or upper swab) turns blue, it indicates that the dye has leaked from the bladder into the vagina, confirming a Vesicovaginal Fistula (VVF). In a Uretero-vaginal fistula (Option C), the swabs would remain white but become wet with urine, because the dye in the bladder never reaches the ureters. In a Urethrovaginal fistula (Option B), the lowest (most distal) swab would turn blue. VVF is a common complication of prolonged obstructed labor or gynecological surgery. The test effectively localizes the site of communication, which is essential for planning surgical repair. Therefore, the "positive dye" result on the middle swab specifically identifies the bladder as the source of the leakage
questions.learning: The 3-swab test (Moir's test) is used to differentiate between various types of urinary fistulae. Methylene blue dye is instilled into the bladder, and three cotton swabs are placed in the vagina at different levels.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a health program, assessment of the fulfilment of objectives, achievement of targets, and short-term goals is carried out through which of the following methods?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Evaluation

Evaluation is the process of assessing whether a health program has achieved its stated objectives, targets, and short-term goals.

It focuses on measuring outcomes and impact after implementation, helping determine program effectiveness.

Monitoring vs Evaluation-

In contrast, monitoring is continuous and process-oriented, supervision ensures correct implementation, and planning precedes execution.
questions.learning: Evaluation Evaluation is the process of assessing whether a health program has achieved its stated objectives, targets, and short-term goals. It focuses on measuring outcomes and impact after implementation, helping determine program effectiveness.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 60-year-old man presents with features suggestive of Cushing’s syndrome. Considering his age and clinical presentation, which condition is most commonly identified as the primary cause of Cushing’s disease in this scenario?
questions.explanation: It is essential to distinguish between Cushing's "syndrome" (the clinical state of cortisol excess) and Cushing's "disease" (the specific condition where cortisol excess is caused by a pituitary tumor). Cushing's disease is the most common cause of endogenous (non-iatrogenic) Cushing's syndrome, accounting for approximately 70% of cases. The primary cause of Cushing's disease is a pituitary microadenoma—a benign tumor of the anterior pituitary gland that secretes excessive Adrenocorticotropic Hormone (ACTH), which in turn overstimulates the adrenal glands to produce cortisol. Ectopic ACTH syndrome (Option C), often from small-cell lung cancer (Option A), is a common cause of Cushing's syndrome in older men with a significant smoking history but is not the definition of Cushing's disease. Adrenal tumors (Option B) cause ACTH-independent Cushing's syndrome. Therefore, in any patient diagnosed with Cushing's disease, a pituitary microadenoma is the most frequent underlying etiology. Diagnosis is supported by high-dose dexamethasone suppression tests and brain MRI
questions.learning: It is essential to distinguish between Cushing's "syndrome" (the clinical state of cortisol excess) and Cushing's "disease" (the specific condition where cortisol excess is caused by a pituitary tumor).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Assertion (A): A nested case-control study can provide an accurate estimate of the relative risk. Reason (R): Cases and controls are selected from a cohort in which incidence data are already available.
options: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.

A nested case-control study is conducted within an established cohort. Since the cohort is followed prospectively, incident cases are identified, and controls are selected from the same risk set. Availability of cohort incidence data allows the odds ratio to closely approximate the relative risk.
questions.learning: Both — A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. A nested case-control study is conducted within an established cohort.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Endocrine · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: 64-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department due to confusion and lethargy. The patient was asymptomatic when her husband left for work in the morning, but when he arrived home, he found her in bed weak and disoriented. The patient's medical conditions include type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension, for which she takes multiple medications. Laboratory testing shows an elevated serum C-peptide level. If her current condition is due to an antidiabetic drug, which of the following is the most likely culprit agent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Glyburide

Sulfonylureas (e.g., glyburide) treat type 2 diabetes by stimulating pancreatic β-cells to release insulin through closure of ATP-sensitive K⁺ channels. This leads to:

• Increased endogenous insulin secretion
• Elevated C-peptide levels (because insulin is produced by the pancreas)

Excess insulin release can cause severe hypoglycemia, especially in elderly patients or with long-acting sulfonylureas like glyburide.

Why other options are incorrect:

• A. Acarbose: Does not increase insulin secretion → hypoglycemia uncommon.
• B. Canagliflozin: Lowers glucose by urinary glucose excretion, not insulin release.
• D. Long-acting insulin: Exogenous insulin lacks C-peptide, so C-peptide would be low.
questions.learning: Glyburide Sulfonylureas (e.g., glyburide) treat type 2 diabetes by stimulating pancreatic β-cells to release insulin through closure of ATP-sensitive K⁺ channels.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 32-year-old man presents after a stab injury to the neck just above the clavicle. His pulse is 120/min and blood pressure is 90/70 mmHg. What is the next best step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Immediate surgical exploration

Penetrating neck injuries are managed based on the patient’s hemodynamic status and the presence of hard signs of vascular or aerodigestive injury.

This patient has:

• Penetrating neck trauma
• Hypotension (BP 90/70 mmHg)
• Tachycardia (120/min)

These findings indicate hemodynamic instability, which is an indication for immediate surgical exploration without delaying for imaging.

Why not the other options?

• B. Supportive treatment and observation: Appropriate only for stable patients without concerning signs.
• C. CT angiography of the neck: Investigation of choice only in hemodynamically stable patients.
• D. MRI neck: Not used in the acute trauma setting.
questions.learning: Immediate surgical exploration Penetrating neck injuries are managed based on the patient’s hemodynamic status and the presence of hard signs of vascular or aerodigestive injury.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient with asthma who is already on inhaled corticosteroids and a long-acting beta- agonist continues to experience exacerbations. Spirometry shows a normal FEV₁, and there is no significant reversibility with a salbutamol challenge. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation: This patient has uncontrolled asthma despite being on low or moderate-dose Inhaled Corticosteroid (ICS) plus a Long-Acting Beta-Agonist (LABA). According to the Global Initiative for Asthma (GINA) stepwise guidelines, the next logical step to optimize anti-inflammatory control is to increase the ICS dose. Long-Acting Muscarinic Antagonists (LAMA) like tiotropium (Option B) can be added in Step 4 or 5, but this is typically done after maximizing the ICS dose. Theophylline (Option C) is rarely used today due to its high toxicity and low efficacy compared to modern inhalers. Biologics like Omalizumab (Option D) are reserved for Step 5 in patients with severe allergic asthma that remains uncontrolled despite high-dose ICS and LABA. Since this patient has not yet maximized their ICS dose, increasing it is the mandated next step

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Given below is a histological section of the thyroid gland. Which of the following is secreted by the cell marked 'X' in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Calcitonin

The structure marked X is the C-cells or the parafollicular cells of the thyroid gland and they secrete calcitonin.

The C-cells (clear cells or parafollicular cells) have a pale staining cytoplasm, they are present between the follicular cells and the basement membrane or between the follicles. They are usually found in the middle third of each lateral lobe of the thyroid and scattered in between the thyroid follicles. They are members of the APUD system of dispersed neuroendocrine cells. They secrete calcitonin which lowers blood calcium.

The thyroid gland is covered by a fibrous capsule with septae dividing it into lobules. These lobules contain follicles lined by follicular cells. The shape of the follicular cells depends on the activity of the gland. They're squamous in the inactive state, cuboidal to columnar in the active state. The cavity of the follicle contains colloid which appears pink in H and E staining.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following marked structure is damaged in respiratory distress syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2

Type II pneumocytes, which are marked as 2 in the above image, are damaged in respiratory distress syndrome.

The cells forming the lining epithelium of alveoli (also called pneumocytes) are mainly of the following types:

• Type I pneumocytes - large flattened cells which present a very thin diffusion barrier for gases. These cells have large cytoplasmic extensions and form the primary lining cells of the alveoli. They are connected to each other by tight junctions.
• Type II pneumocytes (granular pneumocytes) - These are rounded secretory cells bearing microvilli on their free surfaces. These cells secrete the surfactant which decreases the surface tension between the thin alveolar walls and thus prevents alveoli from collapsing during respiration. Type II cells are important in alveolar repair as well.

The below image shows the pneumocytes lining the alveoli:

The alveoli are surrounded by pulmonary capillaries. The alveoli also contain other specialized cells, including pulmonary alveolar macrophages, lymphocytes, plasma cells, neuroendocrine cells, and mast cells.

Respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) is seen in premature infants, due to the decreased production and secretion of the lung surfactant. The surfactant reduces the alveolar surface tension. This phospholipid is synthesized in type II pneumocytes (also called granular pneumocytes) in the endoplasmic reticulum.

The surfactant appears in the amniotic fluid between 28 and 32 weeks of gestation. Mature levels of the pulmonary surfactant are present usually after 35 weeks of gestation. In a premature infant, there is a decrease in both the quantity and quality of surfactant resulting in respiratory distress syndrome.

Administration of antenatal glucocorticoids to mothers who deliver at 24 to 34 weeks can increase surfactant production and reduce the risk of RDS. It includes either giving 2 doses of betamethasone 12mg/dose with 24 hours between each dose, or 4 doses of dexamethasone 6mg/dose, with 12 hours between each dose.

Mild to moderate RDS can be managed with continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP). CPAP is a noninvasive modality of support where a continuous distending pressure (5-7 cm H20) is applied at the nostril level to keep the alveoli open in a spontaneously breathing baby. Severe cases will require mechanical ventilation.

Surfactant administration is reserved for severe cases and moderate cases not improving even with fiO2> 40% in CPAP.

With treatment, it rarely leads to respiratory failure and has a good prognosis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 16-year-old boy presents with exercise intolerance, early fatigue, and painful muscle cramps during strenuous activity. He reports that symptoms improve with rest. There is no significant rise in serum lactate levels after exercise testing. Serum creatine kinase is mildly elevated. Which of the following enzyme deficiencies best explains this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Myophosphorylase

McArdle disease (Glycogen Storage Disease Type V) is caused by deficiency of myophosphorylase, the muscle isoform of glycogen phosphorylase, which is required for breakdown of glycogen to glucose-1-phosphate in skeletal muscle.

• Inability to utilize muscle glycogen during exercise
• Leads to energy deficiency in muscle cells during exertion

Clinical features:

• Exercise intolerance (early fatigue)
• Muscle cramps and pain
• Myoglobinuria (dark urine after exercise)
• “Second-wind phenomenon” (symptoms improve after rest due to use of blood glucose)

Why other options are incorrect:

• Glucose-6-phosphatase: Deficient in Von Gierke disease (GSD I)
• Glycogen phosphorylase: General term; the specific deficient enzyme in muscle is myophosphorylase
• Hexokinase: Involved in glycolysis, not glycogen breakdown

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: An 11-year-old presented with the following growth in the eye as shown below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Limbal dermoid

The image shows the presence of a limbal dermoid.

Limbal Dermoid is a choristoma (a mass of histologically normal tissue in an abnormal location). It consists of collagenous tissue containing dermal elements and covered by stratified squamous epithelium. Limbal dermoid present in early childhood as a subconjunctival mass in the infratemporal limbus. Treatment is indicated for chronic irritation, amblyopia, vision impairment and corneal dellen formation. Small dermoids can be excised, larger lesions may need lamellar keratosclerectomy.
questions.learning: Limbal dermoid — The image shows the presence of a limbal dermoid. Limbal Dermoid is a choristoma (a mass of histologically normal tissue in an abnormal location).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 20-year-old female patient presented to OPD with the given presentation. On examination, it seems gelatinous in consistency. She reports fluctuation in size, mild numbness in hand and occasional pain. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ganglion cyst

The history and image are suggestive of a patient with a ganglion cyst.

Ganglion cyst arises from the leakage of synovial fluid from a joint or tendon sheath and thus contains a glary, viscous fluid.

It can appear anywhere in the wrist but the most common area is the dorsal surface of the scapholunate ligament.

Patients usually present with painless, well-defined, cystic, transillumination-positive, and non-tender swelling. If there is an impingement on a nearby nerve or structure it can cause pain.

It disappears spontaneously, but the aspiration of the swelling or operative removal can be done for reassurance or when there is pressure on the nerve. Even if treatment is done, the rates of recurrence are high.

Other Options:

Option B: Lipomas are benign tumors of adipose tissue. It can occur anywhere and at any depth. It can be encapsulated or diffuse, superficial or deep. On examination, they are nontender and non-pulsatile. Because of the soft consistency, they may appear to be fluctuant but they are not. The slip sign is positive.

Option C: Dermoid Cyst presents as asymptomatic, slowly enlarging, painless, superficial localized swellings over the volar aspect of the hand, especially the distal portion of the digits.

Option D: An extremity hematoma is a localized collection of blood in the soft tissues of an extremity, typically occurring after trauma, surgery, or in patients with bleeding disorders. The hematoma can develop in various tissue planes: subcutaneous, intramuscular, or subfascial compartments.
questions.learning: Ganglion cyst — The history and image are suggestive of a patient with a ganglion cyst. Ganglion cyst arises from the leakage of synovial fluid from a joint or tendon sheath and thus contains a glary, viscous fluid.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An intra-operative image of a child undergoing inguinal hernia repair is shown, with a marked vein in the spermatic cord. What is the likely structure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Testicular vein

The highlighted vein is within the spermatic cord.

The spermatic cord contains :

| Structure | Function

| --------- | --------

| Vas deferens | Transports sperm

| Testicular artery | Blood supply to testis

| Pampiniform plexus (testicular veins) | Venous drainage of testis

| Cremasteric vessels | Blood supply to cremaster muscle

| Genital branch of genitofemoral nerve | Motor supply to cremaster

The testicular vein is part of the pampiniform venous plexus, which surrounds the testicular artery.

Why the other options are incorrect

Femoral vein → Located in the femoral triangle, not inside the spermatic cord.

Obturator vein → Located in the pelvic region passing through the obturator canal.

Inferior epigastric vein→ Runs along the anterior abdominal wall, not within the cord.

During inguinal hernia repair, surgeons must protect:

• Vas deferens
• Testicular vessels

Damage to the testicular vein/artery may cause:

• Testicular ischemia
• Testicular atrophy

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 68-year-old man presents with cough with yellowish sputum. Auscultation revealed bronchial breath sounds. He is hemodynamically stable and not confused. On examination, his respiratory rate is 20/min and blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg. Lab reports show urea levels of 44 mg/dL. What is the next best step in the management of this patient?
options: Give antibiotics and send the patient home
Admit to ICU without mechanical ventilation
Admit to ICU with invasive mechanical ventilation
Consider admission in a non-ICU setting
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Consider admission in a non-ICU setting

This patient should be considered for admission in a non-ICU setting.

Productive cough along with auscultatory findings of bronchial breath sounds in this patient is suggestive of community-acquired pneumonia.

The next step is to determine the need for hospitalization in community-acquired pneumonia based on the CURB-65 score.

CURB-65 scoring:

Clinical factor
Score

Confusion

1

Blood urea nitrogen > 20 mg/dL (> 7 mmol/L)

1

Respiratory rate ≥ 30 breaths per minute

1

Systolic blood pressure < 90 mm Hg or

Diastolic blood pressure ≤ 60 mm Hg

1

Age ≥ 65 years

1

The table below shows the decision based on the CURB-65 score:

Total Score
Decision

0
Treated as outpatient

1 or 2
Admission to the hospital

3 or more
Admission in ICU

Calculating the CURB-65 score for the case given in the question:

• No confusion (score = 0)
• Urea is 44 mg/dL (score = 1)
• Respiratory rate is 20/min (score = 0)
• Blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg (score = 0)
• Age is 68 years (score = 1)

Therefore, the total score is 2, and the patient requires hospitalization in a non-ICU setting (medical ward).

Treatment in a non-ICU setting includes respiratory fluoroquinolones (moxifloxacin) or a beta lactam antibiotic (cephalosporins) plus a macrolide (azithromycin/clarithromycin).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 30-year-old man who regularly wears contact lenses presents with eye pain, redness, and purulent discharge from the right eye. Examination reveals a characteristic greyish- white, serpiginous ulcer on the lower cornea, along with a 4 mm hypopyon and moderate anterior chamber flare. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient’s presentation is highly characteristic of an acute bacterial corneal ulcer, likely caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa, which is a common and aggressive pathogen associated with contact lens wear. The "snake-shaped" (serpiginous) greyish-white ulcer is a classic clinical description for certain bacterial keratitis. The presence of a significant hypopyon (a collection of white blood cells in the anterior chamber) and anterior chamber flare further indicates a severe infectious process. Viral ulcers (Option A) usually present with a dendritic appearance and less prominent discharge. Fungal ulcers (Option C) typically have "feathery" edges and satellite lesions following vegetative trauma. Parasitic ulcers (Option D), such as Acanthamoeba, cause disproportionate pain and a ring-shaped infiltrate. Bacterial ulcers are a medical emergency requiring intensive topical fortified antibiotics to prevent corneal perforation. Therefore, given the acute purulent presentation and contact lens history, a bacterial etiology is the most probable diagnosis
questions.learning: The patient’s presentation is highly characteristic of an acute bacterial corneal ulcer, likely caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa, which is a common and aggressive pathogen associated with contact lens wear.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: At what age is the first dose of hepatitis B vaccine given?
questions.explanation: According to the National Immunization Schedule (NIS) in India and WHO recommendations, the first dose of the Hepatitis B vaccine should be administered as a "birth dose." Ideally, this should occur as soon as possible after delivery, within 24 hours. This birth dose is critical for preventing perinatal transmission from mother to child. Subsequent doses are typically given at 6, 10, and 14 weeks (Options B and C) as part of the pentavalent vaccine. A dose at 6 months (Option D) is not part of the standard primary series. The birth dose provides early protection and significantly reduces the risk of chronic infection in the infant. Therefore, "birth" is the correct and medically essential age for initiating hepatitis B immunization
questions.learning: According to the National Immunization Schedule (NIS) in India and WHO recommendations, the first dose of the Hepatitis B vaccine should be administered as a "birth dose." Ideally, this should occur as soon as possible after delivery, within 24 hours.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the recommended daily protein intake for a 30-year-old woman weighing 55 kg?
questions.explanation: The recommended daily protein intake for a healthy adult is commonly based on body weight. According to standard nutritional guidelines such as ICMR, the average requirement is approximately 0.8 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight per day. For a 30-year-old woman weighing 55 kg: Protein requirement = 0.8 × 55 = 44 grams/day, which is rounded off to 45 grams/day This intake is adequate to maintain nitrogen balance, support tissue repair, enzyme and hormone production, and overall metabolic functions in a healthy adult with normal activity levels. Although some sources mention 1 g/kg/day, especially for easier calculation, the standard recommended dietary allowance (RDA) for adults remains closer to 0.8 g/kg/day, particularly in exam-based contexts like FMGE. Why Other Options Are Incorrect (B) 55 gm: Based on 1 g/kg, slightly higher than standard (C) 60 gm: More than required (D) 70 gm: Excess unless increased demand (pregnancy, illness)
questions.learning: The recommended daily protein intake for a healthy adult is commonly based on body weight. According to standard nutritional guidelines such as ICMR, the average requirement is approximately 0.8 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight per day.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 50-year-old male diagnosed with carcinoma of the larynx is scheduled for treatment and has undergone the procedure shown in the image below. At what level is the incision made for this procedure?
options: At the level of the 2nd tracheal ring
At the level of the 1st tracheal ring
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. At the level of the 1st tracheal ring

The clinical scenario describes a 50-year-old male with carcinoma of the larynx undergoing a tracheostomy, as shown in the image. The incision is made at the level of the first tracheal ring, above the isthmus, in a patient with laryngeal carcinoma, and this procedure is referred to as a high tracheostomy.

Laryngeal carcinoma is an indication of high tracheostomy. It is done at the level of the 1st tracheal ring and an opening is made above the isthmus of the thyroid gland

Tracheostomy involves making an opening and placing a stoma in the anterior wall of the trachea. High tracheostomy is performed above the level of the thyroid isthmus (the Isthmus lies against the II, III, and IV tracheal rings). The only indication for high tracheostomy is carcinoma of the larynx.

It provides an alternative pathway for breathing by bypassing the obstruction. Improves alveolar ventilation by reducing dead space by 30-50% and reducing airway resistance
It uses a cuff to protect the airways from secretions and blood.

Indications of tracheostomy:

* Respiratory obstruction due to infections (laryngo-tracheo-bronchitis, epiglottitis, diphtheria).

* Trauma due to external injury, mandibular or maxillofacial fractures.

* Neoplasms.

* Foreign bodies or edema.

* Retained secretionsInability to cough due to coma, spasm, or paralysis of respiratory muscles.

* Aspiration of pharyngeal secretions.

* Painful cough.

* Respiratory insufficiency due to emphysema, chronic bronchitis

Steps of Tracheostomy:

* Incision: Make a vertical incision in the midline from the cricoid cartilage to above the sternal notch. For a better cosmetic outcome for elective procedures, a 5 cm transverse incision two fingers' breadth above the sternal notch can be used.

* Dissection: Dissect tissues in the midline. Displace or ligate any dilated veins encountered to control bleeding.

* Muscle separation: Separate and retract the strap muscles of the neck laterally to expose underlying structures.

* Thyroid isthmus management: Displace the thyroid isthmus upwards or divide and ligate it with sutures.

* Local anaesthesia: Inject a few drops of 4% lignocaine into the trachea to suppress coughing.

* Tracheal incision: Fix the trachea with a hook and make a vertical incision between the third and fourth tracheal rings(Option D), converting it into a circular opening. Avoid dividing the first tracheal ring to prevent perichondritis and stenosis.

* Inserting the tube: Insert a tracheostomy tube of appropriate size into the tracheal opening and secure it with tapes.

* Avoid tight suturing: Avoid tightly suturing or packing the skin incision to prevent subcutaneous emphysema.

* Dressing: Place a gauze dressing between the skin and the flange of the tracheostomy tube around the stoma to absorb secretions, provide a barrier against infection, and allow air to escape, promoting proper healing.

Pearl PF1486: Types of Tracheostomy

High tracheostomy

* Done through the 1st tracheal ring

* An opening is made above the isthmus of the thyroid gland

* Done in case of malignancy of the larynx

* Increased risk of perichondritis and subglottic stenosis

Mid tracheostomy

* Done through the 2nd - 3rd rings

* Most commonly done tracheostomy

* Isthmus has to be retracted or divided

Low tracheostomy

* Done through the 4th - 5th tracheal ring

* Done below the isthmus

* Done when the airway is blocked at an upper airway level

* Risk of injuring the great vessels of the neck
questions.learning: At the level of the 1st tracheal ring — The clinical scenario describes a 50-year-old male with carcinoma of the larynx undergoing a tracheostomy, as shown in the image.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which types of cancer are associated with exposure to ionizing radiation? 1. Leukaemia 2. Lung cancer 3. Breast cancer 4. Lymphoma Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 3 and 4

Ionizing radiation is a well-established carcinogen that causes DNA damage through direct strand breaks and free radical formation. The risk of malignancy depends on the radiation dose, age at exposure, and tissue radiosensitivity. Hematopoietic tissues and rapidly dividing cells are particularly susceptible.

Why is C correct?

• 1. Leukaemia ✅

• One of the earliest and best-established malignancies associated with ionizing radiation exposure, especially acute leukemia (except CLL).

• 2. Lung cancer ❌

• Although high-dose radiation can increase the risk of lung cancer, lung cancer is classically associated with smoking, radon, and asbestos, and is not considered one of the characteristic radiation-induced cancers in this context.

• 3. Breast cancer ✅

• Exposure to ionizing radiation, particularly during childhood or adolescence, significantly increases the risk of breast cancer.

• 4. Lymphoma ✅

• Ionizing radiation is associated with an increased risk of lymphomas, especially non-Hodgkin lymphoma.
questions.learning: 1, 3 and 4 Ionizing radiation is a well-established carcinogen that causes DNA damage through direct strand breaks and free radical formation. The risk of malignancy depends on the radiation dose, age at exposure, and tissue radiosensitivity.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman presents with chronic dryness of the mouth and eyes. Investigations show positive anti-Ro and anti-La antibodies, and the Schirmer test demonstrates less than 5 mm of tear production in 5 minutes without anesthesia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The combination of xerostomia (dry mouth) and xerophthalmia (dry eyes), known as the "sicca complex," is the hallmark of Sjogren syndrome (Option D). This is a systemic autoimmune disease characterized by the lymphocytic infiltration of exocrine glands. The diagnosis is supported by the presence of highly specific autoantibodies: anti-Ro (SSA) and anti-La (SSB). Furthermore, the Schirmer test result of less than 5 mm in 5 minutes confirms significant objective tear deficiency (aqueous tear deficiency). Scleroderma (Option A) primarily involves skin thickening and multi-organ fibrosis. Dehydration (Option B) causes temporary dryness but would not be associated with specific autoantibodies. Lacrimal duct stones (Option C) would typically cause localized pain and tearing (epiphora) rather than systemic dryness. Given the female gender, specific sicca symptoms, and positive immunological markers, Sjogren syndrome is the most definitive diagnosis
questions.learning: The combination of xerostomia (dry mouth) and xerophthalmia (dry eyes), known as the "sicca complex," is the hallmark of Sjogren syndrome (Option D). This is a systemic autoimmune disease characterized by the lymphocytic infiltration of exocrine glands.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the term used for the average number of children a woman is expected to have over her lifetime if she experiences the current age-specific fertility rates throughout her reproductive years?
questions.explanation: The Total Fertility Rate (TFR) is one of the most important measures of reproductive health and population growth. It represents the average number of children that would be born to a woman during her lifetime (reproductive years) based on current age-specific fertility rates. General fertility rate (Option A) is the number of births per 1,000 women of childbearing age per year. Gross reproduction rate (Option C) specifically counts only the number of "female" children born. Net reproduction rate (Option D) is the most refined measure, as it counts female children who are expected to "survive" to childbearing age themselves. A TFR of 2.1 is generally considered the "replacement level fertility" required to keep a population stable. In India, TFR has been steadily declining and is a key metric for evaluating the success of national family welfare programs
questions.learning: The Total Fertility Rate (TFR) is one of the most important measures of reproductive health and population growth. It represents the average number of children that would be born to a woman during her lifetime (reproductive years) based on current…

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs restrict the availability of thymidylate?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 5-fluorouracil

5-FU acts during the S phase of the cell cycle inhibiting DNA synthesis by restricting the availability of thymidylate.

5-FU acts via two different pathways depending on its dose: G1- S-phase cell cycle arrest and apoptosis at a higher dose and G2-M-phase cell cycle arrest at a low dose.

5-FU:

* Converted in the body to the corresponding nucleotide 5-deoxyuridine monophosphate, which forms a covalent ternary complex with methyl-THFA and thymidylate synthase, resulting in the irreversible inhibition of thymidylate synthase.

* Failure of DNA synthesis occurs due to the non-availability of thymidylate.

* Inhibition of TS by 5-FU depends on THFA, infusion of leucovorin will enhance the efficacy of this drug. Cisplatin and oxaliplatin also synergize with this drug.

* Rapidly dividing cells are most commonly affected, but resting cells are also affected.

* Used as an anticancer drug for many solid cancers such as the colon, rectum, stomach, pancreas, liver, urinary bladder, head, and neck. Topical preparations are used in BCC and actinic keratosis.

* Toxicity includes myelosuppression, mucositis, diarrhea, nausea, and vomiting. Peripheral neuropathy may also occur.

Note:

Monoclonal antibodies recognize the extracellular domain of the EGFR, inhibit ligand-induced signaling, and can elicit an immune response. Cetuximab is a recombinant, chimeric human/mouse IgG1 antibody that binds to EGFR and prevents ligand-dependent signaling and receptor dimerization, thereby blocking cell growth and survival signals. It is used to treat patients with metastatic colon cancers and Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma(HNSCC)

Other options:

Option A: Rituximab is an anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody and is used in the treatment of lymhomas.

Option B: Cisplatin induces its cytotoxic properties through binding to nuclear DNA and subsequent interference with normal transcription, and/or DNA replication mechanisms.

Option D: Methotrexate inhibits purine and pyrimidine synthesis, which accounts for its efficacy in the therapy of cancer as well as for some of its toxicities.  The anticancer activity of methotrexate is by inhibition of dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR).
questions.learning: 5-fluorouracil 5-FU acts during the S phase of the cell cycle inhibiting DNA synthesis by restricting the availability of thymidylate. 5-FU acts via two different pathways depending on its dose: G1- S-phase cell cycle arrest and apoptosis at a higher dose…

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 60-year-old male presents with painless cervical lymphadenopathy and right-sided deafness. On examination, the tympanic membrane was dull on the right side. Moreover, decreased mobility of the soft palate was also noted. What is the viral etiological agent associated with the diagnosis of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. EBV

The given clinical condition is nasopharyngeal carcinoma and Epstein–Barr Virus (EBV) is one of the closley associated etiological agents of this condition.

Specific viral markers are being developed to screen people in high-incidence areas. EB virus has two important antigens: Viral capsid antigen (VCA) and Early antigen (EA).

IgA antibodies of EA are highly specific for nasopharyngeal cancer but have a sensitivity of only 70–80% while IgA antibodies of VCA are more sensitive but less specific. IgA antibodies against both EA and VCA should be done for screening of patients for nasopharyngeal cancer.
questions.learning: EBV — The given clinical condition is nasopharyngeal carcinoma and Epstein–Barr Virus (EBV) is one of the closley associated etiological agents of this condition.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Suction and evacuation is a commonly performed procedure for termination of pregnancy or management of miscarriage, and its safety and effectiveness depend on appropriate timing. At what gestational age is suction and evacuation best performed?
questions.explanation: Suction and evacuation (S&E) is the preferred surgical method for the medical termination of pregnancy or the management of early miscarriage during the first trimester, typically up to 12 weeks of gestation. At this stage, the fetal tissue and placenta can be safely and effectively removed using a vacuum cannula with minimal risk of uterine injury or significant hemorrhage. While it can be performed as early as 6 weeks (Option C), the procedure is most commonly standardized and technically easiest around 10-12 weeks when the gestational sac is well-defined. Beyond 12 weeks, such as at 15 weeks (Option B) or 18 weeks (Option D), the procedure is classified as "dilatation and evacuation" (D&E), which involves larger instruments and higher risks due to the increased size of fetal parts and increased uterine vascularity. S&E remains a cornerstone of reproductive healthcare, offering a rapid and highly effective alternative to medical management, provided it is performed within the established first-trimester safety window
questions.learning: Suction and evacuation (S&E) is the preferred surgical method for the medical termination of pregnancy or the management of early miscarriage during the first trimester, typically up to 12 weeks of gestation.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: At physiological pH, the buffering action in blood is caused by which amino acid?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Histidine

At physiological pH, buffering action in blood is caused by histidine.

The imidazole group of histidine has a pKa value of 6.5-7.4, which is close to physiological pH.

Histidine is a positively charged amino acid which can exist in both its protonated (positively charged) and deprotonated (neutral) forms.

It acts as a buffer by accepting or donating protons (H+ ions) in response to changes in pH, helping to maintain the blood's pH within a narrow physiological range.

Hence, histidine has the maximum buffering capacity at physiological pH.
questions.learning: Histidine At physiological pH, buffering action in blood is caused by histidine. The imidazole group of histidine has a pKa value of 6.5-7.4, which is close to physiological pH.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A lady on oral contraceptive pills presented with white discharge per vaginum. It is not associated with itching or foul smell and stains her underwear yellow in color. Examination of the discharge revealed normal lactobacilli and acidic pH. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Increased normal vaginal discharge

In the given clinical scenario history of vaginal discharge with no itching and foul smell along with normal lactobacilli count with acidic pH is suggestive of normal vaginal discharge.

Leucorrhea is defined as an excessive normal vaginal discharge.

The term leucorrhea should fulfil the following criteria:

• The excess secretion is evident from persistent vulval moistness or staining of the undergarments (brownish yellow on drying) or need to wear a vulval pad.
• It is nonpurulent and nonoffensive.
• It is nonirritant and never causes pruritus.

The physiologic basis involved in normal vaginal secretion is dependent on the endogenous estrogen level. With the rising estrogen level, there is abundant secretory activity of the endocervical glands and the superficial vaginal epithelium becomes rich in glycogen

The normal secretion is expected to increase in conditions when the estrogen levels become high. Such conditions are :

• During puberty—Increased levels of endogenous estrogen lead to marked overgrowth of the endo- cervical epithelium which may encroach onto the ectocervix producing congenital ectopy (erosion) → increased secretion.
• During menstrual cycle

• Around ovulation-Peak rise of estrogen → increase in secretory activity of the cervical glands.
• Premenstrual pelvic congestion and increased mucus secretion from the hypertrophied endometrial glands.

• Pregnancy-There is hyperestrinism with increased vascularity. This leads to increased vaginal transudate and cervical gland secretion.
• During sexual excitement, when there is an abundant secretion from the Bartholin’s glands.

Other options:

Vaginal candidiasis: This condition generally presents with itching and a white, "cottage cheese"-like discharge. The absence of itching and the nature of the discharge described in the scenario rule out this option.

Bacterial vaginosis: This condition is characterized by a thin, gray, foul-smelling discharge. The fact that the discharge in this case does not have a foul smell rules out this option.

Chlamydial infection: Chlamydia infections can cause a range of symptoms, including abnormal vaginal discharge. However, many individuals with Chlamydia are asymptomatic, and the discharge associated with this condition does not typically stain underwear yellow.
questions.learning: Increased normal vaginal discharge — In the given clinical scenario history of vaginal discharge with no itching and foul smell along with normal lactobacilli count with acidic pH is suggestive of normal vaginal discharge.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old male presented with fever of 102°F with foul-smelling sputum for 5 days. On examination, clubbing was noted in the digits. Chest X-ray is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Lung abscess

Fever with foul-smelling sputum suggests an anaerobic lung infection.

Clubbing indicates a chronic suppurative lung disease, commonly seen with lung abscess.

Chest X-ray typically shows a cavity with an air–fluid level, distinguishing it from empyema or pneumothorax.

| Option | Condition | Key Feature | When it is Correct | Why NOT Correct Here | Exam Pearl

| ------ | --------- | ----------- | ------------------ | -------------------- | ----------

| A. Pneumatocele | Thin-walled cyst | Air-filled cavity | Post-infection (esp. staph) | ❌ No fluid level | Thin wall = key

| B. Empyema | Pleural pus | Pleural collection | Fluid in pleural space | ❌ Not intraparenchymal cavity | Lenticular opacity

| C. Pneumothorax | Air in pleura | Hyperlucent lung | Absent lung markings | ❌ No cavity or sputum | No fluid level

| D. Lung abscess ✅ | Necrotic lung infection | Air-fluid level cavity | ✔ Matches all features | ✔ Correct | Foul sputum = key clue

| Feature | Lung Abscess | Empyema

| ------- | ------------ | -------

| Location | Lung parenchyma | Pleural space

| Shape | Round cavity | Lenticular

| Air-fluid level | ✔ Present | Rare

| Sputum | Foul-smelling | Less prominent

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: In a nerve, why is it impossible to generate a new action potential if a second stimulus is applied during the depolarization phase of the current action potential?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sodium channels are opened

During the absolute refractory period (which corresponds to the depolarization phase and early repolarization of the action potential), voltage-gated sodium (Na⁺) channels are already open or in the inactivated state and cannot be reopened by another stimulus. Therefore, no second action potential can be generated, regardless of the strength of the stimulus.

Why not the other options?

• A. Sodium channels are closed: Incorrect. During depolarization, sodium channels are open initially and then become inactivated, which is the actual reason for the refractory period.
• C. Potassium channels are closed: Incorrect. Voltage-gated potassium channels open during repolarization, not during the early depolarization phase.
• D. Neurons are hyperpolarized: Incorrect. Hyperpolarization occurs during the relative refractory period, when a stronger-than-normal stimulus can generate another action potential.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A factory worker working in a plastic pipe factory presented to the OPD with weight loss and right upper quadrant abdominal pain of 6 months duration. He had hepatomegaly. Further investigation revealed that most of the liver was replaced by a hemorrhagic tumor with extensive necrosis. What can be the likely diagnosis in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Angiosarcoma of the liver

The diagnosis is angiosarcoma of the liver.

Angiosarcoma of the liver is usually seen in individuals having occupational exposure to agents such as vinyl chloride, arsenic, or thorotrast. The gross specimen of the liver  shows greyish white lesions, with multiple reddish-brown hemorrhagic foci and several blood-filled spaces .

Option A: Cavernous hemangiomas appear as red-blue, soft nodules, usually less than 2 cm in diameter. Their clinical significance is that they might be mistaken radiographically or intraoperatively for metastatic tumors.

Option B: Metastatic carcinoma of the liver has a gross appearance that shows multiple nodular lesions of variable size, replacing much of the normal parenchyma.

Option D: Primary hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) has a peak incidence around 20 to 40 years of age and is predominantly seen in men. The gross appearance shows unifocal or multifocal or diffusely infiltrative lesions that are paler than the surrounding tissue. The lesions may be greenish due to the presence of bile. Cirrhosis may be seen in about 50% of the cases. Intrahepatic metastases may be seen.
questions.learning: Angiosarcoma of the liver — The diagnosis is angiosarcoma of the liver. Angiosarcoma of the liver is usually seen in individuals having occupational exposure to agents such as vinyl chloride, arsenic, or thorotrast.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Consider the following statements with respect to endometrial cycle: 1. The basal zone is uninfluenced by any hormone. 2. Saw-toothed glandular epithelium is seen in secretory phase. 3. Stratum compactum contains mainly the glands and less stroma. 4. Pseudostratification is seen in proliferative phase of menstrual cycle. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 4

1. Basal zone is uninfluenced by hormones — Correct

• The stratum basale is relatively unaffected by cyclical hormonal changes and remains after menstruation.
• It serves as the source for regeneration of the functional layer.

2. Saw-toothed glandular epithelium is seen in secretory phase — Correct

• Under progesterone influence, endometrial glands become tortuous/coiled (“saw-toothed”) and begin secreting glycogen.

3. Stratum compactum contains mainly glands and less stroma — Incorrect

• The stratum compactum contains densely packed stromal cells and relatively fewer glands.
• The stratum spongiosum contains more prominent, dilated glands.

4. Pseudostratification is seen in proliferative phase — Correct

• During the estrogen-driven proliferative phase, the endometrial glands are relatively straight and show pseudostratified columnar epithelium.
questions.learning: Basal zone is uninfluenced by hormones — Correct • — The stratum basale is relatively unaffected by cyclical hormonal changes and remains after menstruation. • It serves as the source for regeneration of the functional layer.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 21-year-old girl suspects that the college principal is making a conspiracy against her and is planning to fail her in the upcoming exam. She feels that other teachers have also joined the conspiracy and students are helping them too. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Delusion of persecution

Thoughts of being harmed by people around themselves represent delusion of persecution. It is the most common type of delusion.

Delusion is a false, firm, fixed (unshakable) belief which is not in keeping with the patient’s socio-cultural and educational background.

Delusions are of two types based on their origin:

* Primary: Arise de-novo and cannot be explained based on previous experiences, characteristic of schizophrenia.

* Secondary: Delusions that are secondary to other morbid psychological conditions like depressive moods and hallucinations.

Pearl PF1258: Types of delusions

THE TYPES OF DELUSIONS

Delusion of control

False belief that a person’s will, thoughts, or feelings are being controlled by external forces.

Delusion of grandeur or Megalomania

Exaggerated conception of one’s importance, power, or identity.

Delusion of infidelity or morbid jealousy or Othello syndrome

False belief that one’s lover is unfaithful. Sometimes called pathological jealousy.

Delusion of love or erotomania

False belief that another person is in love with them. In De Clerambault syndrome, the woman believes that a man, frequently older and of higher status, is in love with her.

Delusion of misidentification

Capgras syndrome: Belief that a familiar person has been replaced by an exact double i.e. an impostor.

Fregoli syndrome: Person holds a delusional belief that different people are in fact a single person who changes his or her appearance or is in disguise.

Nihilistic delusion

False belief that oneself, others or the world, is non-existent or about to end. When nihilistic delusion is accompanied by ideas concerning bodily function failure e.g. putrefaction of intestine etc, it is called Cotard syndrome.

Delusion of infestation

False belief that one is infested with small but visible organisms. As a monosymptomatic delusional disorder, this is called Ekbom syndrome.

Delusion of persecution

The most common delusion. False belief of being harassed or persecuted.

Delusion of poverty

The person strongly believes they are financially incapacitated.

Delusion of reference

False belief that the behavior of others has a particular and unusual significance, usually of a negative nature. The person may falsely feel that others are talking about them (e.g. the people on television are talking to or about the person).

Delusion of self-accusation

False feeling of remorse and guilt. Seen in depression with psychotic features.
questions.learning: Delusion of persecution Thoughts of being harmed by people around themselves represent delusion of persecution. It is the most common type of delusion.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient presenting with hypercalcemia is found to have multiple pancreatic lesions on evaluation. Further assessment is performed to identify an underlying inherited genetic syndrome. Which of the following statements regarding this condition is correct?
options: Patients should be screened for RET gene mutations
There is an increased risk of thyroid cancer arising from follicular cells
Prophylactic thyroidectomy is indicated in such patients
Menin proto-oncogene mutation is associated with MEN 1
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Menin proto-oncogene mutation is associated with MEN 1

Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 1 (MEN 1), an autosomal dominant syndrome caused by mutation of the MEN1 tumor suppressor gene (menin) on chromosome 11q13. It is classically characterized by tumors of the Parathyroid glands, Pancreatic islet cells, and Pituitary gland (“3 Ps”). In a patient with hypercalcemia (primary hyperparathyroidism) and multiple pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors, MEN 1 should be strongly suspected.

Why not the other options?

• A. Patients should be screened for RET gene mutations: RET mutations are associated with MEN 2A and MEN 2B, not MEN 1.
• B. There is an increased risk of thyroid cancer arising from follicular cells: MEN 2 is associated with medullary thyroid carcinoma, which arises from parafollicular C cells, not follicular cells.
• C. Prophylactic thyroidectomy is indicated in such patients: Recommended in RET mutation carriers (MEN 2) to prevent medullary thyroid carcinoma; not indicated in MEN 1.
questions.learning: Menin proto-oncogene mutation is associated with MEN 1 Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 1 (MEN 1), an autosomal dominant syndrome caused by mutation of the MEN1 tumor suppressor gene (menin) on chromosome 11q13.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 45-year-old patient with a tibial fracture in a cast presented to the emergency department with complaints of intense pain. The cast was removed and on examination, passive extension was painful. The dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses were present and there was a loss of sensation over the first web space. What is the next step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Measure anterior compartment pressure

The clinical presentation of this patient with a history of tibial fracture complaining of intense pain, with painful passive extension and loss of sensation of the first web space upon the removal of the cast, is suggestive of acute compartment syndrome. The next step would be to measure the anterior compartment pressure to confirm the diagnosis.

Acute compartment syndrome refers to the rise in intra-compartmental pressure leading to tissue ischemia and necrosis. The injuries at high risk of developing acute compartment syndrome are fractures of the proximal one-third of the tibia, soft tissue injury, distal radius fracture, and diaphyseal fracture of the forearm. Other high-risk injuries are crush injuries and circumferential burns.

The classic features of ischemia in acute compartment syndrome include the 5 Ps:

• Pain: is the first symptom of acute compartment syndrome. On passive stretching of the muscles, severe pain can be elicited.
• Paresthesia: paresthesia and hypoesthesia are the first signs of nerve ischemia.
• Paralysis: paralysis of muscle groups affected in that compartment is a late sign.
• Pulselessness: usually, the peripheral pulses and capillary return are intact in the early stages, unless there is a major arterial injury. If pulses are absent, arteriography is indicated.
• Pallor: may not always be seen as ischemia occurs at the capillary level.

The diagnosis can be confirmed by measuring the intra-compartmental pressure using a split catheter introduced into the compartment. The difference between diastolic pressure and compartment pressure is known as differential pressure (ΔP). If the differential pressure (ΔP) is less than 30 mm Hg, immediate compartment decompression is indicated.

Treatment:

• Prompt decompression of the affected compartment is done.
• All the dressings, bandages, and cast on the affected limb are removed and the limb is nursed flat.
• Fasciotomy is done if the differential pressure is less than 30 mm Hg
• Fasciotomy wounds are left open and observed after 2 days. If there is necrosis, debridement is done. If the wounds are healthy, they can be sutured without tension or skin grafting can be done.
questions.learning: Measure anterior compartment pressure — The clinical presentation of this patient with a history of tibial fracture complaining of intense pain, with painful passive extension and loss of sensation of the first web space upon the removal of the cast, is…

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient comes to the casualty with a severe headache. His BP was found to be 160/100 mmHg. CT scan revealed a subarachnoid hemorrhage. What is the next best step in the management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Angiography

In this patient with subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), the next step is to do an angiography to see the vascular anatomy and identify the site of bleed.

Trauma is the commonest cause of subarachnoid hemorrhage. Spontaneous SAH usually results from the rupture of an aneurysm or an arterio-venous malformation (AVM). Patients present with a sudden and severe headache which is different from any headache they have experienced before. This is described as a thunderclap headache. Other symptoms include meningitic features like neck rigidity and photophobia, impaired consciousness, intraocular hemorrhages, with or without focal neurological deficits. Compression from a posterior communicating artery aneurysm would result in third nerve palsy.

Non-contrast CT head is the first imaging to be done in a suspected case, which would confirm bleeding in more than 98% of cases. In patients with high suspicion and a negative CT, lumbar puncture is done to detect hemoglobin breakdown products like oxyhemoglobin and bilirubin. After confirming the diagnosis, CT or MR angiography is done to locate the aneurysms or AVM. Digital subtraction angiography remains the gold standard investigation.

The definitive management of subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) is done surgically by craniotomy and clipping or by endovascular embolization known as coiling. This prevents rebleeding of the aneurysm.

Patients with subarachnoid hemorrhage are at risk of developing complications such as rebleeding, cerebral vasospasm, hydrocephalus, seizures, and hyponatremia. Early recognition and management of these complications are essential to improve outcomes. In addition to surgery and nimodipine, other management strategies for SAH include strict blood pressure control, analgesia for headache, antiemetics, and anticonvulsants if seizures occur. Maintaining a close monitoring of the patient's neurological status, intracranial pressure, and electrolytes is also crucial.

Other Options

Nimodipine: Although it is used to prevent cerebral vasospasm and delayed ischemic neurological deficits, it is not the immediate next step in the management of SAH. Angiography is needed first to locate the aneurysms or AVM. It is administered after the procedure.
Surgery: Although surgery is an important management option for SAH, it is not the immediate next step. Angiography must be done first to identify the site of the bleed and plan for the appropriate surgical or endovascular intervention.
Fibrinolytic therapy: This option is not appropriate for the management of SAH as it may exacerbate the bleeding. Fibrinolytic therapy is used in the treatment of ischemic stroke, not hemorrhagic stroke.
questions.learning: Angiography — In this patient with subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), the next step is to do an angiography to see the vascular anatomy and identify the site of bleed.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which vitamin can be deficient in a patient who has undergone gastrectomy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vitamin B12

Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency is common after gastrectomy due to loss of intrinsic factor (IF) production.

• Parietal cells of stomach produce intrinsic factor
• IF is essential for absorption of vitamin B12 in the terminal ileum
• Gastrectomy → ↓ intrinsic factor → impaired B12 absorption

Consequences:

• Megaloblastic anemia
• Neurological manifestations (subacute combined degeneration)

o    Paresthesia

o    Loss of vibration & position sense

o    UMN signs

Why other options are incorrect:

• Vitamin A: Fat-soluble, absorbed in intestine
• Vitamin C: Absorbed directly, not IF-dependent
• Vitamin D: Fat-soluble, not affected by intrinsic factor
questions.learning: Vitamin B12 Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency is common after gastrectomy due to loss of intrinsic factor (IF) production. • Parietal cells of stomach produce intrinsic factor • IF is essential for absorption of vitamin B12 in the terminal ileum •…

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following options best defines the correct sequence of the phases of the demographic cycle?
options: High expanding→ Early stationary → Late expanding → Low stationary → Declining
High stationary → Early expanding → Late expanding → Low stationary → Declining
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. High stationary → Early expanding → Late expanding → Low stationary → Declining

The correct sequence of the phases of the demographic cycle is High stationary → Early expanding → Late expanding → Low stationary → Declining.

India is currently in the "late expanding" stage which is the third stage in the demographic cycle where declining death rates and declining birth rates are seen.

Another important concept of the demographic cycle is the demographic gap which is the difference between birth rate and death rate. The demographic gap is maximum in the early-expanding phase, characterized by a high birth rate and low death rate. As the demography of the country transitions to the late-expanding phase, both birth rate and death rate falls causing a decreasing demographic gap. Although the birth rate is falling in the late-expanding phase, it is still higher than the death rate, which causes the population to increase.
questions.learning: High stationary → Early expanding → Late expanding → Low stationary → Declining The correct sequence of the phases of the demographic cycle is High stationary → Early expanding → Late expanding → Low stationary → Declining.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: What is the appropriate next step in the management of a 22-year-old primigravida at 10 weeks of gestation who presents with nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, inability to tolerate fluids, and recent-onset right upper quadrant pain, and is diagnosed with acute appendicitis?
questions.explanation: Acute appendicitis is a surgical emergency that requires definitive intervention regardless of the patient's pregnancy status. In a pregnant woman, the risk of appendiceal rupture is higher, and rupture significantly increases the risk of fetal loss and maternal sepsis. Therefore, the immediate subsequent course of action is to perform an appendicectomy (Option A). Waiting until the 2nd trimester (Option B) is dangerous, as the infection will progress rapidly. Conservative management (Option C) with antibiotics alone has a high failure rate and is not the standard of care for acute appendicitis in pregnancy. Reassurance (Option D) is inappropriate for a surgical emergency. Laparoscopic or open appendicectomy in the first trimester is generally considered safe for the fetus. The patient's presentation of RUQ pain is common in later pregnancy due to uterine displacement of the appendix, but even at 10 weeks, surgical removal is mandatory

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: In which phase of clinical trials is drug dosing done?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Phase I

The dosing of a new drug is tested in phase I of a clinical trial.

Phase I trials are usually performed on healthy volunteers to check the safety and pharmacokinetic properties of a drug. The participants in this phase do not gain any direct health benefits from taking part. They are generally paid a fee for their time, with the payments being regulated and not related to the risk involved.

In clinical trials, drug dosing typically occurs in Phase I, where researchers establish the optimal dose to achieve desired effects while minimizing side effects. In these phases, they focus on safety, tolerability, and pharmacokinetics.

Dose-ranging, primarily conducted in Phase II trials, involves testing multiple doses to identify the most effective and safe dose range. This phase helps determine the minimum effective dose and maximum tolerated dose, providing critical data for subsequent studies in Phase 3, where the chosen dose is tested for efficacy and safety in a larger population.
questions.learning: Phase I — The dosing of a new drug is tested in phase I of a clinical trial. Phase I trials are usually performed on healthy volunteers to check the safety and pharmacokinetic properties of a drug.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 65-year-old elderly diabetic female presents to the emergency department with complaints of a sudden onset of severe pain in one eye, marked redness, blurred vision, and headache. On examination, there is a hazy cornea with a mid-dilated and fixed pupil with a shallow anterior chamber. What is the likely diagnosis in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Acute angle closure glaucoma

This is a case of acute angle-closure glaucoma, which typically presents with sudden onset of a painful red eye, corneal haze, a mid-dilated fixed pupil, and a shallow anterior chamber.

Angle-closure glaucoma involves a sudden increase in intraocular pressure due to blockage of the anterior chamber angle. It is characterized by severe eye pain, blurred vision, and a mid-dilated pupil, with diffuse redness rather than the circumcorneal congestion seen in uveitis. It has constantly raised IOP >21mmHg, optic disc cupping, and visual field defects.

The primary goal in managing Primary Angle-Closure Glaucoma (PACG) is to prevent optic nerve damage by reducing IOP. In acute attacks, treatment involves aggressively lowering IOP using intravenous mannitol and oral acetazolamide to quickly control symptoms. Topical medications such as pilocarpine, beta-blockers, cholinergic agents, and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors are also used to address the acute episode.

Once the immediate crisis is managed, YAG laser iridotomy (YAG PI) is performed to create an alternate drainage pathway for the aqueous humor, both in the affected eye and the fellow eye. For ongoing management, patients with PACG may require glaucoma medications to maintain target IOP. In cases where maximal medical therapy fails, surgical options such as trabeculectomy or glaucoma drainage devices may be necessary, particularly if there is progressive visual field loss or non-compliance with treatment. Cyclodestructive procedures may be considered for patients with a painful, blind eye or those with recurrent surgical failures.

Signs:

Corneal edema- coloured halos
Conjunctiva- congestion, chemosis
IOP- elevated 40–70 mm Hg
AC- very shallow
Pupil- vertically oval, mid-dilated
Angle- completely closed, Grade 0

Other options:

Option B: Retinal detachment presents with painless, sudden loss of vision, photopsia (flashes), floaters, curtain falling sensation. No corneal haze or painful red eye.

Option C: Open-angle glaucoma is chronic, asymptomatic until late. Gradual painless loss of peripheral vision (tunnel vision).No redness, no acute pain.

Option D: Acute uveitis presents with painful red eye but typically has constricted pupil (miosis), not mid-dilated fixed. Aqueous flare, keratic precipitates may be seen. No shallow anterior chamber.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is the use of Shakir's tape?
questions.explanation: Shakir's tape (also known as Mid-Upper Arm Circumference or MUAC tape) is a simple, cost-effective, and portable tool used for the rapid assessment of nutritional status in children. It is a classic example of appropriate technology, which refers to health solutions that are easy to use, locally adaptable, and accessible to non-medical personnel (like ASHA workers) in resource-limited settings. The tape is color-coded (Red <11.5 cm indicates severe malnutrition) for easy interpretation. Regarding the distractors, intersectoral coordination (Option A) and community participation (Option D) are principles of primary health care that involve teamwork between sectors or citizens, while equitable distribution (Option B) refers to the fair allocation of resources. While the tape facilitates community-level screening, its inherent nature as a simplified diagnostic device classifies it as appropriate technology
questions.learning: Shakir's tape (also known as Mid-Upper Arm Circumference or MUAC tape) is a simple, cost-effective, and portable tool used for the rapid assessment of nutritional status in children.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: For a sick child aged 4 years, which of the following are signs of “severe pneumonia or very severe disease”, as per IMNCI (Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illness) Program? I. Fast breathing (≥40 breaths/minute) II. Child vomits everything III. Stridor in a calm child IV. Chest indrawing Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. II and III

According to the IMNCI (Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illness) guidelines, a child aged 2 months to 5 years is classified as having severe pneumonia or very severe disease if any general danger sign is present or if there is stridor in a calm child.

• I. Fast breathing (≥40 breaths/minute) ✘

• Fast breathing alone is classified as pneumonia, not severe pneumonia or very severe disease.
• For children 12 months to 5 years, fast breathing is ≥40 breaths/minute.

• II. Child vomits everything ✔

• This is a general danger sign in IMNCI and indicates severe pneumonia or very severe disease.

• III. Stridor in a calm child ✔

• Stridor at rest (in a calm child) indicates upper airway obstruction and is classified as severe pneumonia or very severe disease.

• IV. Chest indrawing ✘

• According to the revised IMNCI/WHO guidelines, chest indrawing alone is classified as pneumonia, not severe pneumonia (provided there are no danger signs).

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 17-year-old male patient presents with dull aching pain over the back of his ankle. There is tenderness on firm palpation of the swelling. The following findings are seen on X-ray. What is the likely diagnosis in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Exostosis

According to the clinical scenario and given X-ray, Exostosis of the bone is the most likely diagnosis.

Exostoses can cause chronic pain ranging from mild to debilitatingly severe, depending on the shape, size, and location of the lesion. It is most commonly found in places like the ribs, where small bone growths form, but sometimes larger growths can grow on places like the ankles, knees, shoulders, elbows and hips. Very rarely are they on the skull. Exostoses can be seen in different types: calcaneal spurs, osteomyelitis, Charcot foot, osteochondroma, and hereditary multiple exostoses.

In osteochondroma, the tumour stops enlarging in size once there is a cessation of growth at the epiphyseal plate. It appears as a small bony protrusion at metaphysis on X-ray. They are benign and rarely transform into chondrosarcomas. They are commonly seen around the knee joint (distal femur) or foot.

Option A: Chondrosarcoma are the second most common primary malignant tumors that occurs in any site of the bone. It presents in 3rd to 7th decade of life and is slow growing, with deep pain and/or shows an enlarging mass. Most commonly involves proximal femur, pelvis and proximal humerus.

X-ray features: Large, intraosseous and osteolytic tumors. Irregular and granular calcifications present which shows a characteristic “honeycomb” or “popcorn”appearance.

Option B: Osteoclastoma has a soap bubble appearance on X-ray and typically affects individuals 20-40 years of age. Axial skeleton involvement is not common

Option D: X-ray features of osteosarcoma: Ill-defined, bone forming lesion showing characteristic Codman’s triangle due to periosteal reaction . Sunburst appearance when the periosteum does not have enough time to lay down a new layer.
