questions.learning: Exostosis According to the clinical scenario and given X-ray, Exostosis of the bone is the most likely diagnosis. Exostoses can cause chronic pain ranging from mild to debilitatingly severe, depending on the shape, size, and location of the lesion.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Comment on the report given below: pH 7.17, Na+ 139.7mEq.L, pCO2 25.7mmHg, K+ 5.1mEq.L, p02 97mm Hg, Blood glucose 334mg. dL, SatO2 99%, HCO3 std 17.4mEq.L, BE (-8.6)
questions.explanation: This is a clinical interpretation of an arterial blood gas (ABG). The pH of 7.17 indicates significant acidemia. The bicarbonate (HCO3) level of 17.4 mEq/L is low, and the Base Excess (BE) of -8.6 confirms a deficit of base. These findings define metabolic acidosis. The pCO2 of 25.7 mmHg is low, which represents a respiratory compensation (the patient is hyperventilating) to try and raise the pH. In respiratory acidosis (Option A), the pCO2 would be high. In alkalosis (Options B and D), the pH would be above 7.45. Notably, the high blood glucose of 334 mg/dL (Option C) strongly suggests that the cause of this metabolic acidosis is Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA). DKA is a life-threatening emergency requiring intensive fluid resuscitation, potassium management, and a continuous insulin infusion to shut down the production of ketones
questions.learning: This is a clinical interpretation of an arterial blood gas (ABG). The pH of 7.17 indicates significant acidemia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which medication is preferred for treating migratory polyarthritis and joint pain in a patient with acute rheumatic fever?
questions.explanation: Migratory polyarthritis is the most common major manifestation of Acute Rheumatic Fever (ARF). The joints are extremely painful, but the inflammation responds dramatically and rapidly to salicylates. Aspirin (high-dose) remains the preferred drug for managing the arthritis and general inflammatory symptoms of ARF. Furosemide (Option A) and Digoxin (Option B) are used in the management of heart failure (carditis), but not for the primary treatment of joint pain. Amiodarone (Option D) is an anti-arrhythmic not used in the routine management of ARF. The response to aspirin is so specific that if the joint pain does not resolve within 48-72 hours, the diagnosis of ARF should be reconsidered. Once the acute phase is managed, the most critical intervention is long-term secondary prophylaxis with Benzathine Penicillin to prevent further streptococcal infections and progressive heart valve damage
questions.learning: Migratory polyarthritis is the most common major manifestation of Acute Rheumatic Fever (ARF). The joints are extremely painful, but the inflammation responds dramatically and rapidly to salicylates.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with coronary artery disease presents to you with chest pain and palpitations. The ECG is shown below. Which of the following can be used in the management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Intravenous amiodarone

The clinical scenario along with the ECG points to a diagnosis of ventricular tachycardia. Intravenous amiodarone (class III antiarrhythmic) can be used in the management of this condition.

The patient here complaining of chest pain, and palpitations and has ECG changes showing wide QRS complex tachycardia with absent p waves is likely to have acute ventricular tachycardia. Since the patient is stable and has an underlying coronary artery disease the drug of choice is intravenous amiodarone.

Ventricular tachycardias can be defined as three or more pre-ventricular contractions at a rate >100/minute.

ECG changes include wide QRS complexes, absence of P waves, and ventriculoatrial dissociation. It can be broadly classified as sustained VT or non-sustained VT. Nonsustained VT has QRS complexes lasting <30 seconds while sustained VT lasts for >30 seconds. In monomorphic VT, all QRS complexes look the same. Polymorphic VT has QRS complexes varying in shape or direction in the same lead.

Most monomorphic VT have an underlying cardiac disease. Symptoms of ventricular tachycardia include palpitations, syncope, and shortness of breath.

In a hemodynamically stable patient, amiodarone, procainamide, and lidocaine can be used to treat the condition. In the presence of heart disease, intravenous amiodarone is the drug of choice. In hemodynamically unstable patients, electrical cardioversion is done. Further management depends on the underlying heart condition and frequency of VT. Frequent episodes warrant the use of antiarrhythmics or catheter ablation.

Torsades de Pointes is a type of polymorphic VT occurring with QT prolongation. It can progress to ventricular fibrillation which is treated with defibrillation. Recurrent episodes can be managed with intravenous magnesium sulfate.

Other causes of wide QRS complexes include supraventricular tachycardias with bundle branch block and Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome.

Other options:

Options A and D: Metoprolol is a selective β1-antagonist and a class II antiarrhythmic. It can be used in hypertension, angina, and heart failure. The intravenous form can be used for initial management in acute myocardial infarction.

Option B: Oral amiodarone can be used in the chronic treatment of atrial fibrillation, ventricular tachycardia, and ventricular fibrillation. It has shown a modest beneficial effect on mortality after acute myocardial infarction.
questions.learning: Intravenous amiodarone — The clinical scenario along with the ECG points to a diagnosis of ventricular tachycardia. Intravenous amiodarone (class III antiarrhythmic) can be used in the management of this condition.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is false regarding confounding factor?
options: It can be reduced by matching
It is associated individually with both cause and effect
It is distributed equally in both study and control groups
It is associated with the exposure of the study
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. It is distributed equally in both study and control groups

A confounding factor is a factor that is associated with both exposure and diseases and is distributed unequally in study and control groups. It can be reduced by matching.

For example, if the study is that a sedentary lifestyle can lead to coronary artery diseases, then age can act as a confounding factor as it is individually linked to both sedentary lifestyle and coronary artery diseases.
questions.learning: It is distributed equally in both study and control groups A confounding factor is a factor that is associated with both exposure and diseases and is distributed unequally in study and control groups.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presents with a hypopigmented patch behind the ear with loss of sensation. Neck examination reveals a thickened structure, as shown in the image below. What is this structure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Greater auricular nerve

In the given clinical scenario, the patient presents with a hypopigmented patch behind the ear accompanied by loss of sensation, and neck examination reveals a thickened structure suggestive of leprosy, and the thickened structure is the greater auricular nerve.

Great auricular nerve:

It is the largest ascending branch of the cervical plexus and arises from the second and third cervical spinal nerves. It winds over the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle and ascends upwards. On reaching the parotid gland it divides into the anterior and posterior branches:

* The anterior branch supplies the facial skin over the parotid gland and joins the facial nerve in the gland.

* The posterior branch supplies the skin over the mastoid process, the lower part of the back of the auricle, lobule and concha.

Clinical considerations:

* The nerve can be thickened in conditions like leprosy and can be palpated over the upper part of the sternocleidomastoid muscle. (as seen in the above image). Leprosy is a chronic granulomatous condition caused by Mycobacterium leprae. It affects the skin, cutaneous and peripheral nerves, and mucous membranes. The most commonly affected peripheral nerves are the posterior tibial, ulnar, median, and lateral popliteal nerves. The most frequently involved cranial nerve is the facial nerve. It commonly presents as an area of numbness on the skin or a visible skin lesion, which could be a hypopigmented or erythematous macule.

* Cross-inervation between the somatic sensory supply (great auricular nerve) and the parasympathetic secretomotor fibers to the parotid gland is considered an anatomical basis for the phenomenon of Frey's syndrome (gustatory sweating).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 28-year-old man sustains a head injury while playing soccer, briefly loses consciousness, then regains full awareness and engages normally. Several hours later, he develops a severe headache, confusion, and drowsiness. Which type of brain injury is classically associated with this pattern of a lucid interval following the initial trauma?
questions.explanation: The clinical pattern of an initial loss of consciousness followed by a temporary period of recovery—termed a "lucid interval"—is the classic hallmark of an Epidural Hematoma (EDH) . This condition typically results from a blow to the side of the head, causing a skull fracture that lacerates the middle meningeal artery. The high-pressure arterial bleeding slowly peels the dura away from the skull. During the lucid interval, the patient appears neurologically intact while the hematoma expands. Once the intracranial pressure reaches a critical threshold, rapid deterioration occurs, leading to symptoms like severe headache, confusion, and eventually coma. Subdural hemorrhage (Option A) usually follows a more gradual onset, often in elderly patients or infants. Subarachnoid hemorrhage (Option D) classically presents as a sudden "thunderclap" headache. Parenchymal hemorrhage (Option B) involves bleeding within the brain tissue itself. Because the specific "lucid interval" sequence is pathognomonic for middle meningeal arterial bleeding, Epidural hematoma is the definitive diagnosis
questions.learning: The clinical pattern of an initial loss of consciousness followed by a temporary period of recovery—termed a "lucid interval"—is the classic hallmark of an Epidural Hematoma (EDH) .

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Spanish windlass is a type of which strangulation method?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Garrotting

Spanish windlass is an improvised version of garrotting, and it involves tightening an iron collar (Spanish windlass) around the neck and forcing a spike against the neck into the spinal cord.

This was a form of judicial execution once employed in Spain. The rod-like object used to tighten the ligature is called a Spanish windlass; this may be a ruler, stick, or screwdriver.

Garrotting involves attacking the victim from behind using a ligature. The ligature is thrown over the victim’s neck and then tightened by twisting with a lever.

The image given below shows garrotting.

Option A: Squeezing to death using sticks is called bansdola. The neck or the chest is squeezed between two sticks, one placed in front, and one behind. The neck may also be squeezed with a single stick in front if the victim is lying down.

Option C: Squeezing the neck with the arm and forearm is called mugging. The image below shows mugging.

Option D: Throttling or manual strangulation occurs due to compression of the neck by humans leading to asphyxia. Thumb impression and finger marks may be seen over the victim's neck.
questions.learning: Garrotting Spanish windlass is an improvised version of garrotting, and it involves tightening an iron collar (Spanish windlass) around the neck and forcing a spike against the neck into the spinal cord.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding hepatic adenomas are correct? 1. They are almost exclusively seen in females aged 25–50 years. 2. They are associated with use of oral contraceptive pills. 3. They do not have any malignant potential. 4. Majority are detected incidentally on imaging. Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2 and 4

Hepatic adenoma is a benign liver tumor seen predominantly in young women and is strongly associated with long-term oral contraceptive pill (OCP) use. Most lesions are incidentally detected on imaging, but they carry a risk of hemorrhage and malignant transformation.

Why are the statements correct/incorrect?

• 1. Almost exclusively seen in females aged 25–50 years ✔️: Correct.
• 2. Associated with oral contraceptive pill use ✔️: Correct.
• 3. They do not have any malignant potential ❌: Incorrect. They can undergo malignant transformation (especially β-catenin-mutated adenomas).
• 4. Majority are detected incidentally on imaging ✔️: Correct.
questions.learning: 1, 2 and 4 Hepatic adenoma is a benign liver tumor seen predominantly in young women and is strongly associated with long-term oral contraceptive pill (OCP) use.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is not the mechanism of action of progesterone only pills?
options: Kills the sperms in the cervical canal
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Kills the sperms in the cervical canal

Minipills or progesterone-only pills (POP) do not kill sperm in the cervical canal. Progesterone-only pills act by thickening the cervical mucus (the main mechanism of all POPs except cerazette) that inhibits penetration of sperms, inhibiting tubal motility, and suppressing ovulation.

Other advantages of POPs include a reduction in the incidence of pelvic inflammatory diseases and sexually transmitted diseases (due to thickened cervical mucus).

Due to the inhibition of tubal motility, the absolute risk of all pregnancies including ectopic pregnancy decreases, while the relative risk of ectopic pregnancy increases. But a previous history of ectopic pregnancy is not a contraindication for POP.

POPs do not affect clotting, lipid metabolism, and carbohydrate metabolism. So they can safely be used by women who are obese, breastfeeding, hypertensive, have SLE or a history of thromboembolism, diabetic with vascular disease. Significant adverse effects of POPs are irregular bleeding (mostly scanty), and secondary amenorrhea after longtime usage as it causes endometrial atrophy.

Contraindications for POPs include undiagnosed vaginal bleeding, pregnancy, known or suspected breast cancer, and benign or malignant liver tumors.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Match the following types of larval migrations with their causative organisms:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. A–3, B–2, C–1, D–4

Larval migration syndromes are classified based on the site and pattern of larval movement in humans.

• Cutaneous larva migrans → caused by Ancylostoma braziliense

Presents as serpiginous, itchy tracks in the skin due to larvae migrating within epidermis
• Visceral larva migrans → caused by Toxocara canis

Larvae migrate through internal organs (liver, lungs), causing eosinophilia and organ damage
• Larva currens → caused by Strongyloides stercoralis

Rapidly moving, linear urticarial tracks due to autoinfection
• Swimmer’s itch → caused by Schistosoma cercariae (Non human-Animal or avian Schistosoma)

Cercariae penetrate skin causing pruritic papular rash without completing lifecycle in humans

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 5-year-old child with a history of strabismus (squint) presents for a routine eye examination. Visual acuity testing shows reduced vision in the squinting eye compared to the other eye. Which drug is commonly used to perform refraction in children with squint?
questions.explanation: For a child with a squint (strabismus) and suspected amblyopia ("lazy eye"), a precise refractive evaluation is the most critical first step. 1% Atropine (Option A) is the gold standard cycloplegic agent used for refraction in this population. Atropine provides the most potent and consistent paralysis of the ciliary muscle, ensuring that the child's active accommodation is completely neutralized to reveal the true refractive error. Cyclopentolate (Option B) and Homatropine (Option D) are also cycloplegics but are less potent and typically reserved for older children without squint. Tropicamide (Option C) is a short-acting mydriatic used primarily for fundus examination rather than cycloplegic refraction in young children. Atropine is typically applied as an ointment for three days prior to the examination. Clinicians must warn parents about potential systemic side effects like facial flushing or fever. Correcting the full hypermetropic error revealed by atropine refraction is often the primary treatment for accommodative squints
questions.learning: For a child with a squint (strabismus) and suspected amblyopia ("lazy eye"), a precise refractive evaluation is the most critical first step. 1% Atropine (Option A) is the gold standard cycloplegic agent used for refraction in this population.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: What is the drug of choice for gastrointestinal stromal tumors?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Imatinib

Imatinib is the drug of choice for gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST).

Imatinib is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor. It has a dominant role in tumors involving ABL, KIT, or EGFR kinases. It is the chemotherapy agent of choice in the chronic phase of chronic myelogenous leukaemia (CML) and GIST.

Adverse effects:

* Gastrointestinal symptoms like diarrhea, nausea, and vomiting

* Fluid retention, edema, and periorbital swelling

* Myelosuppression

Gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST) are mesenchymal tumors originating from the interstitial cells of Cajal, located in the gastrointestinal myenteric plexus. The most common mutation is the c-KIT mutation. GIST can also occur with SDH mutation and NF-1 mutation in neurofibromatosis-1.

GIST has specific tumor markers i.e., CD117 (c-KIT mutation) and DOG-1.

Succinyl dehydrogenase deficient (SDH) deficient GIST is commonly seen in Carney’s triad.

Carney’s triad:

* Gastric GIST (succinyl dehydrogenase deficient)

* Pulmonary chondroma

* Extra adrenal paraganglioma

Microscopically, GIST has elongated spindle cells or plumper epithelioid cells, or a mixed pattern.The below image shows the microscopy of GIST composed of bundles, or fascicles, of spindle-shaped tumor cells.

Imatinib can be used to treat GIST with mutations in KIT or PDGFRA. Succinate dehydrogenase (SDH) - deficient GIST is imatinib-resistant, so sunitinib, sorafenib, or regorafenib can be used instead.

During surgical resection of GIST, care must be taken to prevent capsule rupture, which causes seeding of nearby tissues leading to relapse in 100% of the cases. If capsule rupture occurs, adjuvant therapy with imatinib is indicated regardless of tumor extent.

Other options:

Option A: Sunitinib is a multiple kinase inhibitor that is used in imatinib-resistant GIST and pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors.

Option C: Sorafenib is also a multiple kinase inhibitor that is used in the treatment of renal cancer and imatinib-resistant GIST.

Option D: Dasatinib is a BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase inhibitor and is used in imatinib-resistant CML.
questions.learning: Imatinib Imatinib is the drug of choice for gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST). Imatinib is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 22-year-old pregnant lady presented with a fever and was started on antibiotics. The fever did not subside. On further investigation, she was diagnosed to have septic pelvic thrombophlebitis. Which among the following is the next course of treatment for her?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Antibiotics+Heparin

Antibiotics plus heparin is the next course of treatment for septic pelvic thrombophlebitis.

Septic pelvic thrombophlebitis (SPT) refers to the pelvic infection with thrombosis of one/both ovarian veins. The pathogenesis of this disease is due to the spreading uterine infection (secondary to trauma of delivery or surgery) combined with the hypercoagulable state of the pregnancy (thrombus formation).

The patients usually present with constant lower abdominal pain and occasionally with a palpable tender sausage-shaped mass (most diagnostic finding, but rare).

SPT is usually suspected when the fever fails to respond to antibiotic therapy. It can be confirmed by computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the abdomen and pelvis. Patients are treated with a combination of heparin and broad-spectrum antibiotics. Anticoagulation is done to prevent further thrombosis and reduce the spread of septic emboli.

Note: The use of anticoagulation is controversial as not all clinicians favor it. A small randomized study did not demonstrate a benefit, but the majority accept short-term anticoagulation as a part of the treatment regimen.
questions.learning: Antibiotics+Heparin Antibiotics plus heparin is the next course of treatment for septic pelvic thrombophlebitis. Septic pelvic thrombophlebitis (SPT) refers to the pelvic infection with thrombosis of one/both ovarian veins.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following junctions is/are calcium dependent? A. Desmosomes B. Tight junctions C. Adherens junctions D. Gap junctions
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. A & C

Calcium-dependent cell junctions are those that use cadherins, which require Ca²⁺ for proper adhesion between cells.

Calcium-dependent junctions:

• Desmosomes → mediated by desmogleins and desmocollins (cadherins)
• Adherens junctions → mediated by E-cadherin

Calcium-independent junctions:

• Tight junctions → formed by claudins and occludins
• Gap junctions → formed by connexins (connexons) for cell-to-cell communication

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The next step to follow for a mother with Rh-negative pregnancy and antibody titre above critical level (husband Rh-positive) is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. MCA PSV

In an Rh-negative pregnancy with a positive antibody screen and antibody titre above the critical level, the fetus is at risk of hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn (HDFN).

The next step is to assess for fetal anemia non-invasively using the middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity (MCA-PSV) by Doppler.

• A. Umbilical artery Doppler: Mainly assesses placental resistance and fetal growth restriction, not fetal anemia.
• B. Cordocentesis: Invasive and used when fetal anemia is suspected/confirmed, particularly for diagnostic assessment and possible intrauterine transfusion.
• C. MCA PSV — Correct: MCA-PSV >1.5 MoM is suggestive of moderate-to-severe fetal anemia.
• D. Amniocentesis: Historically used for bilirubin assessment, but has largely been replaced by MCA Doppler for fetal anemia surveillance.
questions.learning: MCA PSV — In an Rh-negative pregnancy with a positive antibody screen and antibody titre above the critical level, the fetus is at risk of hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn (HDFN).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the recommended work area per worker in a factory, assuming that any height above a certain limit is disregarded in the calculation?
questions.explanation: The Factories Act in India establishes strict guidelines to prevent overcrowding and ensure worker safety and ventilation. Every workroom must provide at least 500 cubic feet of space for every individual worker employed therein. When calculating this volume, the Act specifies that any height above 14 feet (approximately 4.25 meters) from the floor is not taken into account. This rule ensures that employers provide sufficient horizontal floor area rather than meeting the requirement through very high ceilings in cramped rooms. Options A, C, and D (100, 300, and 400) are below the legal safety threshold. Maintaining this standard is essential for reducing the spread of airborne infections, minimizing heat stress, and ensuring that workers have enough room to operate machinery without accidental collisions. Compliance with these spacing requirements is a critical part of regular occupational health and safety inspections
questions.learning: The Factories Act in India establishes strict guidelines to prevent overcrowding and ensure worker safety and ventilation. Every workroom must provide at least 500 cubic feet of space for every individual worker employed therein.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 56-year-old female patient presented with progressive dysphagia for solids, loss of weight, and loss of appetite. A barium swallow done is given below. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Carcinoma esophagus

A patient with the given history and barium swallow findings of irregular narrowing, mucosal destruction, and shouldered margins of esophagus, are suggestive of carcinoma esophagus.

Esophageal carcinoma is more common in men, with tobacco use and alcohol being the strongest risk factors. The squamous cell carcinoma variant usually affects the upper 2/3rd, and the adenocarcinoma variant usually affects the lower 1/3rd of the esophagus. Clinical features include progressive dysphagia (most common), regurgitation of food, vomiting, odynophagia and weight loss.

On barium swallow, carcinoma esophagus presents with irregular narrowing and ulceration of esophagus. Flexible endoscopy with biopsy is preferred for confirmation of diagnosis. Contrast-enhanced CT and PET can be used to assess distant metastasis. Endoscopic ultrasonography (EUS) is the investigation of choice to assess tumor invasion and lymph node metastasis.

Other options:

Option B:  Diffuse esophageal spasm results in the corkscrew appearance of the esophagus on barium study.

Option C: Esophageal leiomyoma appears as a smooth, semilunar filling defect on barium swallow. it is seen as a discrete ovoid mass that is well outlined by barium.

Option D: Esophageal webs occur in the upper and middle esophagus as a thin membrane that can be identified by the translucent part on contrast radiology.
questions.learning: Carcinoma esophagus — A patient with the given history and barium swallow findings of irregular narrowing, mucosal destruction, and shouldered margins of esophagus, are suggestive of carcinoma esophagus.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is not a recognized clinical use of magnesium sulfate (MgSO₄)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Increase renal perfusion

Magnesium sulfate acts primarily as a central nervous system depressant and anticonvulsant.

Mechanism of action

• Blocks NMDA receptors
• Reduces acetylcholine release at neuromuscular junction
• Stabilizes neuronal membranes

This results in seizure prevention and neuroprotection.

Recognized Clinical Uses

1. Prevention and Treatment of Eclampsia

Magnesium sulfate is the drug of choice for seizure prophylaxis in severe preeclampsia and treatment of eclampsia.

MgSO₄ is superior to diazepam and phenytoin for eclamptic seizures.

2  Fetal Neuroprotection

Magnesium sulfate is given in imminent preterm delivery (<32 weeks).

Purpose:

• Protects fetal brain
• Reduces risk of cerebral palsy

Exam pearl:

MgSO₄ is used for fetal neuroprotection in preterm labor.

3. Prevention of Eclamptic Seizures

In severe preeclampsia, magnesium sulfate prevents progression to eclampsia (seizures).

Indications include:

• Severe hypertension
• Visual disturbances
• Severe headache
• Epigastric pain

Because MgSO₄ can cause respiratory depression, monitoring is essential.

| Parameter | Normal value

| --------- | ------------

| Respiratory rate | >12/min

| Urine output | >25–30 mL/hr

| Patellar reflex | Present

·         Antidote for toxicity:

·         ➡ Calcium Gluconate

Magnesium sulfate does not improve renal blood flow or renal perfusion.

In fact, in severe preeclampsia:

• Renal perfusion is reduced
• MgSO₄ is given only for seizure prevention, not for renal function improvement.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A male patient presented with swelling in his lower limb. The clinical image is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lymphatic filariasis

The image is suggestive of lymphatic filariasis.

Lymphatic filariasis occurs due to the transmission of W.bancrofti by the bite of Culex mosquitoes. The third stage larval forms from the mosquito enter the lymphatics and lymph nodes where they develop into adult worms. The adult worms become sexually mature and mate to release microfilariae which enter the peripheral circulation.

The disease initially causes acute attacks of lymphangitis and lymphadenitis. Early treatment may even cure the disease. The lymphedema may gradually worsen and get associated with the thickening of the skin and fibrosis of lymph vessels or blockage by adult worms. Hydrocele is another common manifestation that occurs due to lymphatic obstruction.

Microfilaria can be demonstrated in blood, chylous urine, exudate of lymph varix, and hydrocele fluid, however, peripheral blood is the preferred choice. The examination of a thick and thin blood smear stained with Giemsa stain shows the microfilaria. Other methods are by examining the unstained blood under a microscope for the actively motile microfilariae and by acridine orange-microhematocrit tube technique.

The best time to collect the blood samples is at night, between 10 pm and 4 am as they are nocturnally periodic.

DEC provocation test: In this test, a small dose of DEC is given 20-50 minutes before sample collection so that the microfilaria appears in the blood even during the daytime.

The image below shows the life cycle of Wuchereria bancrofti.

Other Options:

* Deep Vein Thrombosis is a condition in which a blood clot forms in a deep vein, usually in the legs. It can cause pain, swelling, and warmth in the affected area, but it doesn't lead to the type of severe swelling and disfigurement seen in the image.

* Edems refers to the accumulation of fluid in the body's tissues, leading to swelling. While edema can cause swelling, it doesn't typically cause the extreme and localized swelling associated with lymphatic filariasis.

* Mansonelliasis is a disease caused by another type of parasitic worm called Mansonella. It can lead to symptoms such as skin rashes, joint pain, and fever, but it doesn't typically result in the severe and localized swelling seen in the image.
questions.learning: Lymphatic filariasis — The image is suggestive of lymphatic filariasis. Lymphatic filariasis occurs due to the transmission of W.bancrofti by the bite of Culex mosquitoes.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A female died due to an unnatural cause within 7 years of marriage, and allegations have been raised. Under which section will the inquest be conducted? BNS - Bhartiya Nyaya Sanhita
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 176 CrPC/196 BNSS

The given clinical scenario of a female who died due to an unnatural cause within 7 years of marriage suggests a possibility of dowry death. A magistrate inquest is done under BNSS Section 196 (Section 176 CrPC).

BNSS 196 (Section 176 CrPC) deals with magistrate inquest in which the cause of death is not under natural circumstances. Magistrate inquest may be conducted by the District Magistrate, Sub-Divisional Magistrate, Tahsildar, or any other Executive Magistrate empowered by the State Government.

Indications for Magistrate Inquest:

* Dowry death

* Custodial rape

* Death in police custody or police interrogation

* Death in police firing

* Death in prison, reformatories, Borstal school

* Death in a psychiatric hospital

* Cases of exhumation.

Other options:

Option A: Section 106 BNS (304A IPC) defines the punishment for causing the death of a person by any rash or negligent act, not amounting to culpable homicide, the punishment is imprisonment for up to 2 years, and a fine.

Option B:  BNSS Section 194 (Section 174 CrPC) deals with the police inquest. It is done in suicide, homicide, killing by any animal or machinery or accident, and death under circumstances that raise suspicion of another person committing the offence.

Option D: BNS Sec 89 (IPC 313) deals with the causation of miscarriage of a woman with child (and/or quick with child) without her consent. Only the person causing the abortion is liable to punishment.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Dr. Savita is training her interns who are being posted for rural posting. Which is appropriate for cervical cancer screening?
options: Pap smear + HPV DNA every 5 yearly
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pap smear alone every 3 yearly

Cervical Cancer Screening- The most widely used screening test is the Pap smear (cervical cytology). The Pap smear detects precancerous lesions (CIN) before they progress to invasive cancer. It samples cells from the transformation zone of the cervix, where most cervical cancers originate.

For low-resource settings (such as rural areas), the recommended approach is:

| Age Group | Screening Method | Interval

| --------- | ---------------- | --------

| 21–29 years | Pap smear alone | Every 3 years

| 30–65 years | Pap smear every 3 years OR HPV testing | Depending on resources

Because HPV testing may not be widely available in rural setups, Pap smear every 3 years is considered practical and effective.
questions.learning: Pap smear alone every 3 yearly Cervical Cancer Screening- The most widely used screening test is the Pap smear (cervical cytology). The Pap smear detects precancerous lesions (CIN) before they progress to invasive cancer.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Glucose is absorbed in intestine by?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Secondary active transport

Glucose is absorbed in the intestine by secondary active transport (sodium co-transport).

The energy for glucose transport is provided indirectly, by the active transport of Na+ out of the cell. This maintains the concentration gradient across the luminal border of the cell so that more Na+ and consequently more glucose enter.

Though both secondary active transport and facilitated diffusion play a role in glucose absorption, it is the initial active transport of sodium through the basolateral membranes of the intestinal epithelial cells that provide the eventual force for moving glucose through the membranes as well. So, secondary active transport is the single best answer for this question.
questions.learning: Secondary active transport Glucose is absorbed in the intestine by secondary active transport (sodium co-transport). The energy for glucose transport is provided indirectly, by the active transport of Na+ out of the cell.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 14-year-old male presented with recurrent epistaxis. There is no history of trauma. He also complained of nasal obstruction and rhinorrhea. On examination, there is a firm purplish mass on the posterior nasopharynx. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma

A young male with recurrent epistaxis and complaints of nasal obstruction with a mass on the nasopharynx suggests a diagnosis of Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma.

Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma (JNA) is a highly vascular and locally aggressive tumour seen almost exclusively in adolescent males, associated with significant morbidity and occasional mortality. JNA accounts for only 0.05% of all head and neck tumours. Patients usually present with a triad of progressive nasal obstruction, recurrent epistaxis and a mass in the nasal cavity and nasopharynx.\

It has the potential to cause proptosis, affecting both the orbit and intracranial extension, eventually leading to cranial nerve palsies and loss of vision.  Angiofibroma can be diagnosed using CT, MRI, and magnetic resonance angiography. Anterior bowing of the maxillary wall due to the presence of a mass in the pterygomaxillary space on CT known as the Holman-Miller sign is a characteristic finding of JNA. Recurrence has been reported up to 35%. Management: Surgical excision is the treatment of choice. Recurrent angiofibroma is treated with revision surgery, Radiotherapy is considered where the recurrence tumour is inaccessible.

Other options:

Option A: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma presents in elderly patients of East-Asian ethnicity and smoking history. They present with hearing loss and involvement of cranial nerves.

Option B: The foreign body in the nose presents at an earlier age and doesn't have recurrent epistaxis or a mass on examination.

Option C: Antrochoanal polyp is a type of non-neoplastic nasal polypoidal masses of edematous nasal or sinus mucosa which arises from the mucosa of the maxillary antrum near its accessory ostium. The clinical features include unilateral nasal obstruction, mucoid nasal discharge, and a hyponasal voice.
questions.learning: Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma — A young male with recurrent epistaxis and complaints of nasal obstruction with a mass on the nasopharynx suggests a diagnosis of Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: The World health organisation(WHO) definition of blindness is ________.
options: Best corrected visual acuity of less than 1/60 in the better eye
Best corrected visual acuity of less than 3/60 in the better eye
Presenting visual acuity of worse than 3/60 in the better eye
Presenting visual acuity of worse than 6/60 in the better eye
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Presenting visual acuity of worse than 3/60 in the better eye

The World Health Organisation has adopted the International Classification of Diseases 11 (ICD 11) definition of visual impairment and blindness. As per the new definition, blindness is defined as presenting visual acuity of worse than 3/60 or a corresponding visual field loss to less than 10° in the better eye.

Note: Earlier, the WHO definition of blindness was: Best corrected visual acuity of less than 3/60 in the better eye ( Option B).

Refractive error is the main cause of visual impairment in individuals aged 0-49 years, followed by cataracts, amblyopia, and corneal opacity. However, in the age group >50 years, cataract is the major cause, followed by refractive errors and surgical complications of cataract.

Definitions of blindness and visual impairment as per WHO :

Blindness

Presenting visual acuity <3/60

Mild visual impairment

Presenting visual acuity <6/12 – 6/18

Moderate visual impairment (MVI)
Presenting visual acuity <6/18 – 6/60

Severe visual impairment (SVI)
Presenting visual acuity <6/60 – 3/60
questions.learning: Presenting visual acuity of worse than 3/60 in the better eye The World Health Organisation has adopted the International Classification of Diseases 11 (ICD 11) definition of visual impairment and blindness.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Parathyroid gland post surgery is commonly transferred to:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Brachioradialis

The parathyroid is commonly transferred to the brachioradialis muscle post-surgery. This will facilitate easy removal if there is disease recurrence after surgery.

Parathyroidectomy is indicated in:

1. Symptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism (HPT):
2. Asymptomatic primary HPT with:

• raise in serum calcium >1mg/dl of the normal range
• >400 mg urinary calcium in 24-hour urine test
• < -2.5 Z-score of bone mineral density
• Age <50yr and failed medical treatment

3. Severe cases of secondary HPT

Parathyroidectomy is performed in neck hyperextension (semi-Fowler position). The thyroid gland is mobilized, and the parathyroid gland with adenoma is identified and resected. The parathyroid tissue is transplanted to the non-dominant forearm.

Pockets are made in the belly of the brachioradialis muscle, and one to two pieces of parathyroid tissue measuring 1 mm each are placed into each pocket. A total of 12 to 14 pieces are transplanted. This is a type of heterotopic transplant.

Miami criteria (confirm the absence of another hyperactive parathyroid): A drop of parathyroid hormone intraoperatively, to more than half the maximum value at 10 minutes postresection is considered an adequate resection in a parathyroid adenoma. However, if there is no drop in PTH level, then a multi-gland disease is suspected and the surgery is converted to a bilateral neck exploration.

Complications of parathyroidectomy include:

1. Persistent or recurrent hyperparathyroidism
2. Hypoparathyroidism (presenting as hypocalcemia)
3. Hungry bone syndrome
4. Injury to the recurrent laryngeal nerve
questions.learning: Brachioradialis — The parathyroid is commonly transferred to the brachioradialis muscle post-surgery. This will facilitate easy removal if there is disease recurrence after surgery.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is recommended by the WHO for the management of the second stage of labor?
options: Manual perineal support and warm compresses
Maintain head in deflexion and deliver
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Manual perineal support and warm compresses

Among the given options, manual perineal support and giving warm compresses are recommended by WHO in the management of the second stage of labor.

The second stage of labor refers to the time period between full cervical dilatation and the birth of the baby. For women in the second stage of labor, the following techniques to reduce perineal trauma and facilitate spontaneous birth such as perineal massage, warm compresses, and manual perineal support (hands-on guarding of the perineum) are recommended.

Option A: Mandatory episiotomy is discouraged. Episiotomy is indicated in cases of:

• Shoulder dystocia
• Breech delivery
• Fetal macrosomia
• Operative vaginal deliveries
• Persistent occiput posterior positions

Option C: Head is delivered by maintaining flexion to ensure that the small sub-occipitofrontal diameter distends the vulval outlet instead of the larger occipitofrontal diameter.

Option D: The position that is most comfortable to the mother including upright positions is recommended.
questions.learning: Manual perineal support and warm compresses Among the given options, manual perineal support and giving warm compresses are recommended by WHO in the management of the second stage of labor.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A neonate presents with thickened, edematous intestines protruding from the abdomen without any external covering. What will be the next best line of management?
options: Cover the contents with a silo bag and wait
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cover the contents with a silo bag and wait

The clinical scenario of a neonate presenting with thickened and edematous protruding intestines without any covering points towards a diagnosis of gastroschisis. The next best line of management would be to cover the contents with a silo bag and wait.

A neonate with gastroschisis would need an immediate primary closure. However, in the given scenario, in neonates with thickened and edematous intestines, it may not be possible to return the bowel to the peritoneal cavity immediately after birth. In such cases, a plastic spring-loaded silo bag can be placed over the bowel, facilitating the gradual reduction of the bowel wall edema. This is followed by definitive surgical closure in about 1–2 weeks.

Gastroschisis is an abdominal wall defect located on one side of the umbilicus (right side commonly), allowing protrusion of the intestines, stomach, bladder, and sometimes ovaries or undescended testes. The loops of the bowel are not covered by amnion as they herniate through the abdominal wall directly into the amniotic cavity. The affected bowel loops can be damaged by exposure to amniotic fluid.

The intestines are matted and covered by a thick peel. Longer exposure in utero to amniotic fluid can cause trauma to the intestines. The intestines are also not fully rotated, and these factors increase the risk of intestinal volvulus, postnatal intestinal dysfunction with delayed mobility, and prolonged need for hospitalization and enteral feeding.

Risk factors include teenage pregnancy, recreational drug use, smoking, and genitourinary infection during pregnancy. After birth, careful management is required to prevent twisting or kinking of the blood supply to the intestines.

Management: Immediate surgical intervention is required after birth to prevent complications such as infection, dehydration, and damage to the exposed abdominal organs. In the immediate postoperative period, if abdominal wall closure is tight, aggressive fluid resuscitation may be required to ensure adequate tissue perfusion and prevent metabolic acidosis. Patients are supported with TPN until bowel function returns.

Surgical repair typically involves gently placing the protruding abdominal contents back(primary reduction) into the abdominal cavity and closing the abdominal wall defect surgically. Primary reduction is successful in 50% to 80%, with eviscerated contents placed into the abdominal cavity without excessive tension. Parenteral nutrition is often needed for several weeks to support intestinal recovery.

Note: Covering the bowel with saline-soaked gauze is a temporary measure to prevent fluid loss and infection, but it’s not the next best line of management. The definitive step is silo placement.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A diabetic patient presented to you with visual acuity of 6/9 in one eye. Further investigations revealed pre-retinal hemorrhages with neovascularization at the optic disc. What is the next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pan-retinal photocoagulation

Neovascularization at the disc (NVD) with preretinal hemorrhage = Proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR), which requires urgent treatment.

Management of choice: Pan-retinal photocoagulation (PRP)

• Causes regression of neovascularization
• Reduces risk of vitreous hemorrhage and tractional retinal detachment

Pathophysiology:

• Retinal ischemia → ↑ VEGF → abnormal fragile new vessels
• These vessels bleed → preretinal/vitreous hemorrhage

Why not others:

• Focal laser: For macular edema
• Grid laser: For diffuse macular edema
• Scleral buckling: For rhegmatogenous retinal detachment

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A female at 40 weeks of gestation presents with labor pains and is in the second stage of labor for the last 2 hours. On examination of the abdomen, there are 4 uterine contractions per 10 minutes each lasting more than a minute. On PV examination, the fetal station is at +3 and the suture is in AP diameter and caput +. The fetal heart rate is 70 beats/ minute in the last 20 minutes. Which is the appropriate method of delivery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Outlet forceps

In the given scenario, outlet forceps would be the best choice of instrumental delivery as the fetus is at +3 station, with suture in AP diameter and has caput.

The criteria for the application of different types of forceps are as follows :

Outlet forceps :

• Scalp is visible at the introitus without separating the labia
• Fetal skull has reached the level of the pelvic floor
• Sagittal suture is in direct anteroposterior diameter or in the right or left occiput anterior or posterior position, but rotation is <=45 degrees
• Fetal head is at or on the perineum

Low forceps :

• Leading point of the fetal skull (station) is at +2 cm or more but has not yet reached the pelvic floor, and

(a) Rotation is <=45°, or (b) Rotation is >45°

Mid forceps :

• Fetal head is engaged. Head is 1/5 palpable per abdomen but the station is above +2 cm but not above the ischial spines (station 0).

High forceps :

• Head is not engaged. This type of forceps is not used in current obstetrics.

Note : Ventouse is not the best choice for a fetus with caput, as there is a risk of scalp avulsion. Also, the vacuum cannot be adequately generated owing to the presence of soft tissue swelling.
questions.learning: Outlet forceps — In the given scenario, outlet forceps would be the best choice of instrumental delivery as the fetus is at +3 station, with suture in AP diameter and has caput.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: During the 14th century, what was the prescribed duration of isolation for individuals suspected of having the plague when quarantine measures were enforced?
questions.explanation: The term "quarantine" originates from the Italian word "quaranta giorni," which literally means forty days. This duration was established during the Black Death in the 14th century when the port city of Venice required ships coming from plague-infested areas to anchor offshore for forty days before landing. This specific timeframe was chosen as it was believed to be sufficient for a disease to manifest and for the "cleansing" of the ship and crew. Option A (14 days) is the modern quarantine period used for diseases like COVID-19 but was not the historical standard. Options B (35 days) and D (28 days) are incorrect as they do not correspond to the etymological or historical root of the practice. The choice of forty days may have also had religious significance, echoing the biblical duration of the Great Flood or Lent. This historical precedent laid the foundation for modern public health isolation and containment strategies used in infectious disease control globally

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 30-year-old patient with chronic sinusitis and persistent nasal congestion is being evaluated with a focus on the anatomical pathways responsible for sinus drainage, particularly the bulla ethmoidalis. Which anatomical structure serves as the primary drainage pathway for the bulla ethmoidalis?
questions.explanation: The bulla ethmoidalis is the largest of the anterior ethmoid air cells and a key landmark in endoscopic sinus surgery. It drains directly into the Middle meatus of the lateral nasal wall. Specifically, it typically opens into the hiatus semilunaris or just superior to it. The Superior meatus (Option B) receives the posterior ethmoid cells and the sphenoid sinus (via the sphenoethmoidal recess). The Inferior meatus (Option C) only receives the nasolacrimal duct. The Middle concha (Option D) is the bony turbinate structure that covers the middle meatus but is not a drainage pathway itself. Understanding these drainage patterns is critical for managing chronic sinusitis. Obstruction within the middle meatus (the osteomeatal complex) can lead to the simultaneous involvement of the frontal, maxillary, and anterior ethmoid sinuses. Successful sinus surgery aims to restore the natural drainage pathways through these specific meatuses. The bulla ethmoidalis is often the first structure removed during an ethmoidectomy to gain access to the posterior cells
questions.learning: The bulla ethmoidalis is the largest of the anterior ethmoid air cells and a key landmark in endoscopic sinus surgery. It drains directly into the Middle meatus of the lateral nasal wall.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 3-year-old male has the following buccal mucosa finding. After three days, he presents to your OPD with a rash. What is your diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Measles

The given image shows small red lesions with bluish-white spots in the center on the inner aspects of the cheek opposite to the lower premolar, indicating the presence of Koplik spots. The appearance of these spots, along with a rash appearing three days later, strongly suggests a diagnosis of measles.

The measles virus is a single-stranded RNA virus. Measles infection has 4 phases: the incubation period, prodromal illness, exanthematous phase (characterized by the rash), and recovery phase.

After an incubation period of 8-12 days, the prodromal phase of measles starts with mild fever and is followed by conjunctivitis, photophobia, coryza, cough, and increasing fever. Koplik spots, appearing 1-4 days prior to the rash, are a characteristic sign of measles.

Symptoms gradually intensify over a period of 2-4 days until the first day of the rash. The rash typically begins on the forehead (around the hairline), behind the ears, and on the upper neck as a red maculopapular eruption. It then spreads downward to the torso and extremities, often becoming confluent on the face and upper trunk.

Complications include acute otitis media (most common), pneumonia (the most common cause of death), croup, bronchiolitis, reactivation of tuberculosis, diarrhea, appendicitis, febrile seizures, and encephalitis. Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis is a rare chronic complication of measles.

Other options:

Option B: Leukoplakia appears as a white patch in the oral cavity that cannot be wiped off.

Option C: Scarlet fever is Group A Streptococcus (GAS) pharyngitis and is characterized by a distinctive sandpaper rash. The rash appears as a diffuse, finely papular, erythematous eruption that turns the skin bright red and blanches on pressure. It starts around the neck and spreads to the trunk and extremities.

Option D: Kawasaki disease (KD) is a systemic inflammatory disorder with arteritis of medium to large-sized vessels. It presents with fever, rash (maculopapular, erythema multiforme urticarial, or micropustular), conjunctivitis, and cervical lymph node enlargement.
questions.learning: Measles — The given image shows small red lesions with bluish-white spots in the center on the inner aspects of the cheek opposite to the lower premolar, indicating the presence of Koplik spots.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A software engineer presents to the outpatient department with easy fatiguability. He gives a history of sitting in front of the computer for 12 - 14 hours. He consumes a lot of junk food with very less fruits and vegetables. Hb is 9gm/dl and MCV 120 fl. What is the most likely cause of this patient's anemia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Folic acid deficiency

The given laboratory values showing anemia and increased MCV are suggestive of megaloblastic anemia. This could be due to cyanocobalamin deficiency or folic acid deficiency. The history of inadequate intake of fruits and vegetables points towards folic acid deficiency.

Dietary sources of Vit-B12 are animal products such as meat, fish, milk, and eggs. Dietary sources of folic acid are green vegetables such as lettuce, spinach, asparagus, and broccoli.

Megaloblastic anemia can occur due to Vit-B12 or folic acid deficiency. Inadequate intake, intrinsic factor deficiency, pernicious anemia, gastrectomy, malabsorption, ileal resection, alcoholism, anticonvulsants, oral contraceptives, pregnancy, infancy, disseminated cancer, markedly increased hematopoiesis, folic acid antagonists are some of the causes.

Patient can present with anorexia, weight loss, diarrhea, constipation, glossitis, angular cheilosis, reversible melanin skin hyperpigmentation, paresthesias, muscle weakness, dementia, or psychotic disturbances.

In megaloblastic anemia, DNA synthesis is impaired that leading to ineffective hematopoiesis and distinctive morphologic changes.

Peripheral blood examination shows oval macrocytes, usually with anisocytosis and poikilocytosis. MCV is usually >100 fL. The normal value of MCV is between 80-100 fL. Most macrocytes lack the central pallor of normal red cells and even appear hyperchromic, but the MCHC is not elevated. The reticulocyte count is low. Neutrophils are larger than normal and show nuclear hypersegmentation with five or more nuclear lobules.

Marrow is markedly hypercellular. Megaloblastic changes are seen at all stages of erythroid development. There is nuclear-to-cytoplasmic asynchrony, where nuclear maturation is slower than cytoplasmic maturation. Granulocytic precursors are seen in the form of giant metamyelocytes and band forms. Megakaryocytes may be abnormally large with bizarre, multilobate nuclei.

Peripheral blood smear showing hypersegmented neutrophil:

Other options:

Option A - In cyanocobalamin deficiency, MCV will be increased. But the dietary sources of cyanocobalamin are mainly of animal products. In the given clinical scenario there is inadequate intake of fruits and vegetables. Hence, this is not the answer.

Option C - In iron deficiency anemia, MCV will be decreased.

Option D - In hereditary spherocytosis, MCV will be normal.
questions.learning: Folic acid deficiency — The given laboratory values showing anemia and increased MCV are suggestive of megaloblastic anemia. This could be due to cyanocobalamin deficiency or folic acid deficiency.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 7-year-old female child is brought to the OPD with cramping abdominal pain. On examination, she is found to have rashes on the back of her legs, buttocks and the extensor surface of her forearms. Laboratory analysis reveals proteinuria and microscopic hematuria. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Henoch-Schönlein purpura

The diagnosis in this child with rash, abdominal pain and nephritis is Henoch-Schönlein purpura.

Henoch-Schönlein purpura (HSP), also known as IgA vasculitis, is a common small vessel vasculitis in childhood. It is a type III hypersensitivity reaction characterized by the deposition of IgA in the small vessels of the skin, joints, gastrointestinal tract, and kidney, resulting in vasculitis

Children usually present with the following features:

* Palpable purpura is symmetric and occurs in the lower extremities, extensor aspect of the upper limbs, and buttocks.

* Arthralgia and arthritis- commonly affecting hip, knee, or ankle joints.

* Gastrointestinal manifestations like abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhoea, and intussusception.

* About 30% of the patients with HSP develop renal manifestations, presenting as microscopic hematuria, hypertension, and progressive glomerulonephritis.

Laboratory studies generally show mild leukocytosis, a normal platelet count, and occasionally eosinophilia. Serum complement components are normal.

Most clinical features of IgA vasculitis are self-limiting and resolve in a few days. Supportive management with the maintenance of hydration and pain relief is done. Patients developing nephritis due to IgA vasculitis may need aggressive management with immunosuppressants.

The image given below shows palpable purpura in the lower limbs seen in HSP.
questions.learning: Henoch-Schönlein purpura — The diagnosis in this child with rash, abdominal pain and nephritis is Henoch-Schönlein purpura. Henoch-Schönlein purpura (HSP), also known as IgA vasculitis, is a common small vessel vasculitis in childhood.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Pasteurization is done at ______.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 63 degree Celsius for 30 minutes

Pasteurization: Milk is heated at either

• 63°C for 30 minutes: the Holder method or
• 72°C for 15–20 seconds: the flash process

followed by cooling quickly to 13°C or lower.

All the non-sporing pathogens are killed except Coxiella burnetti, which may survive in Holder method.
questions.learning: 63 degree Celsius for 30 minutes Pasteurization: Milk is heated at either • 63°C for 30 minutes: the Holder method or • 72°C for 15–20 seconds: the flash process followed by cooling quickly to 13°C or lower.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient with a history of liver dysfunction presents to the outpatient department, and characteristic ocular changes are noted on examination. Considering the underlying liver pathology, which substance is most likely responsible for these ocular findings?
questions.explanation: This question reinforces the clinical link between liver dysfunction and specific ocular findings, namely Wilson's disease. As discussed previously, Wilson's disease is a disorder of copper metabolism. In this condition, the liver's ability to excrete copper into bile is impaired, and its incorporation into ceruloplasmin is also defective. This leads to the systemic accumulation of copper. The liver is the first organ affected, presenting as anything from asymptomatic enzyme elevation to fulminant hepatic failure or cirrhosis. The "notable changes" in the eyes refer to Kayser-Fleischer rings (copper in Descemet's membrane) and sometimes "sunflower cataracts" (copper in the lens capsule). Zinc (Option B) is actually used as a treatment for Wilson's disease because it blocks intestinal copper absorption. Selenium (Option C) is a trace element whose deficiency is linked to Keshan disease. Iron (Option D) accumulation causes hemochromatosis, which primarily affects the liver, pancreas, and skin ("bronze diabetes") but does not typically produce the specific corneal rings seen with copper toxicity. Thus, copper is the primary pathological substance
questions.learning: This question reinforces the clinical link between liver dysfunction and specific ocular findings, namely Wilson's disease. As discussed previously, Wilson's disease is a disorder of copper metabolism.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Thickened ventricular wall with normal diastolic function is a feature of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Athlete’s heart

Athlete’s heart is a physiological adaptation to intensive exercise, characterized by mild symmetrical left ventricular wall thickening with preserved systolic and normal diastolic function. It is a benign and reversible condition that must be differentiated from hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

Why not the other options?

• A. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: Causes pathological ventricular hypertrophy with impaired diastolic relaxation (diastolic dysfunction) and may produce LV outflow tract obstruction.
• B. Restrictive cardiomyopathy: Characterized by severe diastolic dysfunction due to a stiff ventricle; wall thickness is usually normal or increased only in infiltrative diseases.
• C. Endomyocardial fibrosis: A type of restrictive cardiomyopathy causing marked diastolic dysfunction.
questions.learning: Athlete’s heart Athlete’s heart is a physiological adaptation to intensive exercise, characterized by mild symmetrical left ventricular wall thickening with preserved systolic and normal diastolic function.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following is/are true about optic neuritis? I. Proportionate loss of colour vision and contrast to visual acuity II. 70% cases of multiple sclerosis are affected III. Treatment is done by oral steroids IV. Optic neuritis presents with normal fundus or disc edema
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Only IV

I. Proportionate loss of colour vision and contrast to visual acuity : FALSE

• In optic neuritis, colour vision loss is disproportionately severe compared to visual acuity
• Especially red desaturation

II. 70% cases of multiple sclerosis are affected :FALSE

• Optic neuritis is common in MS, but:

• \~20-25% present with optic neuritis as first manifestation
• \~50% of MS patients develop optic neuritis during lifetime

III. Treatment is done by oral steroids :FALSE

• Based on Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial (ONTT):

• IV methylprednisolone → speeds recovery
• Oral steroids alone are contraindicated (↑ recurrence risk)

IV. Optic neuritis presents with normal fundus or disc edema : TRUE

• Two forms:

• Retrobulbar neuritis → fundus normal (“patient sees nothing, doctor sees nothing”)
• Papillitis → disc edema present
questions.learning: Proportionate loss of colour vision and contrast to visual acuity : FALSE • In optic neuritis, colour vision loss is disproportionately severe compared to visual acuity • Especially red desaturation II.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: An elderly diabetic woman with a recent history of COVID-19 treatment using steroids and remdesivir now presents with foul-smelling nasal discharge and a black necrotic lesion in the nasal cavity, with erosion of the nasal septum and hard palate. Based on these clinical features, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis is an opportunistic fungal infection caused by fungi of the order Mucorales. This case describes the classic clinical scenario often seen during the COVID-19 pandemic: an immunocompromised patient (due to diabetes and steroid use) developing a fulminant infection. The "black necrotic mass" (eschar) is pathognomonic and results from the fungus's angioinvasive nature, which causes tissue infarction and necrosis. Erosion of the hard palate and nasal septum indicates rapid local spread. Option A (Aspergillosis) can be invasive but rarely presents with such rapid, aggressive necrosis in this specific context. Option C (Foreign body) would cause unilateral discharge but not palatal erosion. Option D (Rhinosporidiosis) presents as strawberry-like friable nasal polyps, usually in patients with a history of bathing in stagnant water. Mucormycosis is a surgical emergency requiring aggressive debridement and systemic antifungal therapy with amphotericin B. Delay in diagnosis often leads to blindness or fatal intracranial extension

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: During measurement of a rifled barrel weapon, the caliber depends on?
questions.explanation: In forensic ballistics, the caliber of a rifled firearm is defined as the internal diameter of the barrel. Specifically, for a rifled weapon, it is measured as the distance between two opposite lands (the raised portions of the rifling). The grooves (Option B) are the recessed portions; the distance between them would be slightly larger than the true caliber. The number of lead pellets (Option C) relates to the "gauge" or "bore" of a smooth-bore shotgun, not a rifled weapon. Mass and velocity (Option D) determine the kinetic energy and wounding potential of the projectile but do not define the weapon's caliber. Accurate caliber determination is essential for matching a fired bullet to a suspect firearm. Each firearm leaves unique land and groove impressions on the bullet, acting as a "ballistic fingerprint" that allows forensic experts to link evidence from a crime scene to a specific weapon
questions.learning: In forensic ballistics, the caliber of a rifled firearm is defined as the internal diameter of the barrel. Specifically, for a rifled weapon, it is measured as the distance between two opposite lands (the raised portions of the rifling).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient came to the emergency room with severe pain in the abdomen. Serum triglyceride level was 1500 mg/dL. Identify the defect?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Apo CII

Very high triglycerides (>1000 mg/dL) with acute abdominal pain suggests hypertriglyceridemia-induced pancreatitis, classically seen in familial chylomicronemia (Type I hyperlipoproteinemia).

• Deficiency of Apolipoprotein C-II (Apo C-II)
• Apo C-II is a cofactor for lipoprotein lipase (LPL)

Pathophysiology:

• Without Apo C-II → LPL cannot be activated
• Impaired breakdown of chylomicrons → massive accumulation of triglycerides
• Leads to pancreatitis, eruptive xanthomas, lipemia retinalis

Why other options are incorrect:

• Apo B-48: Needed for chylomicron formation (defect → abetalipoproteinemia)
• Apo B-100: Required for LDL/VLDL metabolism (familial hypercholesterolemia-like states)
• LDL receptor: Causes ↑ LDL (Type IIa), not severe triglyceridemia

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the cranial nerve passing through the given structure
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. IV

In the given image, the dorsal aspect of the brainstem is marked and the cranial nerve that is passing there is the trochlear nerve (CN IV).

The trochlear nerve is the fourth cranial nerve that originates from the trochlear nuclei within the midbrain at the level of the inferior colliculus. It is the only cranial nerve that emerges from the dorsal surface of the brainstem and has the longest intracranial course. It passes on to the lateral surface of the crus of cerebellar peduncle and lateral wall of the cavernous sinus. The nerve then crosses the oculomotor nerve to enter the orbit through the superior orbital fissure to exclusively supply the contralateral superior oblique muscle.

The main actions of superior oblique are

• Depression in adducted position- The muscle elevates the posterior of the eye causing the front of the eye to be depressed. Patients with trochlear nerve palsy have difficulty in looking downwards when eyes are in the adducted position.
• Abduction
• Intortion of the eyeball.

Other options- Oculomotor (CN III), trigeminal (CN V) and abducens (CN VI) nerves exit ventrally from the brainstem.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child presents with Kawasaki disease with multiple small coronary artery aneurysms. Treatment is?
questions.explanation: In patients with Kawasaki disease who develop small coronary artery aneurysms, low-dose aspirin therapy is typically continued for a duration of 6 to 8 weeks. This timeframe corresponds to the period of highest thrombotic risk during the vascular remodeling process, as these small aneurysms often regress over time. Lifelong aspirin (Option A) is generally reserved for patients with large or giant aneurysms where the risk of thrombosis remains permanently high. A 4-week course (Option B) is usually too short for cases with known coronary involvement. Dual antiplatelet therapy with clopidogrel (Option D) is reserved for more severe cases with higher risks of occlusion. Additionally, the administration of IVIG during the acute phase is crucial to reducing the overall risk of aneurysm formation. Therefore, a 6-week course of aspirin is the standard management for small aneurysms
questions.learning: In patients with Kawasaki disease who develop small coronary artery aneurysms, low-dose aspirin therapy is typically continued for a duration of 6 to 8 weeks.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A married woman at 26 weeks of gestation presents with a history of contraceptive failure and requests termination of pregnancy. According to the provisions of the Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) Act, what is the most appropriate course of action?
options: If no fetal anomaly, continue the pregnancy
questions.explanation: Under the MTP (Amendment) Act 2021, the upper limit for termination due to failed contraception for a married woman (or any woman) is 24 weeks. Since this patient is at 26 weeks, she has exceeded the legal limit for this specific indication. Therefore, if there is no significant fetal anomaly or immediate threat to the mother's life, the pregnancy must be continued. Husband's consent (Option A) is never required. The opinion of 2 doctors (Option B) is required for terminations between 20-24 weeks, not beyond. Medical board permission (Option D) is specifically for terminations beyond 24 weeks but only when substantial fetal abnormalities are diagnosed. Failed contraception is not a valid ground for termination after the 24-week threshold. Clinicians must strictly adhere to these gestational limits to stay within the bounds of the law while providing reproductive healthcare
questions.learning: Under the MTP (Amendment) Act 2021, the upper limit for termination due to failed contraception for a married woman (or any woman) is 24 weeks. Since this patient is at 26 weeks, she has exceeded the legal limit for this specific indication.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman at 32 weeks of pregnancy presents to the emergency department with elevated blood pressure (150/120 mmHg), pedal edema, and a urine dipstick showing 2+ proteinuria. Based on this clinical picture, what is the most likely pregnancy-related diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient’s presentation—hypertension ( mmHg), proteinuria (2+ on dipstick), and pedal edema occurring after 20 weeks of gestation—is the classic diagnostic triad for Pre-eclampsia. Pre-eclampsia is a multi-systemic disorder characterized by new-onset hypertension and end-organ dysfunction, most commonly manifesting as proteinuria. PPH (Postpartum hemorrhage, Option B) occurs after delivery. Abruptio placenta (Option C) involves painful bleeding and a tender uterus, though it can be a complication of severe pre-eclampsia. Placenta previa (Option D) causes painless bleeding. Severe pre-eclampsia, as indicated by a diastolic BP of 120 mmHg, carries high risks of maternal seizures (eclampsia), stroke, and HELLP syndrome. Management involves stabilization with antihypertensives (like labetalol) and magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis, followed by planned delivery, as delivery is the only definitive cure. This 28-year-old patient requires urgent hospitalization and intensive monitoring to prevent life-threatening maternal and fetal outcomes associated with severe gestational hypertension and protein loss
questions.learning: The patient’s presentation—hypertension ( mmHg), proteinuria (2+ on dipstick), and pedal edema occurring after 20 weeks of gestation—is the classic diagnostic triad for Pre-eclampsia.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Despite substantial improvements in immunization coverage, institutional deliveries, and healthcare accessibility under the rural health program, these indicators continued to lag considerably behind those observed in urban populations. Which of the following pillars of primary health care is most likely to be exploited?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Equitable distribution

Equitable distribution is a core principle of Primary Health Care (PHC), ensuring that essential health services are available and accessible to all segments of the population, irrespective of geographic location or socioeconomic status. Persistent disparities between rural and urban health indicators, despite overall improvements, reflect a failure to achieve equitable distribution of healthcare.

Why not the other options?

• A. Appropriate technology: Refers to the use of scientifically sound, affordable, and locally acceptable technologies; it does not address rural–urban disparities in access.
• B. Community participation: Involves active involvement of the community in planning and implementing health programs but does not primarily explain unequal service distribution.
• C. Intersectoral coordination: Refers to collaboration between sectors such as health, education, sanitation, and nutrition to improve health outcomes; it is not the main issue highlighted in the question.
questions.learning: Equitable distribution Equitable distribution is a core principle of Primary Health Care (PHC), ensuring that essential health services are available and accessible to all segments of the population, irrespective of geographic location or socioeconomic status.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 40-year-old man, after being diagnosed with hypertension, strictly follows diet and exercise advice. However, he continues to smoke and says, “My grandfather smoked all his life and lived till 90, so this won’t affect me.” Which of the following defense mechanisms is best illustrated?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Rationalization

Rationalization is a defense mechanism in which a person provides logical, socially acceptable explanations to justify behavior driven by unconscious motives or to reduce guilt/anxiety.

• The person is aware of the facts but distorts reasoning to make behavior seem acceptable
• Common in situations involving health-risk behaviors (e.g., smoking, alcohol)
• Differs from:

• Denial: complete refusal to accept reality
• Minimization: downplaying severity
• Intellectualization: focusing on facts without emotional involvement
