questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is the true statement regarding measures to prevent typhoid transmission in the community?
options: Typhoid vaccine administration is the best method of preventing transmission
Hygiene practices and clean sanitation control is more important than typhoid vaccine
In 10% cases, person to person transmission occurs
Drug resistance in typhoid is not as big a problem as in TB
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hygiene practices and clean sanitation control is more important than typhoid vaccine

The true statement regarding typhoid transmission preventive measures is that hygiene practices and clean sanitation control are more important than the typhoid vaccine. It helps in breaking the chain of transmission.

Typhoid fever is caused by Salmonella typhi and is mainly transmitted to humans by the fecal-oral route.

Clinical features include high fever with chills associated with headache, malaise, cough, sore throat, abdominal pain, and constipation or diarrhea are seen in the early phase. The fever occurs in a step-ladder fashion reaching a plateau in 7-10 days. A maculopapular rash may be seen on the trunk and chest known as rose spots. In the late stages, hepatosplenomegaly, abdominal distension, relative bradycardia, and a dicrotic pulse can occur.

Diagnosis is by isolation of the organism from blood, bone marrow, and stools. Blood culture is mainly used for the diagnosis. Other tests such as the Widal tests are useful.

Management is mainly by sanitation. It is the ultimate method to control typhoid. It breaks the transmission of the disease. It is combined with proper health education.

Antibiotic therapy is started early and the choice of antibiotics depends on the susceptibility of the organism to the drug. In the case of drug-susceptible typhoid, ciprofloxacin is useful.

Drug resistance to typhoid has been emerging. Similar to drug resistance in TB, there are multidrug-resistant (MDR) and extensively drug-resistant (XDR) S. Typhi strains. MDR strains are resistant against at least 1 out of 3 or >3 categorically differentiated antimicrobials, such as ampicillin, cotrimoxazole, and chloramphenicol. XDR are those which are resistant to all except 1-2 antimicrobials.

Ceftriaxone, cefotaxime, and (oral) cefixime are effective for the treatment of MDR enteric fever.

Immunization is a complementary approach in management since the protective efficacy can be overcome by a high inoculum in the case of food-borne diseases.

The typhoid vaccines available are the Vi polysaccharide vaccine and the Ty21a vaccine. Ty21a is a live attenuated vaccine recommended after 6 years and is given orally on days 1,3,5 and 7. Vi polysaccharide vaccine can be given after 2 years as a single dose with a booster dose for every 2 years.
questions.learning: Hygiene practices and clean sanitation control is more important than typhoid vaccine The true statement regarding typhoid transmission preventive measures is that hygiene practices and clean sanitation control are more important than the typhoid vaccine.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 62-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus and chronic sinusitis is brought to the emergency department with a 2-day history of high-grade fever, severe headache, photophobia, neck stiffness, and two episodes of vomiting. On examination, he is confused and febrile (39.5 °C), with neck rigidity and a positive Kernig’s sign. His blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg, pulse is 104/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. Fundoscopic examination shows no papilledema. Empirical antibiotic therapy is planned prior to lumbar puncture. Which of the following is the most appropriate empirical treatment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ceftriaxone + Vancomycin

Acute bacterial meningitis is a medical emergency that requires immediate empiric intravenous antibiotics, ideally after obtaining blood cultures and before lumbar puncture if the LP is expected to be delayed. In adults with suspected community-acquired bacterial meningitis, ceftriaxone plus vancomycin provides broad coverage against the two most common pathogens—Streptococcus pneumoniae (including penicillin- and cephalosporin-resistant strains) and Neisseria meningitidis.

Why not the other options?

• A. Meropenem alone: Has broad-spectrum activity but is not recommended as first-line empiric monotherapy for community-acquired meningitis.
• C. Vancomycin alone: Covers resistant Gram-positive organisms but lacks adequate Gram-negative coverage, including N. meningitidis.
• D. Clindamycin: Has poor CSF penetration and inadequate activity against the common causes of bacterial meningitis.
questions.learning: Ceftriaxone + Vancomycin Acute bacterial meningitis is a medical emergency that requires immediate empiric intravenous antibiotics, ideally after obtaining blood cultures and before lumbar puncture if the LP is expected to be delayed.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which mutation is linked to the Philadelphia chromosome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Reciprocal translocation

The mutation associated with the Philadelphia chromosome is a result of reciprocal translocation.

Fusion of BCR-ABL is created by a reciprocal (9;22)translocation (Philadelphia chromosome. This is detected by cytogenetics, fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH), or polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and occurs in Chronic myelogenous leukaemia (CML). To form the abnormal chromosome, part of the BCR (breakpoint cluster region) gene of chromosome 22 fuses with part of the ABL gene (encodes a tyrosine kinase) of chromosome 9, directing the synthesis of a chimeric protein that has unregulated tyrosine kinase activity and drives cell proliferation.

The peak incidence of CML is in the fifth to sixth decade.

* Clinical features:

* Anemia weight loss, and anorexia.

* Splenomegaly

* Peripheral blood:

* Leukocytosis, exceeding 100,000 cells/mm3, which consists predominantly of neutrophils, band forms, metamyelocytes, myelocytes, eosinophils, and basophils.

* Blasts usually make up less than 5% of circulating cells.

* Bone Marrow:

* Markedly Hypercellular with maturing granulocytic precursors, with an elevated proportion of eosinophils and basophils.

* Low LAP score

Image – Interphase FISH showing (9;22) translocation.
questions.learning: Reciprocal translocation — The mutation associated with the Philadelphia chromosome is a result of reciprocal translocation. Fusion of BCR-ABL is created by a reciprocal (9;22)translocation (Philadelphia chromosome.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 26-year woman presents with six weeks amenorrhea. Obstetrician notices right adnexal tenderness on cervical motion during examination. Which of the following is an incorrect statement?
options: Abdominal pain is the commonest presentation
Oral methotrexate is treatment of choice
Chances of ectopic increase in PID
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Oral methotrexate is treatment of choice

Ectopic pregnancy occurs when the fertilized ovum implants outside the uterine cavity.

Most common location

| Site | Percentage

| ---- | ----------

| Fallopian tube (ampulla) | \~70%

| Isthmus | \~12%

| Fimbria | \~11%

| Ovary / abdomen | Rare

Classic triad of ectopic pregnancy:

| Feature | Explanation

| ------- | -----------

| Amenorrhea | Missed period

| Abdominal pain | Tubal distension

| Vaginal bleeding | Decidual shedding

Role of Progesterone

Progesterone levels may help assess pregnancy viability, but:

• Low progesterone suggests nonviable pregnancy
• It cannot confirm ectopic pregnancy

| Risk factor | Mechanism

| ----------- | ---------

| Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) | Tubal scarring

| Previous ectopic pregnancy | Tubal damage

| Tubal surgery | Structural abnormalities

| Assisted reproductive techniques | Altered embryo transport

Treatment of Ectopic Pregnancy

Methotrexate works by inhibiting trophoblastic cell proliferation.

Route of administration

➡ Intramuscular injection

Common regimen:

• Single-dose IM methotrexate

| Situation | Treatment

| --------- | ---------

| Hemodynamically stable, small ectopic | IM methotrexate

| Ruptured ectopic | Emergency surgery

| Failed medical therapy | Laparoscopy

questions.text: Which of the following is the main arterial supply of palatine tonsils?
options: Tonsillar branch of the facial artery
Descending palatine branch of maxillary artery
Ascending palatine branch of facial artery
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tonsillar branch of the facial artery

The main arterial supply of tonsil is by the tonsillar branch of the facial artery.

Five arteries supply the tonsil:

* Tonsillar branch of the facial artery (the main artery)

* Ascending palatine branch of the facial artery

* Ascending pharyngeal branch of the external carotid artery

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the absolute contraindication for the device depicted in the image below?
questions.explanation: The device shown is an intrauterine contraceptive device (IUCD) such as a Copper-T. The question asks for an absolute contraindication to its use. Undiagnosed vaginal bleeding is an absolute contraindication for IUCD insertion. This is because abnormal bleeding may be due to serious underlying conditions such as endometrial cancer, cervical cancer, or pregnancy-related complications, which must be evaluated before inserting any intrauterine device. Inserting an IUCD without diagnosis may worsen the condition or delay proper treatment. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Anemia : Not an absolute contraindication (though Cu-T may worsen bleeding, caution is needed) (C) Uterine malformations : Relative/functional contraindication depending on severity, not always absolute (D) Uterine fibroids : Not absolute unless they significantly distort the uterine cavity
questions.learning: The device shown is an intrauterine contraceptive device (IUCD) such as a Copper-T. The question asks for an absolute contraindication to its use.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: An elderly male went for a medical examination. Laboratory investigations showed a marked elevation of lymphocytes with marked leukocytosis. The peripheral smear of the patient is given below. What is the appropriate next step for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Flow cytometry

The likely diagnosis based on the given clinical scenario and the peripheral smear showing smudge cells is chronic lymphocytic leukemia. The next step in his management should be flow cytometry.

Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) is a peripheral B-cell neoplasm usually affecting adults, more commonly men. Patients are often asymptomatic at diagnosis. When symptomatic, it presents non-specifically with easy fatigability, weight loss, and anorexia. Generalized lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly are present in most symptomatic patients.

The chromosomal defects in CLL include

• Deletion of 13q (commonest and has a good prognosis)
• Deletion of 11q
• Trisomy 12q
• Deletion of 17p (poor prognosis)

The peripheral blood smear in cases of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) contains small round lymphocytes having condensed chromatin and scant cytoplasm. Some of these cells may get disrupted while preparing the smears, producing smudge cells. An absolute lymphocyte count of >5000/mm3 is required for diagnosis. Hypogammaglobulinemia is commonly seen, making the patient susceptible to infections. A few patients may develop hemolytic anemia or thrombocytopenia due to autoantibodies made by non-neoplastic B cells.

Immunophenotyping using flow cytometry is the investigation done to arrive at the diagnosis. The classical immunophenotypic feature of CLL is CD19+, CD20+, CD 23+, and CD5+.

On lymph node biopsy: Lymph nodes are composed of small lymphocytes admixed with larger activated lymphocytes. The large lymphocytes contain mitotically active cells and gather in loose aggregates, which are referred to as proliferation centers. These proliferation centers are pathognomic to CLL when present.

Expectant management is the treatment of choice for asymptomatic patients with chronic lymphocytic leukemia. The gold standard for therapy is a combination of fludarabine, cyclophosphamide, and rituximab.

Richter’s syndrome is a complication of CLL in which there is a transformation to an aggressive lymphoma, most commonly diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL).

Other options:

Option A: Stem cell transplantation - This is not the first step in the management of CLL. It may be considered in certain high-risk patients or those with refractory disease, but only after confirming the diagnosis and assessing the disease stage.

Option B: Bone marrow biopsy - While it can provide valuable information about the extent of infiltration, it is not the initial test for diagnosing CLL. Flow cytometry is the preferred diagnostic method.

Option D: Start high-dose chemotherapy - This is not the first step in managing CLL. Treatment decisions should be based on clinical stage, prognostic factors, and the patient's overall health. Moreover, asymptomatic patients with CLL are often managed with a watchful waiting approach.
questions.learning: Flow cytometry — The likely diagnosis based on the given clinical scenario and the peripheral smear showing smudge cells is chronic lymphocytic leukemia.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following CT findings is not an indication to perform angiography in a splenic trauma patient under conservative management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Subcapsular hematoma covering 40% surface area

In a splenic trauma patient under conservative management, angiography is indicated if the CT shows a high-grade injury rather than a low-grade injury (subcapsular hematoma covering 40% surface area is a grade II injury).

In splenic trauma patients that are managed conservatively, angiography is indicated if there is the presence of the following CT findings:

* Contrast extravasation

* Presence of pseudoaneurysm

* Significant hemoperitoneum

* High-grade injury

* Evidence of vascular injury

Management of Splenic trauma:

Grade I and II injuries:

* They are usually hemodynamically stable and are managed non-operatively.

* Initially, these patients are managed conservatively with regular monitoring of vitals and serial CECT.

* If the grade of injury is found to increase, then angiography and embolization of the bleeding vessel are done to achieve hemostasis.

* If angiography and embolization fail to achieve hemostasis, or if the patient becomes hemodynamically unstable or if there is a contrast blush, then a splenorrhaphy is done.

Grade III injuries that are hemodynamically stable are managed like that of Grades I and II, while those that are hemodynamically unstable are managed like that of Grades IV and V.

Grade IV and V injuries: These patients are usually hemodynamically unstable and splenectomy is done.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following drugs is associated with calciphylaxis in chronic kidney disease patients?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Warfarin

Calciphylaxis (calcific uremic arteriolopathy) is a rare but life-threatening complication seen mainly in patients with advanced chronic kidney disease (CKD). It is characterized by calcification of small and medium-sized arterioles, leading to painful skin necrosis. Warfarin is a well-recognized risk factor because it inhibits vitamin K-dependent matrix Gla protein, a natural inhibitor of vascular calcification.

Why not the other options?

• A. Calcium channel blocker: Not associated with calciphylaxis.
• C. Non-calcium-based phosphate binder: These (e.g., sevelamer, lanthanum) reduce phosphate burden and may help lower the risk of vascular calcification.
• D. Thiazide diuretic: Not a recognized cause of calciphylaxis.
questions.learning: Warfarin Calciphylaxis (calcific uremic arteriolopathy) is a rare but life-threatening complication seen mainly in patients with advanced chronic kidney disease (CKD).

questions.text: Myosin head detaches from actin by which of the following mechanism?

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a road traffic accident, and a whole-body CT scan is planned as part of trauma assessment. The standard whole-body CT protocol includes all of the following except which one?
questions.explanation: The whole-body CT protocol, often called a "pan-scan," is a rapid screening tool for major trauma to identify life-threatening internal injuries. Standard protocols include CT of the Head (Option D) and Cervical Spine (Option B) to rule out intracranial hemorrhage and spinal instability, as well as CT of the Chest, Abdomen (Option A), and Pelvis to check for visceral injury or internal bleeding. CT of the limbs (Option C) is NOT part of the standard whole-body trauma protocol. Injuries to the extremities are typically assessed via physical examination and targeted conventional X-rays once the patient is hemodynamically stabilized. Scanning all limbs in the primary pan-scan would significantly increase the radiation dose and scan time without necessarily altering immediate life-saving interventions. Therefore, while essential for managing fractures later, CT limbs are excluded from the initial "whole-body" trauma assessment to focus on the brain, spine, and torso

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: As a medical officer posted in rural service, you have been asked to supervise the various preventive measures being taken in your region against malaria. According to the program whose logo is shown below, you would be correct to advise all of the following except:
options: Two rounds of spraying with DDT should be done to provide protection during the entire transmission season.
Long Lasting Insecticide Nets (LLIN) should be provided in areas with Annual Parasite Index ≥ 5.
Indoor Residual Sprays are not suitable for vector control in rural areas.
In case of DDT resistance, 3 rounds of spraying with Malathion should be done to provide protection during the entire transmission season.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Indoor Residual Sprays are not suitable for vector control in rural areas.

Under the Integrated vector management initiative, Indoor Residual Sprays are the main methods of vector control in rural areas.

National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme (NVBDCP) is the nodal agency for the prevention of control of the following vector-borne diseases:

* Kala-azar (also called visceral leishmaniasis)

* Malaria

* Dengue

* Filariasis

* Japanese encephalitis

* Chikungunya.

Integrated Vector Management:

* For adult mosquitoes:

* Indoor residual Sprays are used. It is the main method of vector control in rural areas.

* DDT is the insecticide of choice.

* Two rounds of spraying are done with DDT and in DDT-resistant areas, three rounds of spraying are done with Malathion (if DDT-resistant).

* For the larvae: Larvivorous fish and larvicides are used. This is the main method of vector control in urban areas.

* For personal protection:

* Insecticide-treated bed nets are supplied in areas with Annual Parasite Index (API) ≥ 2.

* Long-Lasting Insecticide Nets (LLIN) are provided in areas with API ≥ 5.

The Drug distribution centers only dispense anti-malarial drugs under the NVBDCP for Malaria.

Important points about the organization for the anti-Malaria program:

* Central Government: Supplies DDT and larvicides.

* State government: Procures the Indoor Residual Sprays (IRS) for the districts.

* District Malaria Office: Key unit for the implementation of the program.

* District Malaria Officer: Has direct responsibility for IRS spraying operations and is assisted by one Assistant Malaria Officer and Malaria Inspectors.

* Medical officer of the PHC:  Has the overall responsibility for the surveillance and laboratory services.

* Multi-Purpose Workers and ASHAs: Carry out surveillance and case detection in the community.

* Drug Distribution Centres: Only dispensing anti-malarial drugs.

* Fever Treatment Depots: Dispense the anti-malarial drugs and collect the blood slides.

Pearl PF1014: Insecticides

Contact poisons

* Natural: Pyrethrum, rotenone, derris, nicotine, mineral oils

* Synthetic:

* Organo-chlorine compounds: DDT, methoxychlor, HCH, lindane, chlordane, heptachlor, dieldrin, aldrin, toxaphene, kepone, mirex.

* Repellants: Benzyl benzoate, indalone, meta-diethyltoluamide, dimethyl phthalate, ethyl hexanediol.

* Organo-phosphorus compounds: Chlorthion (aryl), diazinon (aryl), demethoate, malathion (alkyl), fenthion, parathion (aryl), trichlorfon (alkyl), runnel, abale, naled, chlorpyrifos, fenitrothion, dicapthon.

* Carbamates: Carbaryl, dimetilan, propoxur, pyrolan.

* Synthetic pyrethroids: Prothrin, resmethrin, bioresmethrin, permethrin, proparthin, tetramethrin

* Stomach poisons: Paris green, sodium fluoride.

* Fumigants: Hydrogen cyanide, methyl bromide, sulphur dioxide, carbon disulphide.

Specific Insecticides
Comments

DDT (Dichloro-diphenyl-thrichloroethane)
Insecticidal properties were discovered by Swiss scientist, Paul Muller. Most widely used insecticide. Attacks nerves of insects but doesn’t cause immediate death. White amorphous powder. Contains 70 – 80% of para-para isomers, which is the most active fraction of DDT. Has residual action up to 18 months. Used as a residual spray.Least toxic organo-chlorine compound.

HCH (hexachlorocyclo-hexane)
Synthesized by Michael Faraday. Normal HCH contains 13 – 16% of gamma isomer. Gamma-HCH or lindane has 99% gamma isomer.Short residual action – 3 months.

Malathion
Least toxicity of all organophosphorus compounds. Used as an ultra-low volume spray.

Fenthion
Also called baytex. Used as a residual spray.

Pyrethrum
Vegetable origin – Chrysanthemum cinerariafolium. Nerve poison and is excellent as a space spray.No residual action.Synergistic action with DDT as space spray.
questions.learning: Indoor Residual Sprays are not suitable for vector control in rural areas. Under the Integrated vector management initiative, Indoor Residual Sprays are the main methods of vector control in rural areas.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Caspases are involved in which of the following types of programmed cell death?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pyroptosis and Apoptosis

Caspases = cysteine proteases

• Exist as inactive precursors
• Get activated during programmed cell death

Caspases are central mediators of apoptosis, with initiator and executioner caspases driving programmed cell death.

Pyroptosis is a caspase-dependent inflammatory cell death mediated mainly by caspase-1.

Necroptosis and ferroptosis are caspase-independent forms of regulated cell death.

Hence, caspases are involved in apoptosis and pyroptosis.
questions.learning: Pyroptosis and Apoptosis Caspases = cysteine proteases • Exist as inactive precursors • Get activated during programmed cell death Caspases are central mediators of apoptosis, with initiator and executioner caspases driving programmed cell death.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A one-and-half-year-old child was brought to the hospital with a history of breathlessness, fever, cough, and cold. On examination, respiratory rate was 46/min with chest retractions and no danger signs. Which is the most appropriate management?
options: Give IV antibiotics and refer to higher centre
Oral antibiotics, warn of danger signs, and send home
No need of treatment only home remedies
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Oral antibiotics, warn of danger signs, and send home

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of acute respiratory illness. According to the recent WHO guidelines,  this child can be classified as having 'Pneumonia'. The treatment is oral amoxicillin and home care advice.

Three key clinical signs are used to assess a sick child with cough or difficult breathing:

* Respiratory rate

* Which distinguishes children who have pneumonia from those who do not

* > 50 for infants 2 months to 12 months

* > 40 for children 12 months to 5 years of age

* Lower chest wall indrawing

* Which indicates pneumonia

* Stridor

* Which indicates those with severe pneumonia who require hospital admission.

The following table gives the classification for cough / difficult breathing from 2 months to 5 years of age:

The recent WHO guidelines state that chest indrawing and fast breathing are in the category of pneumonia.

Signs of severe pneumonia are :

* Not able to drink

* Persistent vomiting

* Convulsions

* Lethargic or unconscious

* Stridor in a calm child

* Severe malnutrition
questions.learning: Oral antibiotics, warn of danger signs, and send home The given clinical scenario is suggestive of acute respiratory illness. According to the recent WHO guidelines, this child can be classified as having 'Pneumonia'.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The following Lineweaver-Burk plots depict enzymatic action in the presence of enzyme inhibitors. The enzyme action without inhibitor is represented by a blue line. What type of inhibitors are depicted in images 1 and 2?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1- Noncompetitive inhibition 2- Competitive inhibition

The Lineweaver-Burk plot in image 1 depicts non-competitive inhibition, and that in image 2 depicts competitive inhibition.

Important parameters in a reaction include:

• The affinity of the enzyme for its substrate, given by the Michaelis constant or Km. A low Km reflects a high affinity of the enzyme for substrate and vice versa. The value of Km is given by the substrate concentration at which the reaction velocity is equal to one-half Vmax. It does not change with changes in enzyme concentration.
• Vmax is the maximum velocity of a reaction.

Competitive inhibition is when the inhibitor binds reversibly to the substrate-binding site and competes with the substrate for the active enzyme-binding site. This effect can be overcome by increasing the substrate concentration by which maximum velocity can still be achieved. Therefore, Vmax is unaltered in this type of inhibition. However, the concentration of the substrate required to achieve half of the maximum velocity is increased. Therefore, Km is increased in this condition.

In a Lineweaver-Burk plot, the addition of a competitive inhibitor causes plots with the same y-intercept (Vmax is unaffected) but different x-intercepts (due to increased Km).

Noncompetitive inhibition is by binding of inhibitors to enzymes in locations remote from the active site. Increasing the concentration of the substrate does not overcome non-competitive inhibition. Thus, noncompetitive inhibitors decrease the Vmax of the reaction. They do not interfere with the binding of the substrate to the enzyme. Thus, the enzyme shows the same Km in the presence or absence of noncompetitive inhibitors.

In a Lineweaver-Burk plot, the addition of a non-competitive inhibitor causes plots with the same x-intercept (Km is unaffected) but different slopes and y-intercepts (due to decreased Vmax).

In uncompetitive inhibition, inhibitors bind with the enzyme-substrate intermediate complex and inhibit it. This leads to a decrease in both Vmax and Km.
questions.learning: 1- Noncompetitive inhibition 2- Competitive inhibition The Lineweaver-Burk plot in image 1 depicts non-competitive inhibition, and that in image 2 depicts competitive inhibition.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is an irreversible method of contraception?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Laparoscopic tubal ligation

Among the given options, Laparoscopic tubal ligation is an irreversible method of contraception.

Tubal sterilization can be achieved by three methods which are:

• Electrocoagulation is used for the destruction of a segment of the tube
• Mechanical occlusion of the tube using a silicone rubber band (Falope ring) or a spring-loaded clip (Hulka Clemens clip)
• Suture ligation with or without tubal segment excision such as Pomeroy's method, Uchida's method, Irving's method, etc.

Intrauterine devices such as copper T and LNG-IUDs and implants belong to the category of long acting reversible contraception.

In copper-T (Option B) a copper wire is wrapped around a polypropelene vertical frame. The copper in the device causes an intense local inflammatory response in the uterus that leads to lysosomal activation and activation of other inflammatory processes that are spermicidal. The Cu-T 380A is approved for 10 years of continuous use.

LNG-IUD (Option D) is a T-shaped polyethylene structure enclosed by a cylinder containing levonorgesterl. This hormone is released continuously through the permeable cylinder. The progestin makes the endometrium atrophic and stimulates the production of thick cervical mucus that blocks sperm penetration into the uterus. It also decreases tubal motility, thereby preventing fertilization.

Nexplanon has now replaced implanon (Option C) which was a previously used etonogestrel implant. Nexplanon is a single-rod progestin etonogestrel (68 mg) containing subdermal implant that provides contraception over 3 years. Its mechanism of action is by suppression of ovulation, thickened cervical mucus, and endometrial atrophy. Irregular bleeding is an important side effect of the implant. This method of contraception is reversible in nature.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which method would be most effective for presenting statistical data to highlight the importance of routine antenatal care to a small, uneducated village during a rural health posting?
questions.explanation: When communicating health statistics to a population with low literacy levels, such as an uneducated rural village, visual simplicity is paramount. A pictogram (Option A) is the most effective method because it uses easily recognizable symbols or pictures to represent data, making complex concepts intuitive and engaging. For example, a picture of a mother can represent ten pregnant women, allowing villagers to quickly grasp ratios without needing advanced numeracy. Line diagrams (Option B) are better for showing trends over time but require an understanding of X-Y coordinates. Histograms (Option C) are used to show frequency distributions of continuous data and can appear cluttered and confusing to those unfamiliar with statistical charts. Frequency polygons (Option D) are even more abstract, using lines to connect midpoints of intervals. Therefore, the pictogram's ability to simplify data into relatable imagery makes it the gold standard for community health education in underserved rural settings where traditional literacy is limited

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following cardiac chambers is enlarged in mitral stenosis on chest X-ray initially?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Left atrium

Left atrium (LA) is the first cardiac chamber to get enlarged in mitral stenosis (MS). It is due to the pressure overload of LA. It can be appreciated on the lateral and left anterior oblique views.

Other radiographic changes seen in MS are straightening of the upper left border of the cardiac silhouette, posterior displacement of the esophagus by an enlarged LA, and Kerley B lines due to distention of interlobular septae and lymphatics with edema.

Severe MS causing pulmonary hypertension leads to enlargement of the pulmonary artery, right ventricle, and right atrium. Left ventricle remains unaffected in isolated MS.
questions.learning: Left atrium Left atrium (LA) is the first cardiac chamber to get enlarged in mitral stenosis (MS). It is due to the pressure overload of LA.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 12-year-old boy undergoing combination chemotherapy for non-Hodgkin lymphoma presents on day 7 of his treatment cycle with dysuria, suprapubic pain, and frank hematuria. Urinalysis reveals numerous red blood cells with no evidence of infection. He is diagnosed with hemorrhagic cystitis. His current chemotherapy regimen includes the following agents. Which of the following drug is most likely responsible for his symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ifosfamide

Hemorrhagic cystitis is a characteristic dose-limiting toxicity of ifosfamide (and cyclophosphamide), caused by the toxic metabolite acrolein, which directly injures the bladder urothelium. This complication is preventable with mesna, which binds and detoxifies acrolein in the urine, along with adequate hydration.

Why not the other options?

• B. Vincristine: Causes peripheral neuropathy, autonomic dysfunction (constipation), and SIADH; it is not associated with hemorrhagic cystitis.
• C. Methotrexate: Causes myelosuppression, mucositis, hepatotoxicity, and nephrotoxicity (high doses); hemorrhagic cystitis is not a typical adverse effect.
• D. Doxorubicin: Causes dose-dependent cardiomyopathy, myelosuppression, and alopecia; cardiotoxicity is prevented with dexrazoxane, not mesna.
•
questions.learning: Ifosfamide Hemorrhagic cystitis is a characteristic dose-limiting toxicity of ifosfamide (and cyclophosphamide), caused by the toxic metabolite acrolein, which directly injures the bladder urothelium.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is true about optic neuritis?
options: Relative afferent pupillary defect is seen.
There is no pain on ocular movement.
Multiple myeloma is a common cause.
Oral corticosteroids are the mainstay of treatment.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Relative afferent pupillary defect is seen.

In optic neuritis, relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) or Marcus Gunn pupil is seen. It is elicited by the swinging flashlight test. Normally, both pupils remain constricted. In the presence of RAPD, both pupils dilate on moving the flashlight from the normal to the abnormal eye. This paradoxical response of the pupil to light is called Marcus Gunn pupil.

Other options:

Option B: Pain is aggravated by ocular movement, especially in the upward or downward direction due to attachment of the superior rectus fibers to the dura mater.

Option C: Multiple sclerosis, and not multiple myeloma, is a known demyelinating cause of optic neuritis.

Option D: Oral corticosteroid therapy alone is contraindicated because it does not improve the outcome and is associated with an increased risk of new attacks of optic neuritis. Intravenous methylprednisolone can be used if the patient shows radiological evidence of multiple sclerosis.
questions.learning: Relative afferent pupillary defect is seen. In optic neuritis, relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) or Marcus Gunn pupil is seen.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following disorders follows autosomal recessive inheritance pattern?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cystic fibrosis

Cystic fibrosis is a condition with an autosomal recessive mode of inheritance.

It results due to a defective mutation in the gene encoding for cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR gene). It functions as an epithelial anion channel. It plays an important role in mucociliary transport along the respiratory mucosa. It also helps regulate the amount of exocrine gland secretion.

The defect in the ion channel results in the production of hyper viscous, adherent secretions which can obstruct the airways. Organisms such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus can grow in the sputum. The exocrine pancreas can undergo fibrotic scarring, cyst formation, and acinar tissue loss. The viscid secretions can lead to pancreatic duct obstruction. The flow of digestive enzymes to the duodenum is hence impaired.

Symptoms include sinusitis, steatorrhea, and abdominal pain. Distal intestinal obstruction is a complication due to difficulty in excreting intestinal contents. In neonates, it can present as meconium ileus.

Detection of high levels of trypsinogen is used in newborn screening. Chloride level >60mEq/L in the sweat of affected patients is diagnostic. Hyponatremic hypochloremic alkalosis and hypokalemia may also be seen.

Postural drainage, short-term antibiotics, and inhaled bronchodilators can be used for medical management. The definitive treatment is lung transplantation.

In autosomal recessive inheritance, multiple affected members are seen in the same generation. Other generations are not affected. The following pedigree chart depicts an autosomal recessive pattern of inheritance.

Other options:

Option A - Huntington's disease is a trinucleotide (CAG) repeat disorder with an autosomal dominant mode of inheritance. It is characterized by involuntary movements known as chorea.

Option B - Treacher Collins syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder that presents as mandibular and malar hypoplasia.

Option D - Achondroplasia has an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern and presents with short limbs, saddle nose, and spinal deformity.
questions.learning: Cystic fibrosis Cystic fibrosis is a condition with an autosomal recessive mode of inheritance. It results due to a defective mutation in the gene encoding for cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR gene).

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Medical termination of pregnancy is governed by specific legal and medical regulations. Under certain defined conditions, termination is permitted up to 24 weeks of gestation. In which scenario is medical termination of pregnancy legally allowed up to 24 weeks?
questions.explanation: Under the Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) Amendment Act 2021 in India, the gestational limit for termination was increased from 20 to 24 weeks for specific categories of women. These categories include survivors of sexual assault, rape, or incest, as well as minors, women whose marital status changed during pregnancy (widowhood or divorce), and women with physical disabilities or mental illness. For rape victims, this extension acknowledges the extreme trauma and potential delays in recognizing or reporting the pregnancy. While fetal malformations (Option A) also allow for termination, they are often permitted even beyond 24 weeks if a medical board confirms substantial abnormalities. Contraception failure (Option C) is generally only a valid ground up to 20 weeks for married women or those in stable relationships. Minor status (Option B) is a valid category for the 24-week extension, but in the context of most standard medical examinations, "rape victim" is the classic textbook example for this specific legal threshold
questions.learning: Under the Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) Amendment Act 2021 in India, the gestational limit for termination was increased from 20 to 24 weeks for specific categories of women.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The nerve supply of larynx above the level of the vocal cords is by _______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Superior laryngeal nerve

The nerve supply of larynx above the level of vocal cords is by internal laryngeal nerve which is a branch of the superior laryngeal nerve.

* Sensory innervation of the larynx above the level of vocal cords is by the internal laryngeal nerve.

* Sensory innervation of the larynx below the level of vocal cords is by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

* At the level of vocal cords, it is supplied both by the internal laryngeal and recurrent laryngeal nerves.

The cricothyroid receives its supply from the external branch of the external laryngeal nerve.

Rest all the intrinsic muscles are innervated by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A tuberculosis patient on anti-tubercular treatment presents with a tingling sensation and paresthesia in the lower limbs. He is not a diabetic and occasionally consumes alcohol. Which of the following vitamins must be supplemented to this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Vitamin B6

Vitamin B6 must be supplemented for this patient. The clinical features of tingling sensation and paresthesias in a patient on anti-tubercular treatment are suggestive of the adverse effect of isoniazid.

Isoniazid is the first-line antitubercular drug that inhibits the production of mycolic acid. It is a bactericidal drug against tubercle bacilli.

Adverse effects of isoniazid:

• Peripheral neuritis (paresthesias, numbness, tingling sensation) due to interference with the production of active coenzyme pyridoxal phosphate from pyridoxine. Therefore, pyridoxine 10 mg/day (vitamin B6) is given prophylactically along with isoniazid to prevent neurotoxicity.
• Hepatitis - isoniazid must be stopped at the first sign of hepatotoxicity.
• Rashes
• Anemia
• Arthralgia

Toxicity of isoniazid results in metabolic acidosis and seizures.

Note: Vitamin deficiency in alcoholics includes the following:

• Folate causes megaloblastic anemia. It is treated by supplementation of oral doses of 5-15 mg of folic acid.
• Vitamin B6 results in peripheral neuritis, anemia, and glossitis, and lowers the seizure threshold. It is treated by supplementation of oral doses of 2-5 mg of pyridoxine.
• Thiamine results in Wernicke's encephalopathy. It is treated with 200 mg of intravenous thiamine three times daily, followed by 10 mg/day until complete recovery.
• Vitamin A results in xerophthalmia and night blindness. It is treated with supplementation of oral vitamin A 3000-5000 IU/day.
questions.learning: Vitamin B6 Vitamin B6 must be supplemented for this patient. The clinical features of tingling sensation and paresthesias in a patient on anti-tubercular treatment are suggestive of the adverse effect of isoniazid.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which biochemical cycle/process is used by monoclonal antibodies in hybridoma technology?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Purine salvage pathway

It is the purine salvage pathway that is utilized by monoclonal antibodies in hybridoma technology.

Monoclonal antibodies refer to the antibodies produced by a group of lymphocytes that produce antibodies against a single antigen. These antibodies are produced by hybridoma technology.

In this technology, the B-lymphocytes of mice spleen are immunized with an antigen to produce a specific antibody. These specific antibody-producing B lymphocytes are then fused with myeloma cells that can multiply indefinitely.

The myeloma cells are deficient in the hypoxanthine-guanine-phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT) gene and do not produce immunoglobulins. Therefore, the resulting hybrid cell is producing antibodies against a single antigen indefinitely. These hybrid cells are cultured in a HAT medium (containing hypoxanthine, aminopterin, and thymidine) and the monoclonal antibodies are obtained. It is well-established that nucleotides present in DNA and RNA consist of purine and pyrimidine bases. The synthesis of these nucleotides can occur through either the De novo pathway or the salvage pathway. Consequently, the inclusion of aminopterin in the HAT medium effectively inhibits the De novo pathway, thereby rendering the synthesis of purine dependent on the salvage pathway. However, it should be noted that the salvage pathway exclusively takes place in the presence of the enzymes HGPRT and thymidine kinase. The hybridoma cell is uniquely capable of proliferating on the HAT medium due to its distinct composition. Specifically, the myeloma component of the hybridoma possesses the capacity for repetitive cellular division, while the plasma cell component contains the enzyme HGPRT. Consequently, the hybridoma cells can sustain growth and viability over an extended period when cultivated on the HAT medium.

Hybridoma technology is a method for producing large numbers of identical antibodies (monoclonal antibodies).

Hybridomas are somatic cell hybrids produced by fusing the antibody-forming spleen cells with myeloma cells. The resultant hybrid thus has both the antibody-producing ability of the B-cell and the ability to multiply indefinitely of the myeloma.

The following are the steps involved in hybridoma technology:

• Mice are immunized with an antigen.
• After several weeks of immunization, blood samples are obtained from mice for measurement of serum antibodies.
• When the antibody titer is high enough, mice are commonly boosted by injecting antigen without adjuvant, intraperitoneally or intravenously.
• Then the mice are euthanized and their spleens removed for in vitro hybridoma cell production.
• Fusing antibody-producing spleen cells, which have a limited life span, with myeloma cells (derived from an immortal tumour of lymphocytes) results in a hybridoma that is capable of unlimited growth.
• The cells are cultured in a medium containing hypoxanthine, aminopterin, and thymidine (HAT medium) which allows only the fused cells to survive in culture.
• Monoclonal antibodies are then harvested.

Applications of hybridoma technology

• Listing lymphocyte subpopulations
• Specific cell quantitative preparation
• As an immunosuppressant in therapeutic settings
• Blood component nephelometric assays
• ELISA testing
• Quantitative purification of antigens.
• Common therapeutic applications for monoclonal antibodies
questions.learning: Purine salvage pathway — It is the purine salvage pathway that is utilized by monoclonal antibodies in hybridoma technology. Monoclonal antibodies refer to the antibodies produced by a group of lymphocytes that produce antibodies against a single antigen.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following organisms cause multiple alveolar-like lesions in the liver?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Echinococcus multilocularis

Echinococcus multilocularis causes multiple alveolar-like lesions in the liver.

E. multilocularis leads to the formation of a multilocular hydatid cyst, most commonly affecting the liver. It presents as multiple small cysts in the liver.

Echinococcus granulosus causes a hollow fluid-filled unilocular cyst in the liver. The CT below shows water lily sign, which is seen in the hydatid disease of the lung. It is caused by Echinococcus granulosus. (Option B)

The water-lily sign occurs due to the detachment of the endocyst membrane from the cyst wall, giving the appearance of floating membranes within the pericyst. This mimics the appearance of a water lily. It is classically visualised on plain radiographs (mainly chest X-ray) when the collapsed membranes are calcified but may be seen on ultrasound, CT, or MRI.
questions.learning: Echinococcus multilocularis Echinococcus multilocularis causes multiple alveolar-like lesions in the liver. E. multilocularis leads to the formation of a multilocular hydatid cyst, most commonly affecting the liver.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which one of the following is related to the release of bicarbonate in exchange for chloride in the RBC to maintain electrical neutrality?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Chloride shift

The release of bicarbonate in exchange for chloride in the RBC to maintain electrical neutrality is known as the chloride shift or Hamburger phenomenon.

Chloride shift:

* Upon entering the red blood cell, CO2 is rapidly hydrated to H2CO3 by carbonic anhydrase.

* H2CO3 is in equilibrium with H+ and its conjugate base, HCO3-. H+ can interact with deoxyhemoglobin.

* whereas HCO3- can be transported outside of the cell via anion exchanger 1 (AE1 or Band 3).

* To prevent an imbalance in charge, HCO₃⁻ exits the RBC into plasma, and Cl⁻ enters the RBC via the Band 3 transporter, maintaining electrical neutrality. This is called the chloride shift.

* Because of this chloride shift, the Cl – content of the red cells in venous blood is significantly greater than that in arterial blood.

* Note that for each CO2 molecule added to a red cell, there is an increase of one osmotically active particles in the cell - either a HCO 3 – or a Cl – ion. Consequently, the red cells take up water and increase in size.

Other options:

Option A: The Haldane effect is the phenomenon where the binding of oxygen promotes the release of carbon dioxide from hemoglobin, facilitating its removal. This effect allows for efficient gas exchange in the lungs and plays a crucial role in maintaining the balance of oxygen and carbon dioxide in the blood.

Option B: A right shift of the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve in response to an increase in blood CO2 and hydrogen ions, enhances the release of O2 from the blood in the tissues. This enhances the oxygenation of the blood in the lungs. This is known as the Bohr effect.

Option D: Haber–Weiss reaction is a chemical reaction that generates hydroxyl radicals (•OH), which are highly reactive and contribute to oxidative stress in biological systems. It occurs in the presence of superoxide (O₂⁻) and hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) and is catalyzed by iron (Fe³⁺ or Fe²⁺).

Reaction Steps:

* Superoxide reacts with ferric iron (Fe³⁺) to form ferrous iron (Fe²⁺): O2− + Fe3+→O2 + Fe2+

* Ferrous iron (Fe²⁺) reacts with hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) in a Fenton-like reaction to produce hydroxyl radicals (•OH): Fe2++H2O2→Fe3++OH−+⋅OH

* Overall Haber-Weiss Reaction:
O2−+H2O2→O2+OH−+⋅OH
questions.learning: Chloride shift — The release of bicarbonate in exchange for chloride in the RBC to maintain electrical neutrality is known as the chloride shift or Hamburger phenomenon.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Injury to the posterior interosseous nerve leads to?
options: Loss of extension of the wrist
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Loss of extension of digits

Injury to the posterior interosseous nerve leads to loss of extension of digits.

The posterior interosseous nerve (PIN) is a continuation of the deep branch of the radial nerve. It originates from the radial nerve in the cubital fossa, near the lateral epicondyle of the humerus. After passing through the supinator muscle, it transitions into the PIN.

The PIN is purely a motor nerve and supplies the posterior compartment of the forearm.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which incision is most commonly used for an appendectomy?
questions.explanation: The McBurney incision, also known as the gridiron incision, is the classic surgical approach for an open appendectomy. It is made at the McBurney point, located one-third of the distance from the right anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) to the umbilicus. This muscle-splitting incision follows the fiber direction of the external oblique, internal oblique, and transversus abdominis muscles, allowing for rapid access with minimal muscle damage. Kochers incision (Option B) is a subcostal incision used for cholecystectomy or biliary tract surgery. Midline incisions (Option C) are utilized for emergency laparotomies requiring wide exposure of multiple quadrants. The Battle incision (Option D) is a pararectual incision that is now largely historical due to the risk of damaging nerves supplying the rectus abdominis muscle. Due to its direct access to the cecal base and superior wound healing characteristics, the McBurney incision remains the preferred standard for localized, uncomplicated acute appendicitis when a laparoscopic approach is not utilized
questions.learning: The McBurney incision, also known as the gridiron incision, is the classic surgical approach for an open appendectomy. It is made at the McBurney point, located one-third of the distance from the right anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) to the umbilicus.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following is not required for calculation of creatinine clearance?
options: Volume of serum passing through kidney in 24 hours
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Volume of serum passing through kidney in 24 hours

The volume of plasma passing through the kidney in 24 hours is not used in the calculation of creatinine clearance.

The parameters used to calculate creatinine clearance (CCr) are:

• Urine creatinine
• Serum creatinine
• 24hr urine output

The formula used to calculate creatinine clearance (CCr) is:

UCr × V ⁄ PCr  where,

UCr - Urine creatinine(mg/dl)

PCr - Serum creatinine(mg/dl)

V - Urine volume(ml/24 hrs)

Creatinine is a metabolite of muscle metabolism and is cleared from the body mostly by glomerular filtration. Therefore, the clearance of creatinine is used to assess GFR.

Urine collection for the measurement of creatinine clearance may be subject to practical constraints. Therefore, approximate changes in GFR can be obtained by measuring the serum creatinine concentration, which is inversely proportional to GFR.
questions.learning: Volume of serum passing through kidney in 24 hours — The volume of plasma passing through the kidney in 24 hours is not used in the calculation of creatinine clearance.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In obstetric practice, which factor is most commonly responsible for the development of consumptive coagulopathy, a condition characterized by rapid consumption of clotting factors exceeding their production?
questions.explanation: Consumptive coagulopathy, or Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC), is a severe complication in pregnancy where systemic activation of the coagulation cascade leads to the depletion of platelets and clotting factors. While all the listed options can cause DIC, "placental abruption" (Option B) is the "predominant" or most common obstetric cause. When the placenta separates prematurely, thromboplastin and other tissue factors are released into the maternal circulation, triggering widespread clotting. Intrauterine death (Option A) can cause DIC, but usually only if the dead fetus remains in utero for more than 4 weeks. Amniotic fluid embolism (Option D) and sepsis (Option C) cause extremely severe DIC, but they are much rarer occurrences compared to placental abruption. In abruption, the extent of the coagulopathy often correlates with the size of the retroplacental clot. Management involves rapid delivery and the replacement of blood products (fresh frozen plasma, cryoprecipitate, and platelets) to stabilize the patient's clotting capacity
questions.learning: Consumptive coagulopathy, or Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC), is a severe complication in pregnancy where systemic activation of the coagulation cascade leads to the depletion of platelets and clotting factors.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The upper part of the uncinate process commonly attaches to?
questions.explanation: The uncinate process is a thin, curved bony hook belonging to the ethmoid bone that forms part of the lateral nasal wall. Its upper part commonly extends to attach to the middle turbinate (middle nasal concha). This structure is essential in forming the drainage pathway for the frontal and maxillary sinuses through the ostiomeatal complex. The superior turbinate (Option B) is located higher in the nasal cavity than the uncinate process, so there is no anatomical attachment between them. The inferior turbinate (Option C) is a separate bone located much lower in the nasal passage. The bulla ethmoidalis (Option D) is an ethmoid air cell situated behind the uncinate process; while they form the boundaries of the hiatus semilunaris inferior, they do not serve as an attachment site for one another. Thus, the middle turbinate is the standard attachment point
questions.learning: The uncinate process is a thin, curved bony hook belonging to the ethmoid bone that forms part of the lateral nasal wall. Its upper part commonly extends to attach to the middle turbinate (middle nasal concha).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: 2 medical students are conducting a study to see the effects of acclimatization at high altitudes. Which of the following will not be seen in the same?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hypoventilation

Hypoventilation is not a part of high-altitude acclimatization.

A person constantly exposed to high altitude slowly acclimatizes to the low PaO2 so that the deleterious effects of the same can be reduced. This occurs mainly via the following mechanisms:

* Increased pulmonary ventilation

* Increase RBC and Hb

* Increased diffusing capacity of the lungs

* Increased vascularity of the peripheral tissues

* Increased ability of the tissue cells to use O2, despite low Po2.

Increased pulmonary ventilation: Low PO2 immediately stimulates the arterial chemoreceptors and causes increased alveolar ventilation. The immediate increase may blow off large quantities of CO2, lowering PCO2 and increasing pH which in turn may inhibit the brain stem respiratory centre via peripheral chemoreceptors. But this effect fades away in a few days and the respiratory centre activity returns to normal. Continued exposure to high altitude further increase the ventilation

Increase in red blood cells and hemoglobin concentration: Hypoxia triggers increased RBC production. Hematocrit slowly increases even up to 60%, and blood volume rises and together leading to hemoglobin and myoglobin rise

Increased diffusing capacity after acclimatization: Pulmonary capillary volume expands leading to an increased surface area of diffusion while an increase of pulmonary volume occurs which also increases the surface area of diffusion. Pulmonary arterial pressure rises leading to the opening of normally poorly perfused areas of the lung whereby diffusion further increases

Peripheral circulatory system changes during acclimatization: There is an initial rise in cardiac output to compensate for the low RBC and Hb which later falls to normal once these values rise due to erythropoiesis. Capillary angiogenesis occurs to improve blood flow, especially in the non-pulmonary tissues

Cellular acclimatization. Changes also occur at the cellular level with an increase in numbers of mitochondria and cellular respiration in organisms living at high altitudes than the ones living at sea level.
questions.learning: Hypoventilation Hypoventilation is not a part of high-altitude acclimatization. A person constantly exposed to high altitude slowly acclimatizes to the low PaO2 so that the deleterious effects of the same can be reduced.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is not a radiological finding in a patient with left heart failure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Focal oligemia

Focal oligemia is not a radiological feature of left heart failure. It is seen in pulmonary embolism and is also called Westermark’s sign.

It is defined by a hyperlucent area with decreased vascularity due to oligemia of the involved part of the lung. It is caused by a cutoff of circulation due to an embolus, leading to the loss of visibility of a patch of pulmonary vasculature on an X- ray.

Radiological signs of left heart failure include :

• Cardiomegaly - enlargement of the cardiac silhouette (increased cardiothoracic ratio)
• Upper lobe pulmonary venous congestion (cephalisation of vessels)
• Interstitial edema.
• Kerley B lines - horizontal lines in the periphery of the lower posterior lung fields as shown below.

Other radiological signs of Pulmonary embolism :

• Hampton’s hump - a peripheral wedged-shaped density usually located at the pleural base
• Palla’s sign - an enlarged right descending pulmonary artery
questions.learning: Focal oligemia Focal oligemia is not a radiological feature of left heart failure. It is seen in pulmonary embolism and is also called Westermark’s sign.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 61-year-old university professor presents with a loss of vision in his left eye. He describes the sensation as a curtain being drawn over his affected eye. In addition, 7 days ago the patient noticed what he described as flashing lights and floaters. He gives a history of having cataract surgery in the same eye 3 weeks ago. A B-scan image of his left eye is shown below. What could be his condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Retinal detachment

The given clinical scenario and the B-scan suggest a diagnosis of rhegmatogenous retinal detachment. It is due to the accumulation of fluid between neurosensory retina(NSR) and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) due to a retinal tear.

Definition of retinal detachment: The separation of the neurosensory retina from the RPE.

Types of Retinal detachment:

A. Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment- fluid accumulates after a break (tear) occurs in the retina.

* Causes:

* High myopes

* Retinoschisis-splitting of neurosensory retina plus vitreous degeneration

* Typical retinoschisis-split at the level of the outer plexiform layer

* Atypical retinoschisis-split at the level of the nerve fiber layer

* Trauma

* Pseudophakia

* Aphakia

* The most dangerous type of retinal break is horseshoe tear.

* The most dangerous location of retinal break is the supero-temporal retina.

* Clinical features

* Photopsia-flashes of light due to vitreoretinal traction at the site of the break

* Floaters

* Visual field defect- a black curtain/veil in front of the eye

* Signs

* Hypotony- as the liquefied vitreous in the subretinal space is absorbed through the RPE.

* Shafers sign-pigments in the anterior vitreous (tobacco dusting) are a feature of fresh retinal detachment.

* The detached retina is convex in configuration. The surface is corrugated with undulations.

* Treatment

* Prophylactic laser barrage

* Scleral buckling

* Pneumatic retinopexy

* Pars plana vitrectomy

B. Tractional retinal detachment: Fibro-vascular membranes in the vitreous due to long-standing retinal neovascularization exert traction on the retina.

* Causes

* Proliferative diabetic retinopathy

* Central retinal venous occlusion

* Eales disease

* Retinopathy of Prematurity(ROP)

* Signs

* The detached retina is concave in configuration. No breaks are seen

* Treatment

* Pars plana vitrectomy with endo photocoagulation.

C. Exudative retinal detachment: Exudative fluid from the choroid, collects in the subretinal space leading to retinal detachment.

* Causes

* Inflammatory conditions like choroiditis, posterior scleritis

* Choroidal tumours like melanoma

* Toxaemia of pregnancy

* Malignant hypertension

* Coats disease

* Clinical features

* Floaters due to vitritis but no photopsia

* Visual field defect

* Signs

* The detached retina is convex in configuration. The surface is smooth. No break is seen.

* Shifting fluid is seen.

* Treatment

* Systemic steroids

* Treatment of the cause

The image below shows a fundus which reveals retinal detachment inferiorly from 3-9 o'clock with a tear at 3:30
questions.learning: Retinal detachment — The given clinical scenario and the B-scan suggest a diagnosis of rhegmatogenous retinal detachment. It is due to the accumulation of fluid between neurosensory retina(NSR) and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) due to a retinal tear.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Tetralogy of Fallot is most commonly associated with which of the following:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Down syndrome

Tetralogy of Fallot is most commonly associated with Down syndrome among the given options.

Tetralogy of Fallot: It is the most common cyanotic congenital heart disease.

* The primary defect is an anterior deviation of the infundibular septum (the muscular septum that separates the aortic and pulmonary outflows).

* The primary defect gives rise to the 4 anatomical components of TOF which are:

* Ventricular septal defect (VSD) ( NOT ASD)

* Obstruction to right ventricular outflow - Pulmonic stenosis (PS)

* Right ventricular hypertrophy (RVH)

* Overriding (or dextroposition) of the aorta

* Obstruction to pulmonary arterial blood flow is usually at both the right ventricular infundibulum (subpulmonic area) and the pulmonary valve.

* The degree of pulmonary outflow obstruction determines the degree of the patient’s cyanosis and the age of first presentation.

The heart is typically enlarged and is classically “boot-shaped” due to marked right ventricular hypertrophy.
questions.learning: Down syndrome Tetralogy of Fallot is most commonly associated with Down syndrome among the given options. Tetralogy of Fallot: It is the most common cyanotic congenital heart disease. * The primary defect is an anterior deviation of the infundibular septum…

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman presents with gait instability, memory impairment, behavioral changes, and Kayser–Fleischer rings visible on ocular examination. Which option correctly identifies the gene mutation responsible for this condition and the chromosome on which it is located?
questions.explanation: The symptoms described—neurological deficits (unstable gait, memory loss, mood swings) and the pathognomonic "Kayser-Fleischer (KF) rings" in the cornea—are the hallmark findings of Wilson's disease. Wilson's disease is an autosomal recessive disorder of copper metabolism. The condition is caused by mutations in the "ATP7B gene," which encodes a copper-transporting ATPase essential for biliary copper excretion and the incorporation of copper into ceruloplasmin. This gene is located on "chromosome 13". Option B is incorrect because the ATP7A gene (located on the X chromosome) is associated with Menkes disease ("kinky hair" syndrome), which involves copper deficiency rather than overload. Options C and D are incorrect as they list the wrong chromosome. In Wilson's disease, copper accumulates in the liver and brain (specifically the basal ganglia). Early diagnosis is vital, as the disease is treatable with copper-chelating agents like penicillamine or zinc, which can prevent permanent neurological and hepatic damage
questions.learning: The symptoms described—neurological deficits (unstable gait, memory loss, mood swings) and the pathognomonic "Kayser-Fleischer (KF) rings" in the cornea—are the hallmark findings of Wilson's disease.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with fever, a generalized rash, and the formation of an eschar following a mite bite. Based on these clinical features, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Scrub typhus is a mite-borne infectious disease caused by the bacterium Orientia tsutsugamushi. The diagnostic hallmark, present in about 50% of cases, is the eschar—a small, dark, painless ulcer with a black crust that forms at the site of the mite (chigger) bite. The disease characteristically presents with high fever, headache, generalized lymphadenopathy, and a maculopapular rash. Cutaneous Anthrax (Option A) also features a black eschar but is transmitted by cattle contact and typically lacks the specific febrile/rash syndrome of scrub typhus. African tick typhus (Option C) and Rocky Mountain spotted fever (Option D) are transmitted by ticks, not mites. Scrub typhus is endemic in the "Tsutsugamushi triangle" of Southeast Asia and India. If untreated, it can lead to severe multi-organ complications including ARDS, meningitis, and acute renal failure. Doxycycline is the first-line antibiotic and is highly effective when started early. Clinical awareness of the eschar is essential for rapid diagnosis in endemic regions
questions.learning: Scrub typhus is a mite-borne infectious disease caused by the bacterium Orientia tsutsugamushi. The diagnostic hallmark, present in about 50% of cases, is the eschar—a small, dark, painless ulcer with a black crust that forms at the site of the mite…

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A professional singer develops difficulty in producing high-pitched notes after undergoing thyroid surgery. Her voice is not hoarse, but she is unable to raise the pitch effectively. Which nerve is most likely to have been injured?
options: External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (EBSLN)
Internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (IBSLN)
questions.explanation: The EBSLN innervates the cricothyroid muscle, which is responsible for tensing the vocal cords to produce high-pitched sounds. Injury to this nerve, often occurring during thyroid surgery within Joll's Triangle, results in an inability to raise voice pitch without causing hoarseness, as the vocal cord's ability to adduct remains intact. Professional voice users are highly sensitive to this change. The internal branch (Option B) is purely sensory and its injury leads to loss of sensation above the cords, not pitch changes. The recurrent laryngeal nerve (Option C) supplies the majority of intrinsic laryngeal muscles; damage here causes vocal cord palsy and prominent hoarseness. The glossopharyngeal nerve (Option D) is involved in oropharyngeal sensation and taste, having no role in vocal cord tension
questions.learning: The EBSLN innervates the cricothyroid muscle, which is responsible for tensing the vocal cords to produce high-pitched sounds. Injury to this nerve, often occurring during thyroid surgery within Joll's Triangle, results in an inability to raise voice pitch…

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Chronic liver disease is classified using the Child-Pugh score as follows: Class A: 5-6 , Class B: 7-9, Class C: 10-15. What type of data is this scoring system?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ordinal

The Child-Pugh score is an ordinal scale of data as:

There is a rank order (Class A having a better prognosis than classes B and C) but no regular interval between each class. The final division of prognosis is based on class and not the numerical values arrived at by the summation of a set of variables.

Other options:

Option A: The Child-Pugh score cannot be a nominal scale of data as there is a rank order with class A having better survival statistics than B or C. Nominal data do not have a rank order.

Option C: This is also not merely a qualitative scale as there are scores given to each variable to arrive at the final class.

Option D: The data used in the Child-Pugh score cannot be merely metric as the final division of prognosis is based on class and not the numerical values. Also, there is no definite interval between the classes.
questions.learning: Ordinal — The Child-Pugh score is an ordinal scale of data as: There is a rank order (Class A having a better prognosis than classes B and C) but no regular interval between each class.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A Post-operative immobile patient develops sudden onset severe calf pain. The best investigation to be done is?
questions.explanation: A immobile post-operative patient presenting with sudden calf pain and swelling is a classic scenario for Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT). The best (and first-line) investigation for confirming a suspected DVT is Duplex Ultrasonography. It is non-invasive, highly sensitive, and specific for identifying clots in the leg veins by visualizing the thrombus and demonstrating a lack of compressibility. CTPA (Option A) is the gold standard for pulmonary embolism, not for initial calf DVT diagnosis. X-ray (Option C) cannot visualize soft-tissue clots. While a D-dimer assay (Option D) is a useful screening tool, it is often elevated post-operatively regardless of a clot, making it non-specific and less useful in this specific surgical context. Early diagnosis and initiation of anticoagulation (e.g., LMWH) are essential to prevent the clot from propagating and causing a life-threatening pulmonary embolism. Immobile patients require active thromboprophylaxis with mechanical devices and pharmacological agents
questions.learning: A immobile post-operative patient presenting with sudden calf pain and swelling is a classic scenario for Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT). The best (and first-line) investigation for confirming a suspected DVT is Duplex Ultrasonography.
